title: Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes laying the lumber as blockers for Buffalo Bills
summary: Nowadays, if you’re writing about a Buffalo Bills tight end, it’s probably Dalton Kincaid. But this piece is dedicated to shedding light on the occasionally overlooked aspect of… blocking at the position. While Kincaid has improved in this area, his fellow tight end mates, Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes, have blocking savants through two contests. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Dawson Knox #88 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with his teammates after scoring a touchdown against the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nowadays, if you’re writing about a Buffalo Bills tight end, it’s probably Dalton Kincaid. But this piece is dedicated to shedding light on the occasionally overlooked aspect of… blocking at the position. While Kincaid has improved in this area, his fellow tight end mates, Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes, have blocking savants through two contests. James Cook has seven runs of 10-plus yards through two games. That’s tied for the third-most in football. Knox has been on the field for all of them. Let’s dive into the film to highlight the dirty work done exquisitely by both of now veteran blockers. Here’s the first 10-plus yarder of the season for Cook, a run not possible without two second-level blocks from Knox and Hawes: pic.twitter.com/G7xXbvFCTl — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 That’s a reach block from Hawes on Sheldon Rankins, who’s been one of the more unrated backfield disruptors in football for a while now. On Cook’s 12-yard scamper that ended with a fumble and an O’Cyrus Torrence recovery against the Texans — yes, that run — Hawes stood up and stayed engaged with Danielle Hunter at the point of attack at the line of scrimmage. pic.twitter.com/tBDuhmmKTl — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 No easy task there. Hunter is one of the most physical imposing edge rushers in the NFL. Against the Lions, when Cook had five 10-plus yard runs, the tandem was sensational. First, check this reach and hook from Knox on defensive end D.J. Woonum, in space, to clear a clean cutback lane for Cook to accelerate through the second level. pic.twitter.com/l6rBAde8ye — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 The combination of Hawes and Knox’s blocks were essentially done in perfect rhythm here, just how it’s drawn up, on this long Cook run later in the game. Hawes washed down linebacker Derrick Barnes while Knox ascended to the second level to get a hat on 2025 All-Pro Jack Campbell, one of the largest off-ball linebackers in the game. pic.twitter.com/wsCzrxqpw2 — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 As if the Hunter assignment wasn’t difficult enough, Hawes later took on Aidan Hutchinson crashing inside and handled himself admirably. The subsequent block as Cook started to knife through the line of scrimmage was another Knox stick of Campbell in the whole. pic.twitter.com/KySPe6Uif9 — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 Another sizable gain for Buffalo’s rushing attack. Watch that one again, the cutback lane for Cook was gorgeously paved on that play. Late against the Lions, watch as Hawes cut off Malcolm Rodriguez as the linebacker over pursued, but I urge you to pay attention the snatch-trap utilized by Knox on Hutchinson at the left side of the screen. It ultimately became precisely where Cook ran with the football. And he nearly scored. pic.twitter.com/RFE8f1XB2A — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 No, that’s not a flag on Knox. Hats off to the refereeing crew for not calling a penalty there. Hawes has been especially sturdy as a pass protector too. He’s been credited with zero pressures allowed on 10 pass-blocking snaps, reps that many of which have looked like this (watch him on the right side of the screen): pic.twitter.com/86TFsZExcV — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 Kincaid has been a receiving wizard through two games… and frankly, since the start of 2025. His yards-per-route-run figure is 4.69 through two games after leading all tight ends in YPRR at 2.70 last season. Knox has three catches for 12 yards entering Week 3. Hawes is still looking for his first catch of his second professional season. But we mustn’t forget about the serious value Knox and Hawes are adding to Buffalo’s offense as blockers. Because they’ve been sensational in the trenches, moving defensive lineman, clearing linebackers, and locking down the edges of Josh Allen’s pocket. No wonder t he Bills are second in the NFL in 13 personnel usage right now.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: DeWayne Carter making most of surprising opportunity for Buffalo Bills early in 2026
summary: All signs pointed to former third-round pick DeWayne Carter being cut after the preseason, and now he’s actually playing quality football as a rotational defensive tackle in Jim Leonhard’s scheme. And it took two rather rare occurrences for the former Duke captain to be afforded the opportunity he’s been given in these first two games. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: DeWayne Carter #90 of the Buffalo Bills runs onto the field prior to the NFL game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images All signs pointed to former third-round pick DeWayne Carter being cut after the preseason, and now he’s actually playing quality football as a rotational defensive tackle in Jim Leonhard’s scheme. And it took two rather rare occurrences for the former Duke captain to be afforded the opportunity he’s been given in these first two games. On one of the last defensive snaps of the preseason finale against the Pittsburgh Steelers, rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant suffered a neck injury that ultimately sent him to IR-designated to return. While I can’t be completely sure, it was the likely catalyst for Carter to make Buffalo’s 53-man roster once the three exhibition games concluded this August. The veteran had hardly made an impact in the preseason and was playing well into the fourth quarter in all three contests. When faced with situations like Carter vs. Durant, NFL clubs initially side with the rookie draft picks. But because of the severity of Durant’s injury, Buffalo may not have had much of a choice. And, sure, maybe the powers that be in Orchard Park believed Carter’s experience was more valuable than Durant’s upside. We’ll never know. I thought Carter was a goner. Instead, he was was on the field for 18 snaps against the Texans in Week 1. He only made one tackle, but it was a run stop. A “stop” is an advanced stat that constitutes a “loss” for the offense based on down and distance. He also registered one pressure on seven pass-rush snaps and did not miss any tackles. Then, before Week 2’s game against the Lions, Ed Oliver was a last-minute scratch after injuring his hip during warmups. Another coincidental domino fell, and following some inactive-list shuffling, Carter was set to play even more. He logged 31 snaps in Buffalo’s 10-point victory, made two tackles — one stop — and accumulated a pair of pressures on 20 pass-rush snaps. The beautiful spin move I couldn’t even correct my spelling #Billsmafia https://t.co/R63Er77iV5 pic.twitter.com/ZbRqLOpZ8F — Randall Slifer (@RandallSlifer) September 18, 2026 The sample size is tiny, but Carter’s pressure rate is 11.1%, and he’s nearly halfway to the amount of pressures he registered his entire rookie season (8) on 162 pass-rush snaps in 2024. For a defensive tackle, 10% is the pressure-rate threshold that separates the average from the outstanding. Sure — sample size. But because Carter has two stops on just 21 run-game snaps, he’s standing out amongst his defensive tackle contemporaries. And apparently he’s “winning” on more than half those reps. Bills defensive tackle DeWayne Carter ranks second among NFL DT in ESPN's run stop win rate metric. Carter credited with 11 wins in 21 snaps. — Lance Lysowski (@LLysowski) September 22, 2026 Carter underweight a body transformation during the offseason in hopes of being more capable of contributing on this new Bills defense as a bulkier nose tackle than the one-gap penetrating three-technique he was drafted to be during the Sean McDermott era. He was just under 6’3” and 305 pounds at the 2024 NFL Combine. This summer, Carter said he had gained 20-30 pounds before reporting to training camp at St. John Fisher University. After his Achilles tear that wiped away his entire second season in the NFL after a lackluster rookie campaign, I thought Carter was toast in Buffalo. And maybe he’ll never become a regularly disruptive force. I doubt he will. But the Bills need to take what they can get from him now. He’s appeared on 34% of the defensive snaps through two games and given the defense ample production as a rotational player. Sometimes it takes a multi-layered coincidence for a player to get serious playing time in the NFL. That’s very likely what happened to Carter, and he’s taken full advantage of his opportunity.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Joe Brady tapping into Josh Allen’s bazooka arm, long-ball tendency early in new Buffalo Bills offense
summary: Likely the most obvious observation about the Buffalo Bills offense through two games is how Joe Brady is allowing Josh Allen to play freely. It’s led to 36 points against the Texans in Houston and 41 at home against the Lions. Allen has been sensational, and his phenomenal skill set as been on full display […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills readies to hug quarterback Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills ahead of the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Likely the most obvious observation about the Buffalo Bills offense through two games is how Joe Brady is allowing Josh Allen to play freely. It’s led to 36 points against the Texans in Houston and 41 at home against the Lions. Allen has been sensational, and his phenomenal skill set as been on full display in each contest. Of course, Allen’s arm strength is probably his greatest attribute as a quarterback, and Brady is tapping into every last ounce of it. Through two games, Allen’s average depth of target is 10.5 yards, which is tied for third among all quarterbacks. And it’s the highest aDOT since his rookie season. Allen’s average depth of target was just 7.8 yards in 2025, the 11th-lowest out of 45 qualifying passers. The last time Allen’s aDOT eclipsed 9.0 yards for an entire season was 2022. How about this for another field-stretching metric — 16.7% of Allen’s attempts been have 20-plus air yards. That figure was 11.5% last regular season. On those 20-plus yard targets, he’s completed 5-of-10 deep throws for 198 yards and three touchdowns without an interception — and has forced two pass interference calls, both of which came on DJ Moore targets against the Texans. This isn’t all coaching. Allen is indeed part of this shift in philosophy. He’s ultimately the one making the more aggressive decisions on the field. Per Anthony Prohaska of Cover 1 , 47.1% of Allen’s throws have been made beyond the first down marker, which is the second-highest of his career. When Allen’s arm strength is being deployed at its full potential it makes Buffalo’s offense significantly harder to stop because secondaries are forced to defend much more field vertically compared to a dink-and-dunk attack. On a given play, a defense go from thinking run to a deep shot 20-plus yards downfield in a matter of seconds, which couldn’t be more difficult. And Brady is utilizing play action at a 47.1% clip through two games, the highest in the NFL. Allen’s pedal-to-the-floor aerial attack coupled with Buffalo’s ground game are the foundational elements of the Bills offensive eruption through two games.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills DT Deone Walker has leapt, not stepped, forward in 2026
summary: I am a believer in precise and specific communication. If it takes a few more words to reduce or eliminate the opportunity for a misunderstanding, we should take it. And part of that belief comes with a specific affinity for communication structure. And in communication structure, it’s very important to draw a distinction between “I […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Deone Walker #96 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with teammates after fumble during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images I am a believer in precise and specific communication. If it takes a few more words to reduce or eliminate the opportunity for a misunderstanding, we should take it. And part of that belief comes with a specific affinity for communication structure. And in communication structure, it’s very important to draw a distinction between “I was wrong” and “I’m sorry”. All correctly structured apologies contain a “I was wrong” segment, but not all “I was wrong” communications are an apology, just like all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. An apology contains three main pieces: Recognition of wrong of harm Reasoning Response Recognition is the “I was wrong” part of the apology. You note that not only were you were incorrect in a statement, thought, or action, but you also caused a moral wrong, injury, or insult or some sort through this statement, thought, or action. Reasoning isn’t an excuse as some would note, but instead a communication to the other party that you have been introspective and understand why you were incorrect and what led you to that incorrect conclusion. Response is a call to self-action; a specific behavior that you will or will not do differently in the future. So I don’t have to say I’m sorry for being wrong about Deone Walker (because I didn’t cause a moral wrong, injury, or insult), but I was wrong, so we should talk about it. For starters, let’s pull the exact wording of my reaction to the Deone Walker draft pick in 2025: I am not a huge Deone Walker guy, Especially relative to other players at his position that were available. It feels like he brought all of the negatives of massive size to his scouting report (conditioning, motor worries, playing upright) without the positives (great use of… — Bruce Nolan (@BruceExclusive) April 26, 2025 “I am not a huge Deone Walker guy. Especially relative to the other players at his position that were available. It feels like he brought all the negatives of massive size to his scouting report (conditioning, motor worries, playing upright) without the positives (great use of extension, leverage). Bills are likely hoping they can coach rare size traits, because they simply don’t make many humans like Walker. Rooting for the ceiling.” In his second year, Walker has become a high-level disruptor alongside veteran OLB Gregory Rousseau. The two have arguably been the best players on a Buffalo defense that has looked porous against the pass through two weeks. Walker had 13 pressures on 214 pass rush snaps in 2025, per NFL Pro. He has 7 pressures in 53 pass rush snaps in 2026. His 2026 pressure rate of 17.9% is over double his 2025 mark (8.0%). He has splash plays all over the tape. His impact has been notable and his presence has been felt. I never bought into the “he would have been a top 10 pick if not for the back injury” talk. I was well-aware of the back injury and specifically watched through the prior year tape, but my concerns remained. My comparison was to former Bills defensive tackle Jordan Phillips: a player capable of splash plays to help your team, but one who would balance those plays with enough negatives to make you hesitant to throw a bag at it (I once famously advocated for the Bills to not-resign Phillips on this site, an article that attracted a less-than-stellar reaction from the defensive tackle himself). I had a mid-day three grade on Walker (slightly behind where they took him) but, as noted above, liked other defensive tackles on the board more. But at the risk of being hyperbolic, Walker is trending much more towards being a heavier DeForest Buckner than Jordan Phillips at this point. So what did I get wrong? First off, Walker is playing with exceptional leverage when necessary. Gone is the phenomenon where if his upper body quickness doesn’t get him past an offensive lineman in the first 0.5 seconds of a rep, he’s lost for the remainder of the play pretty much as a rule. Walker is showing the ability to utilize his length as needed: against a second quarter screen pass in Houston, he was first to touch against Texans center Evan Brown, peeked in the backfield to spot running back Woody Marks leaking out to the offensive left, rode and controlled Brown with length and he maneuvered toward the pass placement, and then discarded the block and made the tackle for a -2 yard loss. Right before the first half two-minute warning against Detroit, Walker stacked up Lions left guard Juice Scruggs on a one-on-one on first and 10 before throwing Scruggs to the side and closing on Jared Goff, forcing an incomplete pass short left to wide receiver Jameson Williams. Maybe my favorite rep from Deone Walker this year. pic.twitter.com/9qmGbLHN5G — Bruce Nolan (@BruceExclusive) September 21, 2026 Nobody will or should ever confuse Walker’s playstyle as a “stack and shed” defensive lineman. He’s still primarily focused on utilizing his upper body quickness to win the rep fast and create havoc rather than displacement, but the fact that he shows the ability to win reps with proper use of one of his great gifts (length) is something beyond what I had predicted during scouting. It’s akin to a big wide receiver who has the knock of “doesn’t play big” suddenly starting to play big. Walker’s ability to win different ways (even if one of them occurs far less frequently than the other) is a massive contributor to his long-term outlook in the league because it let’s him keep the high-level reps he always had without bringing with him the lowlights. The second item that jumps off the film with Walker is his body composition and conditioning. Even prior to his back injury, Walker’s conditioning contributed to him playing higher and higher the longer the game went on, exacerbating the downsides of his height and leading to leverage issues. Coming into the 2026 season, Walker shed about 10 pounds and looks to be in excellent shape (see the Buckner comp above), leading to more energetic reps later in the game for a Bills defensive line that lacks depth and more ability to exert the bursts of strength necessary to pull off the plays like the two “stack and shed” examples listed above. Better conditioning and playing with better extension have allowed the best traits of Walker to shine while minimizing some of his biggest downsides from this college scouting report. Evaluation is distinct from projection when discussing NFL Draft prospects. Just because Walker didn’t do it with enough frequency for me to feel comfortable assigning a high grade to him prior to the draft, doesn’t mean he couldn’t do it at the NFL level. He had the tools, but being able to parse out players who have the tools and will use them differently in the NFL versus players who have the tools and will not use them differently in the NFL is a matter of evaluating coaching and the player on a football character level. If Walker continues on this trajectory, he’ll join Josh Allen on my personal “sure glad I missed on them” list of Bills draft picks over the last decade. I’m not sorry, but it sure looks like I was wrong. You absolutely love to see it. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!
author: Bruce Nolan

title: Buffalo Bills clean up penalties in Week 2 vs. Detroit Lions
summary: For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. In Week 1, the Buffalo Bills seemed like they received a flag on just about […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Detail view of the Highmark Stadium sign during an NFL game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. In Week 1, the Buffalo Bills seemed like they received a flag on just about every other play. They cleaned up things quite a bit this week against the Detroit Lions, but there were still some big goofs I bet they’d have rather had back. Let’s take a look. And oh yeah, there’s video of some of the flags this time seeing as I had my usual time. Extra time really. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts Last week the Buffalo Bills had ten flags that counted and 12 total. This week was five and six, so exactly half no matter how you slice it. It’s always nice when the graphs look like a staircase going up too. That means the Bills were below average and the opponent above. We’re starting off with some good signs. In a bit of a weird league twist this week, the count went down which is normal. However, the true count (includes offset and declined) went up. That means more flags were thrown than Week 1, but less were accepted. They’ll both go down over the season I’d wager, but it’s a fun twist for this week. Penalty Yards Here’s why we dive deeper than most places on flags. The Bills weren’t really too far off average here on assessed yards despite the low count. The Lions had an above average count and are almost perfect on the yards. Perhaps the gap between the two teams wasn’t that large? Making it even more complicated this week is the true yards, which add in yards negated due to penalty, looks more like what you’d originally expect. The Bills are still fine, but the Lions take a big leap up. Penalty harm Buffalo Bills Last week the Bills crossed the “bad day line” of 10.0 total Harm and landed at 13.2 in my proprietary assessment scale. How did they do with half the penalties? They had 10.7 total Harm this week. It’s an improvement but much slighter than the raw count would have suggested. I’m going to focus on three of the flags, but if you have questions on the other ones, pop into the comments and let me know. Let’s take a peek at the three. pic.twitter.com/c6r8gYiM5b — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 22, 2026 The Landon Jackson tripping call was late in the second half and as you can see pretty justified. The Lions were already in field goal range and didn’t have time to run another play. So while this did push Detroit 13 yards closer (half the distance to the goal) and gave up a free down for a total of 2.3 Harm, the free down was irrelevant in this situation and the thirteen yards probably doesn’t lead to a missed field goal try. This is a good time to point out that Harm is a starting point for dialogue and is not intended to be an absolute grading scale on how bad a penalty hurt the team. It just identifies which ones had the highest potential for a harmful impact. Let’s transition then to two flags that for sure did hurt the Bills. The Davison Igbinosun flag for defensive holding would appear to be five yards in most analysis. Here at Buffalo Rumblings though, we recognize that the fact it occurred on fourth down was a HUGE deal. That adds 3.0 Harm for the three downs it gave the Lions free of charge. From ended drive to first down. There’s a pretty clear penalty on this one too, so it’s hard to say this self-inflicted wound wasn’t earned. With the drive continuing, the Bills made a couple of good plays on defense and forced a 3rd & 7. Now, if Christian Benford isn’t called for defensive pass interference there’s a very good chance the Lions are going for it anyway. But 4th & 7 at the nine-yard line sounds like better odds than 1st & goal at the one. While the Igbinosun flag was the right call, I didn’t see anything in the film that changes how I felt watching from the stadium. That ball was uncatchable. Oh well, the Bills won but they made it harder for themselves, especially on the touchdown drive featuring the bailouts from Igbinosun and Benford. Detroit Lions The Lions though had an even worse day, with 16.7 Harm. Like with the Bills, I’ll focus on just a couple of these, but feel free to ask questions on any I leave out. For the formula lovers, the Tyler Lacy face mask call is a fun one. The flag itself was assessed as 15 yards or 1.5 Harm. It also gave up a down as it occurred on second, earning another 1.0 Harm. Finally, it negated a three yard tackle for loss for 0.3 Harm or 2.8 total. Larry Borom’s holding flag wiped out 19 yards by Jahmyr Gibbs in addition to the ten assessed yards. Luckily it was first down and didn’t cost the team anything there. Now for the flip side of above, it wasn’t just the Bills that insisted their opponent score on a particular drive, and you could say the Lions did it even worse. pic.twitter.com/qNYiWwGs5w — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 22, 2026 There are a few cardinal sins when it comes to flags, and one of the worst is negating a turnover. Roger McCreary did just that at the beginning of the second quarter when Buffalo was up 14 to zip. Negating a turnover is always assessed at 4.0 Harm, the number of downs/opportunities you cost your team. Even worse, McCreary’s flag came on third down. The automatic first down meant Buffalo got some free chances at a touchdown. At this point, the five yards assessed seems trivial but we count ‘em anyway. The Lions were now in quite the pickle. They were yet to have had any good answer for Buffalo’s offense and now they handed the Bills 1st & goal at the four-yard line. Not great. Then Jack Campbell was called for defensive holding. Half the distance to the goal put Buffalo at the two-yard line, but that’s not the biggest part of the story. Detroit had just sacked Josh Allen for seven yards. First down and two to go is a whole heck of a lot different than second down with eleven to go. Would the game’s outcome have been different without the Lions practically giving away points? Who knows really. As noted above, the Bills gifted the Lions in similar fashion. If we’re hypothesizing in one direction, it needs to go in the other which balances things out. For the short version of things though, both teams would have liked to have avoided a few flags.
author: Skarekrow

title: Greg Rousseau taking game to new heights early in 2026 season for Buffalo Bills
summary: Greg Rousseau is becoming a huge win for age-related draft analysis. Even after sitting out his second season at the University of Miami due to COVID, the Buffalo Bills selected Rousseau with one of the final picks in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft just a few weeks after his 21st birthday. He […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills looks on from the field during an NFL game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Greg Rousseau is becoming a huge win for age-related draft analysis. Even after sitting out his second season at the University of Miami due to COVID, the Buffalo Bills selected Rousseau with one of the final picks in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft just a few weeks after his 21st birthday. He was one of the youngest players in that draft, and surprisingly was able to shoulder a full-time workload as a rookie at defensive end. Since then, he’s been a steady yet mostly unspectacular edge rusher in Buffalo. His regular-season pressure rate has hovered between 14.0% and 14.9%. Quite impressive, really. That is until the first two games of 2026 within Jim Leonhard’s scheme. Rousseau’s pressure rate is a massive 23.1% entering Week 3, and he already has four sacks on the year, matching his rookie-year total and just one shy of the five he accumulated as a 23-year-old in 2023. Just 26 years old, Rousseau has probably just entered the the prime of his career, and he’s already played 3,507 snaps — counting playoffs — in his NFL career. Along the way, he’s learned a variety of ways to collapse the pocket, work around tackles, and track the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage. Like on his first sack of the season, a strip-sack of C.J. Stroud in the first quarter of opening weekend against the Texans, watch how he swiped away the chipping tight end, then worked back to the inside as he felt the quarterback stepping into the pocket. pic.twitter.com/AKyqtmiHjX — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 Textbook. The clean, around-the-corner wins are flashy. The big-time sack producers understand how to follow the quarterback as he glides around in the pocket. The game-sealing sack late in the fourth quarter was a tremendous display of his maturity rushing the quarterback. Against the impossibly large and lengthy Trent Brown, Rousseau used an inside-arm stab before climbing around Brown’s outside shoulder before getting his right arm on the football as Stroud unsuccessfully attempted to evade the rush again. pic.twitter.com/CGbgryC1jX — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 That play was a fine example of why length matters along the defensive line. Not only to establish first contact at the point of attack… but to have the reach to get your hands on the football once you enter the pocket. Right when Rousseau has the offensive tackles thinking he’s a lanky-ish, finesse rusher… he can deploy a nasty straight-arm bull rush, like he did hear against the typically serviceable swing tackle Larry Borom. pic.twitter.com/Jo85WftYOA — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 His second sack against the Lions was the byproduct of bad offensive schematics from the Lions — as Rousseau was left with a tight end on him in pass pro. Obviously, Rousseau quickly worked through the tight end and forced another fumble on a sack. pic.twitter.com/LgzghItwoD — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 Referencing yesterday’s article on Buffalo’s pass rush converting pressures to sacks at a much higher clip than at any stage of the Sean McDermott era, Rousseau is a key aspect of that. Rousseau entered this season with a career 14.6% pressure-to-sack rate himself, and only in 2023 was that single-season rate higher than 15% — it was 21.4%. Thus far in the 2026 campaign, Rousseau has four sacks on 16 pressures, good for a 25% pressure-to-sack rate in Leonhard’s new scheme. And check where he is in the Pass-Rush Win Rates as compiled by PFF and SumerSports. By year No. 6 in the NFL, we almost always know precisely who a player is. But at his age, Rousseau has ample experience and really is entering the peak physical timeframe of his professional career. And, this season, he looks well on his way to realizing all the upside that was a key element of his draft profile all the way back in 2021.

title: Panthers vs Falcons Game Review: What do we know
summary: There are now three things that I am certain of in this world: death, taxes, and the Carolina Panthers using the Atlanta Falcons for a ‘get right’ game. I don’t know why, but quite frankly I don’t care to overthink it. Whether it’s Sunday’s 34-3 blowout or 2025’s franchise record breaking performance from Bryce Young, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jaelan Phillips #5 of the Carolina Panthers sacks Jack Strand #18 of the Atlanta Falcons during the third quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Butch Dill/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are now three things that I am certain of in this world: death, taxes, and the Carolina Panthers using the Atlanta Falcons for a ‘get right’ game. I don’t know why, but quite frankly I don’t care to overthink it. Whether it’s Sunday’s 34-3 blowout or 2025’s franchise record breaking performance from Bryce Young , nothing heals the Panthers wounds like a trip to Mercedes Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. With that said, what if I told you that there’s an argument to be made that the team’s performance between Week 1’s barn burner versus the Chicago Bears and this most recent blowout of the Falcons weren’t all that different? I imagine the general reaction would range from a dismissive scoff to some choice not-safe-for-work words. Fair enough, because that’s an insane assertion for me to make and wrong on many levels. I’m going to do it anyway, though. Welcome to this week’s game review where I try to tell you how the Panthers performance against the Falcons was not actually that much better than the game that preceded using some definitely-not-cherry-picked stats. Let’s get into it. Statistic vs. CHI @ ATL Penalties on CAR offense 7-49 9-63 3rd down conversions 4-9 (44%) 6-14 (43%) Red zone TD 5-5 (100%) 3-7 (43%) Pressure rate allowed 11.6% 15.4% EPA / play 0.18 0.14 So, the Panthers offense in Week 2 were called for more penalties, slightly less efficient on 3rd down, significantly less efficient in the red zone, allowed more pressure on the quarterback and were overall efficient as an offense according to their EPA per play. Let me be clear, I am not saying the Panthers offense performed poorly. Far from it, as averaging an 0.14 EPA/Play for a season would have been good for the best offense in the NFL in 2025. As far as week-to-week comparisons go, though, the Offense was better against the Bears. Statistic vs. CHI @ ATL RB Production 28-224 (8.0 ypc) 27 – 123 (4.5 ypc) RB Production minus K. Monangai 61 yd rush 27-163 (6 ypc) 27 – 123 (4.5 ypc) NFL NGS Average receiver separation 3.14 yards 2.7 yards Completion % over expected 11.4% -14.5% Opposing QB turnover worthy plays 1 4 Listen, we’re talking about a difference of 56 points scored here so the numbers were going to be significantly improved against Atlanta. Just hear me out as I am going somewhere with this. If you take out the outlier 61 yard rush by Kyle Monangai, the Bears and Falcons had the exact same number of runs against the Panthers (27). While the Bears running backs ran for an insane 6 yards per carry, the Falcons’ backs ran for a still strong 4.5 yards per carry. This suggests that while improved, the overall rushing defense was still below average against the Falcons. However, the difference of performance between the two quarterbacks the Panthers have faced is where the crux of my argument lays. The Bears receivers had an above average amount of yards of separation. Generally, the more separation your receivers have, the more likely a quarterback is to complete a pass, and vice versa. The more likely a quarterback is to complete a pass, the higher their expected completion percentage will be. The inverse of this is also true – less receiver separation, the less likely a quarterback is to complete pass. Consider now that Caleb Williams was managing to complete 11.4% more of his attempts than expected while the Falcons gruesome twosome at quarterback completed 14.5 overall less of their attempts. This is not even accounting for the fact that Williams’ average intended air yards was literally 8 yards farther than Jack Strand. In other words, Williams made the hard plays look easy and the Falcons quarterbacks made the easy plays look hard – hard enough to sink their entire offense with poorly placed footballs and 5 turnovers. This is, of course, a fairly simplified view that does lack a some nuance. Those of you who are optimists (as I like to think I am) may believe that it takes a talented improvisor like Williams who can run 20 mph and turn off-script plays into big gains to dismantle the defense. The pessimist amongst you will wonder what may have happened if the Falcons had deployed even average quarterback play. The question I ask is did the Panthers play that much better this week, or did the Falcons just play that much worse than the Bears did in Week 1? I’d love to hear where you stand in the comments below. That’s all I have for you this week! So far the Panthers have faced against elite quarterback play and then the best efforts of Cooper Rush and Jack Strand. Who is to say what they get against the Cleveland Browns next week, though. Until then, keep pounding.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Colin Simmons
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: AUSTIN, TX - SEPTEMBER 05: Defensive end Colin Simmons #1 of the Texas Longhorns rushes around offensive lineman William Boone #71 of the Texas State Bobcats during the college football game the Texas Longhorns and the Texas State Bobcats on September 5, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Texas Longhorns edge defender Colin Simmons. Bio Simmons (6’3”, 240 lbs.) came into college as one of the best pass rushing prospects in the country. He led his high school to back-to-back state championships, winning Defensive MVP of the game both times. In his freshman year at Texas, Simmons posted nine sacks and 14 tackles for loss in 16 games for the Longhorns, earning him National Freshman of the Year, Freshman All America, and SEC All-Freshman honors. Heading into the following season, Simmons was named to the preseason All-SEC first team and preseason All-American first team. He improved in his sophomore season, notching 12 sacks and 15.5 tackles for loss in just 13 games, indeed being named to the All-SEC first team and to the All-American second team. The true junior has started hot for the Longhorns this year as well, already being credited with 3.5 tackles for loss and two sacks in three games so far. He is on the watchlist for many awards, including the Lott, Bronko Nagurski, Weurfful, Lombardi, Walter Camp, and Chuck Bednarik trophies. Strengths/Weaknesses Simmons is considered the consensus best pass rusher in the 2027 class (assuming he doesn’t return to school). He has an insane first step and converts that elite short area speed into power, bending around tackles with loose hips and ankles. He also has a knack for turnovers, forcing six fumbles and grabbing one interception across his first two college seasons. While not the biggest or strongest, Simmons is able to set a solid edge against the run and has the motor to chase down cutbacks and backside runs. Simmons’s size is a question mark for some NFL scouts. At just 240 lbs., stronger offensive lineman can push him around when they get their hands on him. He also has a couple discipline and technique issues to address, namely missed tackles and committing penalties. Projection Simmons will likely be the top edge defender taken in the 2027 NFL Draft baric anything drastic happening between now and April. His pass rush prowess and playmaking ability definitively outweigh some of the lack of discipline and weight questions. Simmons has the three down ability that modern NFL teams need and will likely be a day one starter. If he continues on his current trajectory, he could easily be a double digit sack player while being an above average edge setter at the next level. His abilities make him scheme versatile as a plug and play edge, so the Panthers should do their due diligence regardless of the defensive scheme and coaching staff. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Colin Simmons is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Bears-Vikings Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears Fans!  Well, this is a much sadder second installment in our series than I initially thought it would be after the game on Sunday. So welcome back to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag: the referees.  Let’s briefly review the project:  Upon Further Review exists to answer […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears Fans! Well, this is a much sadder second installment in our series than I initially thought it would be after the game on Sunday. So welcome back to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag: the referees. Let’s briefly review the project: Upon Further Review exists to answer the questions about the calls on the field with film, the rulebook, and a consistent grading scale: Each week I isolate the flags and no-calls that went against Chicago and against the opponent, grade every one as Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, or Horrible, then roll those grades into four numbers: a Calls-Against-Bears rating, a Calls-Against-Opponent rating, an overall referee performance score, and a differential that shows which sideline got the better of the crew. I also pull the most controversial calls from around the league so we can see what call this week has NFL fans screaming, “wait, what?” and NFL rules analysts assuring us, “always has been.” Week 1 was a 59-point win and a pile of flags that mostly evened out. Week 2 is the first loss of the series, and it was a 9–3 slop-fest in the rain that Chicago donated on offense — then didn’t get back from Land Clark’s crew when it mattered. This week the accepted tape is mostly self-inflicted: Bradbury, Roush, grounding, a drive that started at the Minnesota 30 and ended in a punt. The Bears Tax, however, reared its ugly head in this game, and I have all of the gory details. Three no-calls in the fourth quarter, including forcible head/neck contact and a lift-and-slam on Tyson Bagent on the last two snaps from the 12, with the backup now in concussion protocol. The Vikings earned their 9–3 victory with some stellar plays in the downpour that killed near-certain Bears scoring opportunities. But that doesn’t mean the stripped ones didn’t play their own role in the Bears’ defeat. Below is every accepted flag, in order, with the player when named, the yardage, the game clock, and the score when the penalty was enforced. First Quarter MIN 3, CHI 0 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding / Levi Rodriguez (MIN), roughing the passer — offsetting — 7:42. Chicago has reached 1st-and-10 at the MIN 35 after converting 3rd-and-1. Williams throws incomplete short right; Rodriguez is in on the play. Both flags come out. Down is replayed. Not in the official 8–58 / 3–25. Braxton Jones (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 7:00. 2nd-and-7 at the MIN 32. Monangai runs left tackle for 8 yards to the 24. Jones is flagged on the edge. Play comes off the board: 2nd-and-17 at the MIN 42. Williams dumps to Monangai for 4, then scrambles 6 on 3rd-and-13 to the 32. Santos still makes the 50-yarder at 5:03. MIN 3, CHI 3 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 2:57. After Wentz’s aborted snap turns 3rd-and-2 into 4th-and-24 and Thorson punts, Raymond fair-catches at the CHI 42. First play of the drive: Bradbury flinches. 1st-and-15 at the 37. Anthony Van Ginkel (MIN), defensive offside, 5 yards — 1:53. 3rd-and-12 at the CHI 40. Williams goes deep left to Odunze, incomplete, but Van Ginkel is in the neutral zone. Replay the down: 3rd-and-7 at the CHI 45. Chicago (team), delay of game, 5 yards — 1:47. Six seconds after the offside gift, the play clock expires in shotgun. 3rd-and-12 at the 40 again. Williams throws deep middle for Burden. Byron Murphy intercepts at the MIN 36. Second Quarter MIN 3, CHI 3 Jaylon Johnson (CHI), illegal use of hands — declined — 13:15. 3rd-and-4 at the MIN 42. Wentz hits Jefferson over the middle for 16 yards to the CHI 42. Johnson’s flag is picked up. Catch and first down stand. Minnesota will kick Reichard’s 49-yarder at 8:18. MIN 6, CHI 3 Dallas Turner (MIN), roughing the passer, 15 yards — 6:18. Chicago is answering. 2nd-and-10 at the CHI 40. Williams completes short right to Raymond for 5, to the 45. Turner hits Williams after the throw. Automatic first: 1st-and-10 at the MIN 40. Swift loses 2. Chicago later converts 4th-and-3 to the MIN 30 — then the next four flags live on this same drive. Sam Roush (CHI), illegal shift, 5 yards — 3:02. 1st-and-10 at the MIN 30, already in field-goal range. Williams hits Loveland for 14 yards to the 16. Roush is flagged for an illegal shift. Replay first down: 1st-and-15 at the MIN 35. Loveland’s catch does not count. Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 2:35. 1st-and-15 at the MIN 35. Swift right guard for 3, to the 32. Bradbury holds. Enforced from the tackle: 1st-and-22 at the MIN 42. Caleb Williams (CHI), intentional grounding, 13 yards — 2:13. Shotgun, 1st-and-22 at the MIN 42. Wilson’s pressure. Williams throws it into the dirt short right with no eligible in the area. Loss of down: 2nd-and-35 at the CHI 45. Two-minute warning next. Garrett Bradbury (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 2:00. After an 11-yard screen to Swift makes it 3rd-and-24 at the MIN 44, Bradbury false-starts in shotgun. 3rd-and-29 at the MIN 49. Incompletion to Kmet. Taylor punts 37 yards. Four accepted flags, 33 yards, MIN 30 to a punt from midfield. Third Quarter MIN 6, CHI 3 No accepted flags. Christian Darrisaw (MIN), illegal formation — declined — 6:49. 3rd-and-2 at the MIN 32. Wentz is sacked. Formation flag is picked up. Minnesota punts. Chicago (team), illegal formation — declined — 4:20. 3rd-and-10 at the CHI 27. Raymond catch for 7. Flag is declined. Chicago punts. Fourth Quarter MIN 6, CHI 3 Josh Oliver (MIN), false start, 5 yards — 14:43. Minnesota 2nd-and-10 at its own 12. Oliver jumps. 2nd-and-15 at the MIN 7. They still get enough to punt from the 21. Raymond starts Chicago at the 33 — the drive that will reach the 1 (Swift fumble) and the 5 (Rodgers block). Tyrique Stevenson (CHI), defensive holding, 5 yards — 4:05. 1st-and-10 at the MIN 32. Wentz throws deep right for Jefferson, incomplete. Stevenson is holding. Automatic first: 1st-and-10 at the MIN 37. Hockenson then picks up 19 to the CHI 44. Chicago burns timeouts. Reichard’s 39-yarder at 1:09 makes it 9–3. MIN 9, CHI 3 No accepted flags on the final Bears drive. The two RTP no-calls on Bagent (3rd-and-2 head/neck; 4th-and-2 Turner lift-and-slam) belong in the no-call column, which we will get to forthwith. Upon Further Review — Week 2: Bears 3, Vikings 9 Crew: Land Clark . Official totals: Chicago 8 penalties, 58 yards . Minnesota 3 penalties, 25 yards . The scale. Every accepted flag — and every no-call we put on the ledger — gets one of four grades: Correct — the rule and the tape agree. Arguable — judgment call; you can see both sides. Incorrect — the tape says the crew got it wrong. Horrible — bright-line foul (or non-foul) a wing official should not miss. The weight. Impact, 1 to 4, stacked on the grade: 1 — housekeeping (false start that doesn’t kill a scoring chance). 2 — drive disruption (down-and-distance flip, stalled series). 3 — scoring situation / red-zone / automatic first that feeds points. 4 — wiped score or takeaway, dead drive flipped into points, or a last-snap foul that would have been 1st-and-goal. Snapshot: Flags For and Against Welp, here we are, analyzing the flags that, at least arguably, cost us the game. title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Whiplash
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: So I may have gotten a little bit ahead of myself tracking the Bears to eclipse the single season scoring record set by the Denver Broncos at […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson looks on in the rain before a game against the Minnesota Vikings at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Matt Marton-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: So I may have gotten a little bit ahead of myself tracking the Bears to eclipse the single season scoring record set by the Denver Broncos at 606 points. Ben Johnson’s stated goal and the 59 point showing in Week 1 got me dreaming big. Now, with the Caleb Williams injury and the terrible Week 2 showing, I’m feeling whiplash. A lot has been said about the Caleb Williams injury and I’ll just say, I was thinking we were dealing with an Achilles tear and how the rest of the season was essentially over. Incredible news that Caleb is looking at a condensed rehab and will hopefully be back on the field by the Green Bay game in Week 5. Garrett Bradbury might have had the worst day of anyone on Sunday. I know Ben Johnson wants that veteran presence at center, but Logan Jones has the hairline of someone who has refinanced his mortgage – I think he can step in and do the job. To give Bradbury some benefit of the doubt here, the wet conditions seemed to really mess with his game – extra concentration to complete the snap combined with bad footing put him in conflict all day. The autumnal equinox has come and gone, and we are officially in the fall season. I have failed to complete my summer checklist for the umpteenth year in a row, but this year was particularly bad with the heat and humidity. Good riddance. I’ve been impressed with the rookie defensive backs thus far. Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad have both played well in their first NFL action. Maybe not a surprise for Thieneman, the first rounder, but Muhammad stepping in early has been a pleasant surprise. This secondary will be tested with this schedule so it’s nice to see early returns on the rookies. Speaking of rookies, the second Ben Johnson draft class has had mixed results with Sam Roush’s poor Week 2 performance and Zavion Thomas’s lack of snaps. But that’s what September football is all about – figuring out what you have and what you don’t. Remember, Luther Burden was brought along slowly last year before catching fire late in the season. Give these guys a chance. I drafted Colston Loveland in the third round of the redraft fantasy football league I’ve been in forever. Let’s just say that the early returns aren’t great on that investment. It sure felt like the Bears paid some additional penalty tax in that game against the Vikings, particularly that late hit out of bounds on the punt return that didn’t draw a flag. I’ve never seen anything more obvious that didn’t draw a flag in my life. And then the guy flopped and it looked like he might’ve drawn a flag against the Bears before the refs picked it up. That would have been an insane double taxation moment had they marched off 15 against the Bears on a clear Vikings penalty, so I guess we should be thankful for that… After rewatching the game, I came away with the thought that I’d seen that game before, but in reverse, many times. How many times have the Bears played on a sloppy field that reduced the game to a messy field position game, getting the defensive plays when needed, and pulling out an ugly victory? Seems like a million. Bears fans got a taste of their own medicine as the Bears did have two drives that looked like TDs that came away with zero points. The first ended with a Swift fumble at the goal line. The second was disrupted with the injury to Williams where he had the angle for a score before eventually getting a 23-yard field goal blocked. Ridiculous odds of those two things happening in the same game. Bad luck, hopefully that’s the end of that. As the Bears shape their new identity under Ben Johnson, does it challenge anyone to think that maybe they would be better off playing in a dome where weather won’t slow down their high-flying offense? Detroit put up those great offenses under Johnson in part because they were never slowed by a bad weather game. Just a thought. It doesn’t matter because the Bears are never going to actually build a new stadium. They’re just going to keep torturing fans with new updates every few weeks that lead to more annoying questions from everyone you run into on the streets and over the the holidays with family. I thought Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson bounced back after their rough Week 1 performances. I also think both defenses benefitted from the wet conditions. It’ll be a real test on Monday to see if these two can be a viable tandem this year. Pete Crow Armstrong is going to win the NL MVP this year with an incredible season for the Cubs. The last time the Cubs had an MVP was Kris Bryant in 2016. The Bears haven’t had an MVP since Walter Payton in 1977. In fact, they’ve only had 3 players in their 100+ year history to win the award – Harlon Hill in 1955 won one of the league MVP awards, and Sid Luckman took the honors in 1943. The Cubs have had 5 since Payton won his (Ryne Sandberg, Andre Dawson, Sammy Sosa, Bryant, PCA), and we’re not exactly talking about the most successful baseball team here. I need to see a Bears MVP season in my lifetime. I dug into the history of the Chicago Bears scoring 50 or more points in the regular season and was shocked (well, it’s the Bears so not that shocked) that they’ve only done it 14 times in their history. And they’ve never done it more than once in a single season. I have a feeling that we’ll soon be talking about number of times Ben Johnson’s Bears have scored 50 versus the rest of Bears history. My money is on Ben to eventually win that one.

title: Chicago Bears week 3 power rankings roundup
summary: It’s easy to predict the fall when the rise is so rapid, so fast and the follow up is such a face plant. Now we’re getting the “maybe Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson isn’t good” takes flying. Every week, someone is in the comments saying power rankings don’t matter. I’m here to tell you, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyrique Stevenson Sr. #29 of the Chicago Bears reacts against the Minnesota Vikings during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s easy to predict the fall when the rise is so rapid, so fast and the follow up is such a face plant. Now we’re getting the “maybe Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson isn’t good ” takes flying. Every week, someone is in the comments saying power rankings don’t matter. I’m here to tell you, hot takes following one game don’t matter. Ignore the noise. The fact is, even with the Minnesota Vikings blitzing around 80 percent of the Bears’ offensive snaps, Chicago was the only team at Solider Field to run multiple plays in the red zone. The Bears were the only team with multiple goal-to-go plays run. Those sequences ended with zero points, due to turnovers or execution, not coaching. With that rant out of the way, let’s look at this week’s power rankings. WCG – Aaron Leming 13. Chicago Bears (1-1) Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBA (Pending Caleb Williams’ health) Early reports are that Williams avoided a serious injury, and although he might miss a few weeks, the team hasn’t ruled him out for Week 3’s Monday night matchup against the Eagles. Assuming backup quarterback Tyson Bagent can keep them above water, this should be a Wild Card contender at worst. Staying “alive” over the next two games will be key, and it starts with the Eagles on Monday night at Soldier Field. Profootballtalk – Mike Florio Bears (No. 3; 1-1): Don’t sleep on West Virginia native Tyson Bagent. Obviously written before the news . Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 14. Chicago Bears (1-1, LW: 10) The fear over Caleb Williams’ injury has subsided since it seems like a fairly minor hamstring injury, and yes his extremely distressed reaction to a hamstring strain was odd. At least it wasn’t a major injury. What needs to be addressed is how the Bears’ offense was inept just one week after putting up 59 points at Carolina. The Bears scored three points against Minnesota and that was with Williams playing three-and-a-half quarters. It would have been better had it not been for a D’Andre Swift fumble at the 1-yard line and a blocked field goal. The rainy weather was certainly an issue, but it’s not like the Bears won’t be playing more bad weather games. They’re still having trouble getting Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland (14 combined catches in two games) involved. One bad game doesn’t mean the Bears are in trouble on offense, but one great game might not make them the highest scoring offense in NFL history either. “The weather was a major factor in this game,” Bears head coach Ben Johnson said, according to the team’s site. “It was the big story of this game. Both defensive coordinators did a great job making it very challenging for the opposing offense. I thought that was the tale of the tape.” CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 12. Chicago Bears (9) The offense really struggled against Minnesota and now it will be without Caleb Williams for some time. They have problems. NFL.com – Nick Shook 16. Chicago Bears (8) The NFL’s highest-scoring offense in Week 1 finished with just three points in Sunday’s rain-soaked loss to the Vikings. The Bears’ Week 2 experience was a nightmare that became even worse when they lost Caleb Williams to a hamstring injury. It sounds like the star quarterback avoided total disaster, but as we saw in the final minutes of Sunday’s game, if Caleb isn’t available or is physically limited, the Bears’ ceiling plunges. ESPN – Courtney Cronin 11. Chicago Bears (1-1) Week 2 result: Lost to the Vikings 9-3 Week 2 ranking: 7 One thing we know about the QB1: Caleb Williams’ hamstring injury isn’t serious. The Bears dodged a major bullet with the right hamstring injury Williams sustained late against the Vikings. Coach Ben Johnson labeled Williams as week-to-week, and while the QB is expected to miss some time, Johnson is confident that backup Tyson Bagent can operate the offense. It understandably won’t look the same as when Williams is under center, but the scheme will not change. Chicago gave Bagent a two-year, $10 million extension in 2025, and his experience with Johnson in preseason games is why the coach believes “we’ll be fine.” USAToday – Nate Davis 13. Chicago Bears (4): Seems like the real ‘Madden’ curse here is that the Bears may have to wait at least another year for their first 4,000-yard passer.

Richardson, WR Stephen Carlson, TE Qadir Ismail, TE Miller Moss, QB Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Keidron Smith, S Deantre Prince, CB Marcus Davenport, DE Nick McCloud, CB Practice squad injured: Anthony Johnson Jr. (S) Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: Chicago Bears Hot Take Tuesday: Shut Up, Losers
summary: As Chicago Bears fans, we have seen the crazy amount of attention (largely negative) that our quarterback, Caleb Williams, receives. full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears is carted off the field after an injury against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images As Chicago Bears fans, we have seen the crazy amount of attention (largely negative) that our quarterback, Caleb Williams, receives. We mostly take it in stride because we know how ridiculous most (all?) of the comments are and how they simply are not grounded in reality. We all know what happens on Sunday. Caleb Williams goes down on a non-contact injury; he yells out in pain or frustration (or both) and is helped to the sidelines before he is taken on a cart to the locker room. The losers and frauds just couldn’t wait to jump all over this one. We have former NFL player Emmanuel Acho (who can’t get hired by a network) desperately looking for attention on social media, screaming out that you can’t take the cart because carts are only for career-ending injuries. You have Will Compton, who had two seasons in the league when he wasn’t at the bottom of the roster, who literally tweets this: People forget I played through a Grade 2+ hamstring at the bottom of my ass, and picked off Kirk Cousins and RG3 at practice in 2013 — Will Compton (@_willcompton) September 21, 2026 Hopefully he’s kidding, but this was on the heels of him ripping Caleb Williams for yelling about a hamstring injury so who the hell knows? You have the clowns at Barstool, led by Dave Portnoy, insinuating that Caleb Williams is some sort of soft, girly man (who might be gay). You have clowns like Peter Bukowski piling on. Here’s a quick message to all of you (and all the anonymous posters on social media too cowardly to put their actual name next to a post): Shut up, Losers. Shut. Up. Losers. Seriously, enough with your toxic masculinity BS. All of you saw that Caleb Williams had painted nails at USC in 2023, and you made up your mind about him. You decided he was a diva. You decided he was too weird for the NFL. You decided that only a gay person would paint his nails. You embraced your homophobia, and you’ve let it run rampant for years. Now you can go away. Nobody needs to hear from you. There’s a reason that Acho can’t keep a job. Nobody wants to be associated with his takes. That’s why all he has is an independent YouTube show. I feel bad for his brother Sam, who was one of the classiest people who has ever walked through Halas Hall, and his brother is soiling his name. Former players like Compton deciding how a player should react after an injury is just sad, attention-seeking behavior. It’s embarrassing for them. Sadly, they are too dense to realize it is. Suddenly, one of the most sacked QBs ever in 2024, who didn’t miss a snap, by the way, isn’t tough enough for you? This cart take is hilariously stupid. Anyone want to tell Dave Portnoy about the time Rob Gronkowski injured his knee, was taken off on a cart, only to miss one game. ONE GAME! Gronk is clearly a girly man. He’s not tough at all. Sorry to bring up a bad memory, but does anyone want to remind Bukowski about the time that Aaron Rodgers got knocked out in the first half by the Chicago Bears in 2018, was taken off on a cart, and he returned to the game and brought the Packers back to a victory? Jaxson Dart was carted off the field and stood on the sidelines the entire second half in this past game on Monday Night Football. I know he’s going to be out a few weeks, but was his use of the cart acceptable? Is the cart only for career-ending injuries and broken limbs? How about you say more dumb things that show you only played 20 games in the league and clearly know nothing about it? These people are desperate to find their confirmation bias. It’s pretty pathetic. Some of them have tried to walk it back. Some of them have doubled down. All of them are fools. I remember a man who was in the public eye. This man painted his nails. This man dyed his hair. This man wore women’s clothing. This man hinted that he might be bisexual. This man regularly went to gay clubs, drag queen shows, and embraced the entire LGBTQ+ community. He was an athlete. He was a prominent athlete. He was considered the ultimate badass. His name was Dennis Rodman. These same toxic jerks that want to crush Caleb for having a pink phone cover, painting his nails, or not handling the injury the “right way” are the same ones that thought Rodman was just being Rodman and was fun and awesome. It’s an embarrassing double standard. And the keyboard warriors on social media, probably the same ones that think children are using kitty litter in school bathrooms, are questioning Caleb Williams’ toughness. The same 30- or 40-something that turn into a 5-year-old child when they get the sniffles and call their Mommy to come over and bring them soup. All of them just expose themselves for who they are. All of this has been an incredibly stupid topic driven by incredibly stupid people. In closing, Jarrett Payton said it best, “Get my quarterback’s name out of your damn mouth.” Well said.

title: Bears sign long snapper Scott Daly off Saints’ practice squad
summary: The Chicago Bears have signed veteran long snapper Scott Daly from the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad, Brad Biggs of the Chicago Tribune reported on Tuesday. By signing Daly onto their 53-man roster, the Bears have effectively signaled they’ll be moving on from current long snapper Beau Gardner, whom the team signed as an undrafted […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 15: Scott Daly #46 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Houston Texans during a football game at NRG Stadium on September 15, 2024 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have signed veteran long snapper Scott Daly from the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad, Brad Biggs of the Chicago Tribune reported on Tuesday. By signing Daly onto their 53-man roster, the Bears have effectively signaled they’ll be moving on from current long snapper Beau Gardner, whom the team signed as an undrafted rookie this offseason. UPDATE: It’s now official; the Bears have signed Daly to the active roster, waived Gardner, and also signed corner Nick McCloud to the practice squad while releasing offensive lineman Kyle Hergel. Bears fans will certainly remember Daly, as he was the team’s long snapper in both 2024 and 2025. He was initially brought in to replace the injured Patrick Scales, and the decision was eventually made for him to remain the team’s long snapper in 2025. Though the Bears didn’t extend him this offseason, it appears they’ve decided to go back to the stability that Daly provided. Daly, a 32-year-old Downers Grove native, served as the Saints’ starting long snapper in Week 2 after incumbent starter Zach Wood suffered a calf strain. He’s been on three teams in 2026 alone, spending the offseason with the Buccaneers, serving a two-week stint on the Packers’ practice squad, and spending just a few days with New Orleans. The Saints signed him to their practice squad on Sept. 18. This doesn’t come as much of a surprise that the Bears would make a move at long snapper, as Gardner has been shaky to start the year. He’s been high on a few snaps, and Cairo Santos had a chip-shot field goal blocked in Chicago’s 9-3 loss to the Vikings on Sunday. The Bears rank just No. 27 in the NFL with a 68.8 kicking score by Pro Football Network’s metrics heading into Week 3. Gardner was the Patrick Mannelly Award winner as the best collegiate long snapper out of Georgia last year, but he’ll likely have to wait for his next chance to see NFL action. As of this writing, no move has been made regarding his roster status, but teams typically only keep one long snapper on the roster.

title: 2-0 Bengals get a slap in the face from a new NFL ranking and a Texans player
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0, atop (alone) the AFC North, and the team and its fans have every reason to be excited about what the 2026 Bengals are capable of and will do. However, not everyone sees it. Some look at the fact that the two teams the Bengals faced are both 0-2, the Bucs […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0, atop (alone) the AFC North, and the team and its fans have every reason to be excited about what the 2026 Bengals are capable of and will do. However, not everyone sees it. Some look at the fact that the two teams the Bengals faced are both 0-2, the Bucs losing at home to the lowly Browns in Week 2, and some seem to forget that the city of Cincinnati exists at all. PFF is a great example. They released their power rankings, which were derived from the quality of each team as defined by Point Spread Team Ratings (whatever that means), and to say that it’s ridiculous is a massive understatement. Not only do they have the 2-0 Bengals all the way down at No. 15 behind several teams not nearly as good, but they’re also three spots behind the 0-2 team they beat on Sunday. I’m not exactly sure what algorithm PFF used to come up with this garbage, but it should be scrapped for good. And then there’s the lack of respect from a vanquished foe. Texans wide receiver Kayshon Boutte recently told the media the Bengals didn’t do anything out of the ordinary to beat Houston; it was all Houston’s doing. You know, the whole, ‘they didn’t win, we lost’ thing. “We beat ourselves,” he said. “They wasn’t really doing nothing that we couldn’t handle. We just gotta be better in the red zone. We went there multiple times, came up with zero, bull—- offense.” This is the kind of thing players don’t pay much attention to, but fans tend to latch on. The Texans were outmatched on Sunday in almost every way, and especially when Boutte and his bullsh*t offense were on the field. It’s hard for CJ Stroud to find one of his receivers downfield when he’s running for his life. The Bengals didn’t allow him to get comfortable often, and it’s very clear it was something the Texans’ offense “couldn’t handle.” Al Golden may not be putting this stuff on the bulletin board in the locker room, but fans remember. We don’t get no respect! No respect at all! Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0 after defeating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at home in Week 1 and then the Houston Texans on the road in Week 2. It’s the latter of these wins, though, that has turned heads. The Bengals scored 20 points, but that’s nothing special. What was special was their defense keeping the Texans out of the end zone throughout the entire game, and completely dominating the line of scrimmage all afternoon. Now the Bengals have a shot to do something only nine teams have done in franchise history—start a season off with a 3-0 record. They travel to Pittsburgh to open up AFC North play against the Steelers, who are coming into Week 3 with a 1-1 record. But how important is a 3-0 record? Well, according to RotoWire, it’s a pretty good indicator of what’s to come. “We sorted every team from 2016 through 2025 by its record through three games and tracked where each season finished,” wrote RotoWire’s Thomas Leary . “The table splits cleanly in two worlds: the 3-0 and 2-1 teams, who make the playoffs more often than not, and the 1-2 and 0-3 teams, who mostly don’t.” Hopefully the Bengals will fit into the first category and remain unbeaten. We’re one bit of communication, or one block in the second level away from Chase [Brown] getting a one-on-one with the safety, and then we’ll see how that plays out.” The Bengals will be wearing white jerseys and black pants on Sunday in Pittsburgh, according to Bengals.com’s Michael Hull . Chiefs, Bengals, Vikings head the surprise early contenders entering Week 3 The Bengals defense has been impressive for the second week in a row. He’s playing corner at a high level right now. He’s had two back-to-back solid games. He’s been in great position.”

title: Stars of the Game: Ja’Marr Chase and the Bengals defense shine in Houston
summary: Joe Burrow, Zac Taylor, and Dan Pitcher made it clear throughout the week after the Bengals’ Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Week 2 game at the Houston Texans: they needed to do a better job getting the ball to Ja’Marr Chase. After just two receptions for 12 yards, one of which […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Ja'marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals catches a touchdown pass against the Houston Texans during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Burrow, Zac Taylor, and Dan Pitcher made it clear throughout the week after the Bengals’ Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Week 2 game at the Houston Texans: they needed to do a better job getting the ball to Ja’Marr Chase. After just two receptions for 12 yards, one of which went for -4 yards, the tone was set heading into Houston; Chase would get the ball early and often. The best part of the week between Weeks 1 and 2 is that Chase said all the right things. He kept his head down and just went about his business. Chase let his actions speak louder than his words, and whoa, did his actions speak volumes on Saturday. Here is a look at our stars of the game from the Bengals’ 20-6 win over the Houston Texans. 1. Ja’Marr Chase: 7 rec., 75 yds, 2 TD Chase had three receptions in the first quarter on Sunday, making his presence felt. The Bengals established him early, setting him up for big plays later in the game and a catch that will forever be on his highlight reel and in his future Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement video. Chase’s 32-yard touchdown reception was a kill shot. Joe Burrow had just hit Tee Higgins for a 23-yard reception on 3rd&4 to get to the Texans’ 32-yard line. Now, it was 1st&10. The Texans had just flubbed a 34-yard field goal attempt and gotten stopped on 4th&Inches. They were on their heels. Burrow sensed that, and he went for the home run play. Good lord, Chase’s catch is incredible. It’s so many things woven into one: body control, concentration, and footwork. Not to mention, it came against Derek Stingley Jr., one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL. But Chase wasn’t done there. On his second touchdown, it’s classic Burrow and Chase. Ja’Marr Chase knows what Joe Burrow will do when he’s out of the pocket. As soon as Burrow waved his thumb in the direction he wanted Chase to go, Chase sprinted to the right side of the end zone and hauled in a back-breaking 18-yard touchdown to put the Bengals up 17-3. It was very reminiscent of Burrow to Chase on a scramble drill against San Francisco in 2021 and against Philadelphia in 2024. This time, though, the play came in a Bengals win. There was no need to worry about Chase after Week 1. He was in a great headspace despite small numbers, and now he’s coming off a terrific performance going into an AFC North game at Pittsburgh. 2. Dexter Lawrence: 3 TKL, 1 TFL,1 QBH Dexter Lawrence single-handedly changed the game on Sunday in Houston. Lawrence only needed three tackles and one tackle for loss on the stat sheet because he does so many other things to impact the game. That said, Lawrence’s fourth-down stop on David Montgomery in the second quarter is why the Bengals traded for him. It’s that kind of play, stuffing a run on fourth and TWO INCHES to completely swing the momentum of the game. The Bengals needed a stud and beast in the middle of their defense to make plays like that to swing games when they are on their heels. That’s who Lawrence is. He’s the undisputed leader of the Bengals’ defense, the guy in the center up front who sets the tone. Lawrence’s fourth-down stop is his first big, game-changing play as a Bengal. It won’t be the last time you see him make a play like that this season. 3. Joe Burrow: 20/31, 207 yds, 2 TD, 105.2 Passer Rating Back tightness, Houston’s defense, clunky offense at times? None of it mattered for Joe Burrow on Sunday, who diced up the Texans and played a clean game despite taking five sacks. This is one of my favorite Joe Burrow games in his career. Given the week leading up to the game and the opponent, Burrow displayed a calm and toughness that made him one of the NFL’s best quarterbacks in 2021 and 2022. There’s no question Burrow is still one of the NFL’s best quarterbacks. Yes, he hasn’t posted prolific numbers yet this season. However, he’s still been productive through two games. Burrow only needed to throw for 207 yards on Sunday for the Bengals to have success against Houston, or, as he said, he only needed to be “incredibly average.” Here is one way to interpret that quote: this is Burrow’s floor, and that’s been good enough for the Bengals to win their first two games of the season. Just wait till Burrow starts putting up elite numbers on offense. 4. Demetrius Knight Jr.: 12 TKL, 1 QBH Knight led the Bengals in tackles on Sunday, and it was one of the first times in his young career I thought he looked like he belonged on an NFL field as a linebacker. He finally looks like a guy who can rally to the ball, take the right angle for a tackle, and knows where the ball is going. If Knight is leading the Bengals in tackles in a game, that’s really good for this revived Bengals’ defense. He was awesome on Sunday, and this is a performance he can build on.
