title: Should the Colts expect more from their players?
summary: I had to take a beat after the marathon Sunday Night game. This old-timer made it all the way, but had to answer the 5:30 a.m. bell the following morning. I was spent most of Monday and jotted down some notes, but I just didn’t have the focus to make it coherent. There is no […]
full_text: I had to take a beat after the marathon Sunday Night game. This old-timer made it all the way, but had to answer the 5:30 a.m. bell the following morning. I was spent most of Monday and jotted down some notes, but I just didn’t have the focus to make it coherent. There is no question that the Colts fan base expects more from their coaches and management. There are enough posts out there detailing those deficiencies, that even though I have joined in from time to time, I won’t take this opportunity to pile on. I’m not even going to say that the posts are unfair. I do believe that the attention absorbed by the staff, makes it pretty easy to be a player. When you have not won a game since the Berlin road trip last year, there are plenty of outlets for our anger and I sometimes wonder why the players are often shielded from the criticism. Not all players are exempt from our ire, but it is usually not based on play on the field. Someone might get a thumbs down, stock down, or some other designation for not having a good game, but we seem be far more tolerant of the play, than those who are in charge of putting them on the field. I watched many cases of our defenders simply being beat by their offensive counterpart. The plan to play more man-to-man coverage can never work if your player is not up to the challenge his man presents. There are plays where our defenders, mostly the LBs, are not paying attention to their surroundings. I may be wrong, but aren’t LBs often the most instinctive players on the field? I wouldn’t think that you could get through college without, “A nose for the football.” Not being able to diagnose a play, or find a player is only half of our current player difficulties. On the occasions where a play has been diagnosed and a player has put themselves in position to make a play, the tackle is not being made. There is reaching, lunging, and bumping, but we are bringing guys to the ground, not taking them to the ground. I see too many cases of one of our defenders stopping in their tracks to see which way the ball carrier is going to go, rather than going full bore and blowing them up. I also see them running along side in what looks to be an attempt for the runner to actually come to them. Lastly we appear to give up extra yards while trying tug at a players arms in an effort to get the turnover, in hopes that it would mask how poorly the play had been defended. The LBs are not the only culprits, as our lockdown guys have been anything but. I don’t know where you instill attitude of beating your man on every play, but we seldom exhibit it. I understand growing pains, but they should be occasional lapses, rather giving look of being lost. Key may end up being okay, but that first play of the game was just stupid. You held contain for nearly the duration of the play, but when it got bottled up and you decided to engage, you went in blind and attempted to tackle big Grove. I did think that Taylor-Britt brought in a little attitude and that Gushiken showed good ball skills, until he was beat, giving up the longest play at the most critical time. Man, I thought Wohler hit him hard enough to dislodge the ball, but credit Thornton for making the play. If Treadwell would have caught his ball with that much authority, the game narrative may be different right now. I don’t have as much of a gripe with the offense. Allen looked a little less this week. Maybe the distraction of the impending suspension got in his head? A little more drive might have bailed DJ out of that interception. The O-line was steady and you can tell they like it when Jones lines up under center. If Warren is to be what we believe he can be, he needs to get closer to the 11 targets that Kelce got last night and it needs to good for more than 4 YPC. This may be an odd observation, but he doesn’t appear to land very well? A little out of control, unbraced, or not with the looseness that someone who is a little liquored up might have. Don’t tell me you don’t know that roll. Ta-da! Just my two cents on where some of the blame should be placed. I will say that the Chiefs got great reviews for beating us and not just the “A win is a win” narrative. They believe Mahomes to be fully back and playing his best to pull one out. Most would give the Mora “Playoffs?” line to me if I said that we might have to turn the tables on both them and the Raven in the playoffs, but I haven’t lost complete confidence. I still believe that we have talent, but I sometimes wonder if the players want it as badly as we do. I don’t know how you have galvanizing events? It seems like the players need something to rally around? The Browns found a way to rally around a Mike Tomlin quote of “Browns gonna Brown”. Our D could use a little incentive or something to spark them. Yogi said that 90% of the game is half mental. There is still room for some physical in there and the crew needs to tap into being more physical. As far as the game, it was a good one to watch. I, like many, watched with some belief that we could win and also with some sense of impending doom. I do not know exactly our ceiling at this point? The Pierce loss is going to hurt and we need to go 4 – 2 or better against the division to have any real shot at winning it. Let’s get a couple of more games under our belts, before claiming we know how this movie ends.

title: The Good and the Bad from the Chiefs’ Week 2 win
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs won an exciting overtime game against the Indianapolis Colts, 33-30. The Chiefs’ pass offense looked crisp, the run game continued to make a difference, and Kansas City got enough stops without cornerback Mansoor Delane to win. After every win, I like to look at two things that went well for the […]
full_text: (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs won an exciting overtime game against the Indianapolis Colts , 33-30. The Chiefs’ pass offense looked crisp, the run game continued to make a difference, and Kansas City got enough stops without cornerback Mansoor Delane to win. After every win, I like to look at two things that went well for the Chiefs and one thing that didn’t. Let’s start by talking about the impact of nose tackle Khyiris Tonga: The Good Khyiris Tonga brings a different element to the Chiefs’ defense For years, the Chiefs scraped by at nose tackle with cheap veterans, primarily Derrick Nnadi and Mike Pennel since 2019. Both could eat blocks and occupy space, but neither consistently impacted the run game. This offseason, Kansas City finally upgraded, signing Tonga to a three-year, $21 million contract. After bouncing around early in his career, Tonga broke out with New England by stabilizing its run defense. The early returns have been promising. Khyiris Tonga pt 1 pic.twitter.com/BCkco29Zie — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 Khyiris Tonga pt 2 pic.twitter.com/4F6zvX7o1c — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 Khyiris Tonga pt 3 pic.twitter.com/VyrNw9wbhr — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 Khyiris Tonga pt 4 pic.twitter.com/lZEDdzbzpj — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 The most underrated part of Tonga’s game is his initial burst. He fires off the ball and beats blockers to the spot, especially on zone runs. On the backside, guards have to get around his hips to seal him, which is difficult because Tonga explodes off the ball and chases plays down. He combines that burst with the strength to control blocks and eat space. Tonga even got the better of left guard Quenton Nelson in the first clip, directing him toward the running back and closing the hole. That combination of explosiveness and power gives the Chiefs a disruptive presence against the run. Tonga could be especially important when Kansas City faces the Bills. The Chiefs incorporating play action into their passing game I’ve written about this before, but I’ve believed the Chiefs needed to run more play action with the skill-position personnel they have. Kansas City’s weapons struggle to get off press coverage and create their own separation. Running play action can help mitigate this, as you can create natural rubs with the run fake and condense the formation, forcing cornerbacks to play off receivers. The issue is that with the Chiefs’ lack of run game for years, it was hard to get any team to buy the run fake Kansas City would present. Defenders would drop into coverage, so the fake did nothing. Now that the Chiefs have running back Kenneth Walker, teams have to respect the run threat much more, which has opened up Kansas City’s play-action passing concepts. Mahomes went 14/17 on play-action passes for 137 yards and two touchdowns against the Colts. Patrick Mahomes completed 32 of 47 passes for 382 yards and 3 touchdowns in the Chiefs' Week 2 win, recording a career-high 14 completions on play-action passes. He totaled 137 yards and 2 touchdowns on 17 play-action attempts. #INDvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/DiYyyXrqV3 — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 21, 2026 Mahomes play action to Worthy pic.twitter.com/0TEXEs7Byq — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 23, 2026 One of the first plays of the game showed the impact of the Chiefs’ improved run game on play action. The Colts are in Cover 2, but the WILL linebacker bites on the play fake and gets completely out of position. With the field corner occupied by Kelce in the flat, the MIKE linebacker must choose between tight end Noah Gray’s sail route and receiver Xavier Worthy’s backside dig. He covers Gray, leaving Worthy wide open. Mahomes play action pt 2 pic.twitter.com/q4TGrCbZoz — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 23, 2026 This is a good example of how condensed formations can help wide receivers get free releases. Wideout Rashee Rice motions inside to an F position off the line of scrimmage. This makes it look like he’s going to run block. When it’s a pass, Rice gets a free release. The Colts are playing Cover 1, but the motion gives Rice a leverage advantage on cornerback Sauce Gardner, who has no chance at recovering to Rice on the over route. Mahomes PA flat to Walker pt 1 pic.twitter.com/9GO3rj6lS0 — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 23, 2026 Mahomes to Walker PA flat pt 2 pic.twitter.com/pX2fUahqQI — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 23, 2026 The Chiefs ran this exact formation and play twice, including on a critical third down in overtime. Worthy motions across the formation, then Kansas City runs a quick boot to the flat for Walker. The first time, Indianapolis linebackers bump with the motion, giving Walker easy leverage. The second time, Gardner travels with Worthy, vacating the flat. It’s a quick-hitting concept that attacks linebackers who can’t match Walker in space. The pass offense can’t build entirely around play action, but using it more will make the offense smoother. It creates cleaner receiver releases, slows linebackers against the run, reduces the burden on the offensive line, and simplifies Mahomes’ reads by giving him one or two primary options plus a checkdown. Overall, it’s something the coaching staff should keep refining; it gives them a new and important lever to pull in big games. The Bad The Chiefs setting the edge against pin-pull runs The Chiefs defense wasn’t as dominant as Week 1, but the Colts deserve credit. They ran effectively, added bodies in protection, and consistently used hot routes to neutralize the blitz. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed struggled in space against slot receiver Josh Downs, but cornerback Nohl Williams and safety Jaden Hicks played well. Without Delane, the Chiefs will be more vulnerable in coverage, but they did enough to win. My biggest concern was edge-setting. On both Jonathan Taylor touchdowns, Indianapolis used pin-pull concepts to create a wide edge, and the Chiefs struggled to set it. Jonathan Taylor pin-pull TD part 1 pic.twitter.com/WkUHUVd0xJ — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 Downs motions across the play, and Sneed travels with him, eliminating him from the run fit. The center and right tackle pull around the edge, with the tackle easily widening Tranquill. The center doesn’t have to block anyone because Hicks takes a poor angle and gets caught inside. But the play is really lost on tight end Tyler Warren’s block against rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas. Warren gets enough torque to seal Thomas inside and drive him three or four yards off the line. Thomas can’t lose his outside shoulder here. pic.twitter.com/Kt4kP9Oa4z — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 22, 2026 On this touchdown, the Chiefs don’t travel the corner with motion, keeping Kristian Fulton in the run fit. Unfortunately, Fulton has to take on Quentin Nelson with a full head of steam and gets pancaked. Hicks can’t beat the center to the hole, Drue Tranquill gets caught in the trash, and Nick Bolton has too much ground to cover. Defensive end George Karlaftis doesn’t get pinned like Thomas, but he still can’t shed the tight end to make the tackle. You could argue he was held, but it wasn’t called, and he needs to get off that block. These are only two plays, but they’re on tape now. Teams will keep running at Thomas and Felix Anudike-Uzomah because they’re light, so the Chiefs need to improve their edge setting.

Harbaugh said Tuesday that evaluations on Dart’s knee were still ongoing and declined to comment further on his timeline to return. “It’s an ongoing conversation about the health of a player, of a person,” Harbaugh said on a video call with reporters. “We’ve got to prepare for the range of possibilities.” Broncos’ Sean Payton accused Seahawks of cheating, sparking ‘Cold War,’ Mike Macdonald says | The Athletic According to Macdonald, the Seahawks scouted video of roughly 100 plays posted by fans on social media from Broncos training camp practices and used them to prepare for Payton’s team ahead of the 2024 season opener. “It’s like public knowledge. So we took like 100 plays from their training camp,” Macdonald said with a laugh. The Seahawks won the game, Macdonald’s first as head coach, 26-20. Bears QB Tyson Bagent in concussion protocol; Case Keenum could start Week 3 | NFL.com This always made a lot of sense, even before Goedert was sidelined. The team placed rookie TE Eli Stowers on IR at the start of the season, and Grant Calcaterra was put on IR at the end of training camp. With just Johnny Mundt and E.J. Jenkins left, the TE room gets an immediate boost by adding Ertz. The former Eagles draft pick has spent his time away from Philly with the Cardinals and Commanders, and has been a consistent factor in the redzone — regardless of the overall effectiveness of those offenses. Ertz is also just 11 receptions away from breaking Harold Carmichael’s franchise record (589) in Philadelphia to become the team’s leader all-time in catches. title: Chiefs Film Review: Patrick Mahomes has monster game in Week 2
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Indianapolis Colts in a closely contested 33-30 game that came down to the final possession in overtime. The game was back and forth for most of the evening, but Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes elevated his team to victory. Mahomes put up 382 passing yards and three touchdowns with 32 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after a play during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Indianapolis Colts in a closely contested 33-30 game that came down to the final possession in overtime. The game was back and forth for most of the evening, but Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes elevated his team to victory. Mahomes put up 382 passing yards and three touchdowns with 32 completions on 47 attempts and a quarterback rating of 114. The game marked the 14th-highest passing yardage total Mahomes has thrown for in his career. The performance came at the right time as the Chiefs needed every bit of his arm talent and pocket presence to beat the Colts. Let’s take a look at how he did it. Settling in Last week, Mahomes struggled through the game to find any rhythm in his first game back after his ACL injury last season. This week, the Chiefs coaching staff allowed Mahomes to ease himself into the game with some easy completions based on run action looks. This look is too easy for Mahomes, and a great "layup" to start the game and help him build rhythm. The run action pulls the defense, and Worthy ends up wide open. pic.twitter.com/ENVb6ior5q — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 Last week, Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker had a big performance , naturally meaning the Colts defense was ready to attempt to stop him. After an opening burst of 19 yards by Walker, the Chiefs would go to a play-action look on their second play of the game. On the snap, the linebackers and most of the Colts’ defense would flow toward Walker. With the Chiefs in 13 personnel, this appears to be a run-first look, but Mahomes pulls the ball and quickly finds Xavier Worthy over the middle, who was wide open on a crossing pattern with the Colts looking to defend the boundary against the run. The pass isn’t spectacular, and maybe even a touch underthrown, but it establishes an easy completion for Mahomes and sets him in the right direction for success. Mahomes with a perfectly placed ball to Kelce on the out. Confident throw with some zip. He leads Kelce into the end zone with the pass, taking advantage of good field position. pic.twitter.com/lk6iomlndV — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 In a two-by-two set, the Chiefs run a high-low concept with tight end Travis Kelce and wide receiver Xavier Worthy to attack the Colts’ man coverage. With two corners and a high safety in defense of the combo, Worthy runs the high route holding up the safety and creating space, while Kelce creates just enough separation on his out route to give Mahomes a good window. Mahomes puts some zest on the ball and fires it to Kelce, who turns in stride upfield after the catch. Kelce blasts his way into the end zone to give the Chiefs the lead. KC in "11 personnel," but Thornton and Rice condense into tight alignment, mimicking KC's 13-personnel set. Run action look with Rice inserting through the gap creates instant space and allows Mahomes to lead him into a big gain. Look at the LB's react to the run action. pic.twitter.com/IabV66KZfI — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 Out of a condensed look, receiver Rashee Rice goes from shifting pre-snap to inserting in the line of scrimmage to run his route, which creates immediate separation from him and the cornerback, while allowing Mahomes to hit him in stride. Working the pocket Mahomes was uncomfortable during week one in the pocket and the Denver pass rush, but this week after settling in with some easy throws and building his confidence, he quickly started creating plays himself in the pocket. Pressure in the pocket quickly, but Mahomes stays calm and works around it. Good job finding Rice in the window after stepping up past the interior pass rush. pic.twitter.com/ju9BxFHY2g — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 On the snap, pressure quickly comes from the interior, but Mahomes is unfazed. By simply sliding away from the pressure and stepping up in the pocket, he avoids the rush completely and keeps his eyes locked in downfield. He uses good anticipation to find the hole in the defense, and fires a pass into Rice for a nice gain. Pocket collapses quickly and forces Mahomes to roll out to his right. The edge tried to jam Kelce, but he created just enough separation, and Mahomes rips one to him while falling away. pic.twitter.com/e00VZ15XrF — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 On the snap, the Colts bring pressure through the backside B-gap, which forces Mahomes to roll ot his right. The pass rush is well coordinated, but Mahomes stayed cool and recognized that Kelce is being covered by a defensive end. The idea is to jam Kelce straight off the line, but Mahomes is buying extra time; this gives Kelce just enough time to create separation and give his quarterback a window to throw. Deep shots After not looking to go deep much in Week 1, Mahomes found wideout Tyquon Thornton — his favorite deep target in 2025 — twice downfield this game, resulting in explosive gains. After a dormant week one, Mahomes and Thornton picked up where they left off last season. Worthy's route holds the defense in place as Thornton blows by the safety. Mahomes has time in the pocket and lets it fly. Beautiful throw. Just short of the end zone. pic.twitter.com/LmCtXtzRx7 — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 The Chiefs line up with a trips variation on the left side of the field, and on the snap both Thornton and Worthy run deep routes agaisnt the zone defense on a third-and-medium distance. The defensive backs are playing the sticks, and there is only one true “deep safety”. Worthy pulls the defenders’ attention, but Thornton keeps tracking downfield, and Mahomes fires a dart to set up first down and goal. Later in the game, the duo would connect once more. Thornton has a great route to beat the man coverage. Great job shaking free to the outside, and Mahomes has the time to step into the pass. Perfect pass; Thornton takes a hit but holds on. Chemistry on display between the two. pic.twitter.com/0fBrzu9bCp — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 The Colts mixed and matched zone and man coverage all day, and on the snap they attempt to go with man coverage while rushing five. Mahomes hits the top of his drop, and drifts just a bit to buy Thornton to win his route and get to the spot on the deep out. Mahomes puts it on the money, and Thornton holds on despite taking a big shot. Trusting the team So many times through the course of his career, Mahomes has played the role of Superman, but on Sunday night, we saw him trust his teammates to help make critical plays down the stretch, specifically Walker. Condensed formation for KC with Worthy showing the eye candy. The defense reacts to the motion/line showing the run, and this allows Walker to come free out of the backfield. No heroics needed from 15, dump it down and let K9 do the rest. Rice with a good block. pic.twitter.com/ePqlGghLvr — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 22, 2026 Late in overtime, the Chiefs needed one yard to pick up a first down and keep the drive alive. Once more, they come out with receivers tight on the line of scrimmage, mimicking their 13-personnel look. With eye candy from Worthy, Mahomes reverses on the snap and rolls out. With most of the defense set up to play the run and/or stop the speed play, all Mahomes has to do is float a pass over the free rusher’s head to Walker. After securing the catch, Walker turns up field sets them up for the game-winning field goal. The bottom line Mahomes was outstanding on Sunday, through a combination of making layups, working the pocket, and connecting on big plays down the field. The Chiefs offense has been firing the first two weeks of the season, but seeing Mahomes…

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 3 Roundup: Chiefs settle into top 5
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 2 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Indianapolis Colts on “Sunday Night Football” in overtime. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN: 4 (Up from 8) One thing we know about the QB1: Patrick Mahomes can deal from under center. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Andy Reid of the Kansas City Chiefs on the sidelines in overtime of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 2 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Indianapolis Colts on “Sunday Night Football” in overtime. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN : 4 (Up from 8) One thing we know about the QB1: Patrick Mahomes can deal from under center. With the addition of running back Kenneth Walker III, Mahomes has shown that he can be surgical when passing from under center, especially on play-action passes. On under-center plays, Mahomes threw a touchdown against the Colts and has already recorded 107 passing yards. It’s one of the biggest changes from last season, when the clear majority of the Chiefs’ snaps with Mahomes were in the shotgun — 80.6% of their formations (excluding quarterback kneel-downs), third most in the league. — Nate Taylor — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 4 (Up from 7) Rookie spotlight : Mansoor Delane The first-round cornerback had an interception on the first drive of the season but has been out since then due to a shoulder injury. It hasn’t been a problem for the Chiefs, though, who seem to have drafted well in 2026. Defensive lineman Peter Woods and edge rusher R Mason Thomas are already contributing, and fifth-round running back Emmett Johnson has 10 rushes for 39 yards and four catches for 64 yards despite limited playing time. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 4 (Up from 8) Kenneth Walker III could become one of the best free-agent signings ever. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 5 (Up from 10) They are 2-0 and the passing game came alive in the victory over the Colts. Patrick Mahomes looked like Patrick Mahomes again, which is not good for the rest of the league. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 6 (Up from 7) Kenneth Walker might have the second-biggest impact of anyone in the NFL through two weeks, behind Josh Allen. In Week 1, Walker set a career best by forcing 14 missed tackles. In Week 2, he forced 15 missed tackles. When the Chiefs needed a game-winning drive in overtime, he was involved in five of their six offensive plays. Included in that was a 22-yard gain on a catch that got the Chiefs into easy field-goal range. For the first time in a while, the Chiefs have balance on offense and that’s helping Patrick Mahomes. “It’s fun for me, just him running the ball, our offensive line driving off the ball the way that they’re driving off,” Mahomes said. “It’s making defenses have to account for that. I mean, if not, we’re going to run the ball for 200 yards or whatever we did the week before, and so you want to be able to do it all.” — Frank Schwab USA Today : 5 (Up from 6) It’s early yet − way early, obviously − but the Super Bowl MVP backfield of QB Patrick Mahomes and RB Kenneth Walker III is on pace to pass for nearly 5,000 yards and rush for nearly 2,500, respectively. — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 3 (Up from 5) There’s a lot we can say and should say about the Chiefs’ storming out of the gate this year. But the one that I am the most curious about, and need the most information on, is how Travis Kelce got into the best shape of his life in his late thirties post-wedding. Normally that is the time in a man’s life to really embrace the dad bod. — Conor Orr FOX Sports : 8 (Up from 12) They needed all of overtime to escape the Colts, but look at what Patrick Mahomes did with 382 yards and three touchdowns. There’s no more doubt: The Chiefs are back. — Ralph Vacchiano

title: Week 3 AP NFL Power Rankings: Chiefs remain top 5; Raiders rise
summary: We’re in the swing of things now. Two weeks are in the books, and once again, parity runs rampant in the NFL. It seems there is the cream of the crop in the top few teams; then there are the clear bottom feeders—and in the middle lies a bunch of teams that could win or […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Travis Kelce #87 and Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs run onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re in the swing of things now. Two weeks are in the books, and once again, parity runs rampant in the NFL. It seems there is the cream of the crop in the top few teams; then there are the clear bottom feeders—and in the middle lies a bunch of teams that could win or lose on any given Sunday. This week’s talking points will be the quarterback injuries that wreaked havoc across the league. Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, and Jaxson Dart were all forced out of their games. It remains to be seen how long each player will miss this season. For now, each team dropped in our power rankings. Injuries to the quarterback don’t spell disaster, however, as the Seahawks remain at the top of the league with Drew Lock under center, while the Vikings crash into the top of the rankings under the strong play of quarterback Carson Wentz. Let’s see how the rankings shook out this week from the crew. Biggest riser: Las Vegas Raiders +9 Biggest faller: Houston Texans -12 This week, along with myself, staff voters were: Maurice Elston, Caleb James , Ron Kopp Jr., Rocky Magana and Jared Sapp. 1. Seattle Seahawks (1st) Jaxson Smith-Njigba is the only Seahawk to score a touchdown this season. Four so far. And so far, so good. 2. Buffalo Bills (3rd) Yikes, that Bills’ defense. But when you have Josh Allen in September, it doesn’t matter. 3. San Francisco 49ers (4th) Even back on American soil, the 49ers were dominant. 4. Kansas City Chiefs (5th) Inexplicable special-teams blunders, Mahomes’ dimes, Kelce finding an open hole against zone defense, Depression-era play calls, and a weird game against the Colts. We’re so back. 5. Cincinnati Bengals (6th) The Burrow-Chase connection was renewed. And the Bengals defense looked stout against an offense that shredded the Bills the week prior. It looks like the Bengals are back in the AFC mix. 6. Philadelphia Eagles (9th) Say what you want, but all Jalen Hurts does is win football games. 7. Baltimore Ravens (2nd) It was John Harbaugh before. Who’s the scapegoat for a fourth-quarter collapse now? 8. Los Angeles Rams (11th) Now that is the Rams team we expected to see. 9. Minnesota Vikings (16th) KOC, head coach Kevin O’Connell, is putting on a coaching masterclass in Minnesota to start the year. 10. Chicago Bears (8th) You would have to take me off an NFL field in a wheelchair or ambulance if I attempted to play. But these Caleb Williams memes are hilarious. 11. Jacksonville Jaguars (10th) The Jaguars couldn’t complete the win in Denver on Sunday. But Trevor Lawrence is a different player this year. 12. New England Patriots (14th) Dominating win against the Steelers…but is anyone overly impressed? 13. Denver Broncos (12th) It took almost seven quarters, but the Broncos’ offense made their 2026 season debut. 14. Detroit Lions (13th) This team has completely lost the toughness and grit promised by head coach Dan Campbell. 15. Green Bay Packers (17th) Everything for the Packers just seems like a struggle right now. 16. Dallas Cowboys (19th) Quarterback Dak Prescott now owns every passing record in Cowboys’ franchise history. But he’s tied for fewest Super Bowl wins. 17. New Orleans Saints (23rd) “Poor man’s Josh Allen” Tyler Shough currently leads the NFL in passing yards. 18. Las Vegas Raiders (27th) Kirk Cousins’ good boy persona just doesn’t fit the vibe of the Raiders…yet, he’s turned back the clock and is balling out to start the season. 19. Houston Texans (7th) With Nico Collins on the sideline, the Texans’ offense had no juice. Lucky for them, they play in the AFC South. 20. Carolina Panthers (26th) Okay, Bryce Young…I’m starting to take notice. 21. New York Giants (15th) A hopeful start to the season took a big blow, depending on the severity of Dart’s injury. 22. Indianapolis Colts (24th) Is it the right move to actually go for it on 4th and 8 in overtime rather than giving Patrick Mahomes the ball again? 23. Pittsburgh Steelers (18th) The Steelers benefitted from playing the Falcons in Week 1… this is not a good football team. 24. Arizona Cardinals (22nd) I was convinced wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. would be an All-Pro from the beginning of his career. Right now, he looks like an all-time bust. 25. Los Angeles Chargers (20th) Their AFC West offseason crown was even shorter-lived than usual. How long will the national media make excuses for Justin Herbert? 26. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (21st) Baker has taken a two-week vacation since he got paid. 27. New York Jets (29th) Same old Jets. A 10-point blown lead in the 4th quarter. (And still no interceptions). 28. Washington Commanders (25th) Tom Brady said what we were all thinking on the broadcast. 29. Cleveland Browns (32nd) The Browns are the Browns. Or so we thought? 30. Tennessee Titans (31st) They were cooling off cleats with water bottles in Nashville on Sunday. The heat got to the Titans as their first win remains elusive. 31. Atlanta Falcons (28th) This team is going nowhere fast. Worth a call to see if Drake London is available? 32. Miami Dolphins (30th) Ryan Fitzpatrick said his former team could realistically go 0-17. It’s hard to believe that’s possible—but they look like a team tanking.

title: Chiefs Mailbag: Will the real Kansas City defense please stand up?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! It took a full 70 minutes, but the Chiefs are 2-0 thanks to a 33-30 overtime victory over the Indianapolis Colts Sunday night. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Chris Jones #95 of the Kansas City Chiefs chases Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts during a run in the second quarter of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! It took a full 70 minutes, but the Chiefs are 2-0 thanks to a 33-30 overtime victory over the Indianapolis Colts Sunday night. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds ahead of a trip to South Florida to face the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. MrAustin.Sr asks: Which defense is REALLY our defense, last week vs the Denver Broncos or the defense we ran out there for the Colts? This will sound like a cop out, but the answer is probably somewhere in between. I think there are some context factors we should consider. The Chiefs had probably been working on the Broncos game plan since midway through training camp. Also, Week 1 was defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s fifth opportunity to game plan against the Denver quarterback Bo Nix’s offense. He clearly made adjustments to keep Denver from repeating some of their success in the pair of 2025 matchups. Many laughed off the Colts after being blown out by the Baltimore Ravens in Week 1. However, Indianapolis was also among the league’s best offenses in the first half of last season. Indianapolis started 8-2 while averaging 32 points per game. Yes, the wheels fell off down the stretch, but the Colts have definitely shown the ability to score big early. My biggest concern coming out of the Broncos win was how the defense would react to a team that doesn’t abandon the run early, as Denver did. Hopefully, the team sees some areas to address because it did not go well. The combination of star running back Jonathan Taylor and the Colts’ offensive line is likely a challenge few opponents can replicate. The biggest issue for the Chiefs’ defense is how long the unit can afford to continue a heavy workload for cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who surrendered a passer rating of 132.6 when targeted in Week 2. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones treated Sneed like an “easy button,” and the Chiefs’ pass rush had little to do to be effective. Like most things early on, we will need a larger sample. If the Chiefs struggle with the Dolphins — who have surrendered nine sacks through two games and needed a garbage-time touchdown to reach 13 points on Sunday — it will be more concerning. Will007 asks: Is it time to start worrying about the wide receivers room or is just the first two games the Chiefs played two teams with good secondaries? There are two possibilities to ponder with the wideouts. For many, the question is whether the Chiefs have someone in-house who can be a no-doubt No. 1 passing game option. That answer is undoubtedly no. A different assessment is whether the Chiefs have the potential to replicate the 2022 receiving corps featuring complementary pieces that propelled quarterback Patrick Mahomes to an MVP season. That one is probably a “maybe.” Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton and Jalen Royals combined for 200 receiving yards and a pair of touchdowns against Indianapolis. To be fair, 31 of those yards came to Rice on the final play of regulation that never had any chance of proving fruitful. But the Chiefs’ receivers did show signs of the “sum of the parts” approach that has worked well in prior seasons. While you cannot expect tight end Travis Kelce or running back Kenneth Walker to keep up their early-season pace, they are crucial to the Chiefs succeeding with an underwhelming group of wideouts. Which player gets targets will likely change weekly depending on the opponent. Second-year man Jalen Royals entered the night widely forgotten. Royals only saw two targets, but both came in key situations, and the coaches clearly saw something in the Colts’ defense they felt he could exploit. Whenever rookie Cyrus Allen’s turn finally comes, it will probably be a similar development. Andyreidsmustache_ asks: Has the coaching staff finally seen enough from Tyquan Thornton to actually make him a more prominent part of the offense, if not an outright starter? I’d already put him head and shoulders above Worthy at minimum. I think the Kansas City wideout group is so matchup dependent that I am rarely concerned with who is nominally starting. I do think Sunday previewed what can be done with Thornton. His 86 receiving yards in Week 2 were more than a tenth of his career production over his first four seasons. Thornton has never shown the yards-after-the-catch elusiveness to have the value in the short passing game that the other wideouts bring. However, he is easily the Chiefs’ most dependable deep threat since Tyreek Hill left after 2021. As Walker demands more defensive focus, Thornton should find more deep opportunities as he did on Sunday night. Worthy’s start to the season has been frustrating, but I still think it is early to write him off completely. Remember that over three years with the New England Patriots , Thornton definitely looked like the far inferior player. RoyalsFanBill asks: Who is our primary kick returner going forward? The Chiefs seem to be trying to make running back Brashard Smith the focused returner. Rookie Emmett Johnson took one kickoff Sunday night. While both appear to have more juice than Remigio, I would be wary of using both backup running backs as the return tandem because of the risk of having both options behind Walker injured at the same time. Perhaps the Chiefs are seeing that Remigio’s speed limitations lead to penalties because it takes him longer to reach his blockers. Hopefully, Smith will get more opportunities on punts and kickoffs as the season goes on. FoxBot2021 asks Will AP ever just be happy the team wins? Or will everything always be nitpicked because people wamt a “perfect victory”? A long time ago — in a Chiefs Kingdom that seems far, far away — I watched the 2002 squad steal a Week 1 victory because Cleveland Browns linebacker Dwayne Rudd threw his helmet in celebration before time expired and drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. An untimed down allowed a 30-yard game-winning field goal. When I see the current state of social media during Chiefs games, I wonder if we would even feel permitted to celebrate that moment if it happened today. My opinion is that now multiple generations have grown up playing Madden and believe that anything short of a three-touchdown margin of victory doesn’t truly count as a win. The truth is, the NFL is a tough business, and the margin between perceived good and bad teams is rarely as wide as fans believe. Players know how short their careers can be, and you should expect every team’s best shot every week. The first month of the season is increasingly unpredictable as teams enter the campaign with less preseason action than in previous generations. Several teams that entered 2026 with lofty expectations would have taken a tight overtime victory over how their own Week 2 contests went. Eight squads are 2-0, and the Chiefs are one of them. It would be naive to think there aren’t areas for improvement. But sometimes a game turns out closer than expected — and it’s ok just to be happy with the win. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with a road game in Miami on Sunday. Keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

full_text: Good morning, Chargers fans! Following the placement of Charlie Kolar and David Njoku on injured reserve this week, the Chargers are signing former Dolphins and 49er tight end Hayden Rucci to the active roster. He will join Oronde Gadsden II as the only two tight ends on the Chargers roster as of Wednesday morning. Rucci played his collegiate football at Wisconsin where he caught 17 career passes for 200 yards and one touchdown. At the NFL Combine, Rucci measured in at 6’5 and 247 pounds. He ran his 40 in 5.04 seconds, jumped 32 inches in the vertical, and had a short shuttle time of 4.40. In four career games played (all in 2025 with the Dolphins), Rucci played 39 total snaps. Most of those came as a run blocker (29) where he finished with an overall season run block grade of 56.6. And now for today’s links. title: Chargers Week 3 Power Rankings Roundup:
summary: A second consecutive loss to begin the season has the Chargers plummeting down power rankings even more this week. For the first time since Jim Harbaugh took over as head coach, you’re be hard-pressed to find an outlet that still views the Chargers as a top-20 team. How could they not, though? They’re one of […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Oronde Gadsden #86 of the Los Angeles Chargers completes a catch for a touchdown during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images A second consecutive loss to begin the season has the Chargers plummeting down power rankings even more this week. For the first time since Jim Harbaugh took over as head coach, you’re be hard-pressed to find an outlet that still views the Chargers as a top-20 team. How could they not, though? They’re one of the few 0-2 teams right now and the product on the field makes fans feel like they were hoodwinked all offseason. It’s preposterous that all of the highlight reels and hype from training camp was filled with that much smoke. It just doesn’t compute and it looks like the coaching staff feels almost shaken as the fan base. But luckily it’s a long season and while it doesn’t look very likely, there’s still a non-zero chance the Chargers can turn this around and become the team they were supposed to be. That’s enough hope to clean on to, right? …Right? ESPN – #22 “For the past two Sundays, this Chargers’ offense has looked like a unit that hadn’t practiced together before. Herbert looks lost and, at moments, angrier than he has ever been at the helm of a flat offense. He had three fumbles (all recovered) and two interceptions Sunday, though one was because of a dropped pass by tight end David Njoku. This new offense under coordinator Mike McDaniel was supposed to elevate this team into a championship contender. Instead, its star quarterback looks almost unrecognizable.” – Kris Rhim CBS Sports – #23 “They are in major trouble. They are 0-2 and face a brutal seven-game stretch that could have them out of the playoff race by midseason. Ouch.” – Pete Prisco theScore – #24 “It’s a long season. The Chargers have been football’s most disappointing team; even their best players have no answers for their offensive struggles. But there’s a lot of season left, and that should give L.A. fans some optimism despite a terrifying stretch from Weeks 3-10.” – theScore staff Bleacher Report – #25 “ There isn’t a team in the NFL that should be freaking out more two weeks into the season than the Los Angeles Chargers. Of that there is zero doubt. ” “ The Chargers were supposed to be contenders. And with two straight home games against perceived tomato cans, the Chargers were supposed to start the season hot. ” “Instead, the Chargers are winless. The offense hasn’t scored more than 14 points in a game. The defense has allowed 52 points to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders. ” “ Now? That soft schedule becomes Mortal Kombat “fatality” time. Between now and the bye, the Bolts face Buffalo and Seattle (both on the road) before hosting the Broncos and traveling to Arrowhead to face the Chiefs. ” “Given that schedule and what we have seen from this team to date in 2026, the Chargers may well be cooked by Halloween.” — Brad Davenport Pro Football Talk – #25 “At least they do really good schedule-release videos.” – Mike Florio The Athletic – #27 Rookie spotlight : Jake Slaughter It was a bad omen when free-agent center Tyler Biadasz suffered a torn ACL in training camp, thrusting Slaughter, a second-round pick, into the starting lineup for a team that was expected to contend. The Chargers’ collapse certainly hasn’t been his fault, but his presence in the lineup is more evidence (if we needed any) that this team is suffering through some kind of curse.“ – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall NFL.com – #29 I find it hard to believe that, after two weeks, the Chargers are here, below the Browns, Jets, Titans and Commanders. And yet, they haven’t played better than any of those teams to this point. Justin Herbert still rips a few beautiful throws per game, but there’s no telling whether his teammate on the receiving end will actually hang on to the ball. The mistakes and sloppiness on both sides — pre-snap penalties, dropped passes, fumbles, blown coverages — are too frequent, and this team looks nothing like one coached by a Harbaugh. Los Angeles was in position to win Sunday, and ended up losing by 12 to a Las Vegas team that won three games last year. There’s plenty to correct and a brutal schedule ahead for the Bolts, whose 0-2 start might only be the beginning of their problems.” – Nick Shook
author: Michael Peterson

title: Chargers-Raiders Winners/Losers: Omarion Hampton giveth then taketh away
summary: The Chargers are in a weird spot with their second-year running back. Omarion Hampton has arguably been the biggest bright spot of the offense through two games. But, he’s also turned the ball over twice in as many games. If I were to have predicted that Hampton and Justin Herbert would have a combined five […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Omarion Hampton #8 of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers are in a weird spot with their second-year running back. Omarion Hampton has arguably been the biggest bright spot of the offense through two games. But, he’s also turned the ball over twice in as many games. If I were to have predicted that Hampton and Justin Herbert would have a combined five turnovers through the team’s first two games, you would have laughed and said that’s just downright pesseimistic. Well, here we are. For the second week in a row, change and urgency are at the forefront of Week Three’s preparation. Unsurprisingly, there was once again more bad than good. Here are this week’s winners and losers from Sunday’s loss. Winners Chargers run defense The Chargers held Ashton Jeanty to a paltry 48 yards on 21 carries (2.3 YPC) and overall held the Raiders as a team to 2.0 yards per tote on 29 total attempts. The run defense has been a rare bright spot for the Chargers through two weeks, but it all means nothing if the secondary cannot find a way to hunker down on the backend to stop allowing explosive pass plays in critical moments. RB Omarion Hampton’s production I do want to give Hampton his flowers in some way because the Chargers offense would honestly look even worse if he wasn’t there to churn out the gritty yards on the ground. He finished Sunday with 115 yards of total offense (94 rushing, 21 receiving) and his second touchdown of the season. It’s early, but his current pace puts him at 1,164 rushing yards which would be the most by a Chargers running back in quite some time. Take away the fumbles and his pace would honestly be much more impressive, but this is reality of his situation. He has to eat those plays and get back to work. Losers RB Omarion Hampton’s ball security Hampton was picked in the first round of the 2025 NFL Draft for a reason. He’s a complete back who runs angry on every carry. He’s built to be a workhorse back in this league, but you can’t be a workhorse if you’re giving the ball away once a game. That’s exactly what Hampton has done by turning it over against both the Cardinals and Raiders. Even after having over 100 yards of offense and a touchdown on Sunday, the only thing people will remember about Hampton in that game was the lost fumble during a drive where the Chargers were down only three points with the ball marching across midfield. There was 3:52 on the clock in regulation. A touchdown on this drive, if the Chargers ate the clock behind Hampton, would have given them a 4-point lead and dumped all the pressure on Cousins and the Raiders to find the end zone with very little time remaining. It’s not just that the Chargers are turning the ball over in general, but also how and when they’re doing it. Each of Hampton’s fumbles came when the Chargers were within one score coming off a great defensive stop. This fumble came after they forced a three-and-out. That’s beyond inexcusable. S Genesis Smith A rough day for a rookie who likely played more snaps than he was prepared for. Smith was the culprit on the Raiders’ first touchdown of the game when he seemingly was one a separate page from R.J. Mickens while sitting in a two-deep look. On the play, wideout Tre Tucker stemmed vertically towards Smith who immediately opened his hips and allowed Tucker to gain inside leverage. When Tucker broke on his deep post route, Smith was already nowhere near able to make the play while Mickens was sitting on a deep comeback route on the other half of the field. It was an excellent play design by Klint Kubiak to beat that two-high look, but there also can’t be a world where it wasn’t a massive blown assignment, as well. Smith’s action were counterintuitive to any normal two-deep coverage. If anything, it looked like he thought they were rolling to a three-deep look due to him instantly opening up. On another player, the Raiders were facing a third-and-long. The Chargers came out in a Cover 4 look but rolled down into a Cover 3 with Smith as the down safety. At the snap, there are zero players in the middle of the field for the Chargers. Zero. Smith is the only player in this coverage that needed to drift down and be a centerfielder around the second level. When the ball was snapped, Smith just…didn’t move. He hugged the left hash and left a wide open throw on the right seam the Raiders used to convert on the money down. WR Quentin Johnston That 65-yard touchdown pass to Quentin Johnston from the preseason seems like a decade ago. After looking like he may be a perfect fit for McDaniel’s offense, Johnston has been one of the most disappointing pass-catchers through the first two games of the season. While currently leading the team in targets (11), Johnston only has three receptions for 24 yards, ranking T-5th, and 5th on the team, respectively. On Sunday, Johnston dropped a perfectly thrown Cover 2 hole shot by Herbert that would have been a chunk play at a time the team needed to build momentum. Other times through two games when he’s been targeted, it doesn’t look like he’s giving 100 percent effort, especially when he’s needed to come back to the football and outmuscle defensive backs. After two solid seasons for Johnston, this year could end up being a disastrous campaign for him if things continue. CB Cam Hart Hart may have intercepted a pass on Sunday, but it somehow did not make up for the rest of his day. After the Chargers defense got a much-needed stop on third down, Hart was flagged for illegal hands to the face which moved the chains for the Raiders. In coverage, Hart allowed three receptions on five targets for 60 yards, including the 42-yard with under a minute left that helped the Raiders kick a field goal before halftime. That helped break the 7-7 tie the Chargers just created and allowed Las Vegas to gain a ton of momentum heading into the break. Hart has been a solid player for the Chargers thus far in his young career, but Sunday’s showing was a low point against a team who entered the game with one of the worst receiver rooms in the entire league.
author: Michael Peterson

summary: Good morning, Chargers fans! At 0-2, the trajectory of the Bolts this season is firmly downward. full_text: NORMAN, OKLAHOMA - NOVEMBER 22: Defensive tackle David Stone #0 of the Oklahoma Sooners prepares to rush against the Missouri Tigers in the fourth quarter at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium on November 22, 2025 in Norman, Oklahoma. Oklahoma won 17-6. (Photo by Brian Bahr/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Chargers fans! At 0-2, the trajectory of the Bolts this season is firmly downward. A look at the league’s No. 1 most difficult schedule from Week Three on could very well turn in to a top-five pick in next year’s draft if things don’t take a drastic turn. However, this new updated 2027 mock draft from Yahoo Sports still has the Chargers picking at No. 17, meaning they believe the Bolts will settle in and finish with around 8-9 wins this year. That sounds like a miracle at the current moment, but something the fan base will surely take if they could have it. At pick No. 17, analyst Curt Popejoy has the Chargers selecting Oklahoma defensive tackle David Stone. Stone stands 6’3 and looks incredibly-lean for someone listed at 315 pounds. He has the mass to play anywhere along the interior of the line all while also offering the upside of a pass rush with his excellent get-off and notable length. Defensive tackle likely isn’t the position the Chargers will need to address the most come next year’s draft, but picking a blue-chip player at an impact position in today’s NFL is always a strong backup option if there is not an elite offensive lineman or skill player available when they’re on the clock. And now for today’s links. title: Brandin Cooks back in the NFC West
summary: Brandin Cooks was drafted in 2014 by the New Orleans Saints and at this point, Cooks is a veteran journeyman of the NFL. He’s play for the Saints, the New England Patriots, the Los Angeles Rams, the Houston Texans, the Dallas Cowboys, the Buffalo Bills (any teams I missed?), and he’s now signing to the […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 8: Wide receivers Brandin Cooks #3 of the Dallas Cowboys and Cooper Kupp #10 of the Los Angeles Rams talk on the field following a joint practice at Cowboys training camp on August 8, 2024 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brandin Cooks was drafted in 2014 by the New Orleans Saints and at this point, Cooks is a veteran journeyman of the NFL. He’s play for the Saints, the New England Patriots, the Los Angeles Rams, the Houston Texans, the Dallas Cowboys, the Buffalo Bills (any teams I missed?), and he’s now signing to the San Francisco 49ers practice squad. For Cooks and the Rams, it was a fairly successful stint. Heck, had he and the Rams won the Super Bowl in the 2018 season , Cooks may have been the MVP with over 100 receiving yards. Had Jared Goff and Cooks connected on a touchdown, who knows? Maybe Cooks spends more time with the Rams than he did. Maybe Goff does too. But the past can’t be changed, and instead, the Rams didn’t win that Super Bowl, Cooks seemed to get hurt often, and though Cooks was a solid Ram, he’s not likely to go down as an all-time great Ram. That being said. Cooks has put together a solid if not great NFL career in terms of production, longevity and as far I am aware he’s a drama free type player. There’s a lot to like about Cooks, and the 49ers are giving him a chance to compete in 2026. With the way the 49ers are looking right now who’s to say, maybe Cooks finds himself in another Super Bowl. We’ll see. Source: Niners signing veteran receiver Cooks to practice squad (espn.com) “Free agent wide receiver Brandin Cooks is signing with the San Francisco 49ers ‘ practice squad, initially to get up to speed for games, a source told ESPN’s Adam Schefter on Tuesday. Cooks, 32, joins a Niners team that has lost wideouts Ricky Pearsall , De’Zhaun Stribling and Demarcus Robinson to injury this season. Meanwhile, veteran wide receiver Mike Evans will need to be managed this week with a hip injury. Cooks was the 20th pick in the 2014 draft by the Saints out of Oregon State , and he spent the first three years of his career with New Orleans. He returned to the Saints in 2025 but was waived in November after he requested his release. Cooks then joined the Buffalo Bills for the remainder of the campaign” No QB has more games with 4-plus TD passes than Matthew Stafford since 2021 (ramswire) “On Monday night, the NFL’s reigning MVP, Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, was simply sensational, getting back to basics in his four-touchdown performance. Slicing and dicing the New York Giants ‘ defense, Stafford found Terrance Ferguson, Kyren Williams, and Davante Adams twice for his passing scores that led to a 28-6 win. According to Pro Football Focus, Stafford’s performance was his 10th game with at least four passing touchdowns since 2021, which is tied with Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott for the most within that timeframe. Of course, 2021 was his first year with the Rams.“ Rams WR Davante Adams Raises Fascinating Matthew Stafford-Sean McVay What-if (sports.yahoo) “During an appearance Tuesday on The Pat McAfee Show, future Pro Football Hall of Famer Adams wondered what it could have been like if Stafford and McVay had been together much longer on the same team. “If Matthew Stafford was here with Sean McVay for his whole career, they would be saying, ‘ Is this guy literally the best QB that’s ever played,” Adams said.“ Poona Ford and Aaron Donald are Rams’ perfect pairing up front (ramblinfan) “With Donald back in the rotation, Ford’s value to the defense has skyrocketed along with that of Kobie Turner and even Braden Fiske. While Donald commands offensive lines’ attention, LA finally has defenders who can make them pay for leaving them one-on-one. Ford is among them. Double teams smothered LA’s short nose tackle was smothered in the season opener. Conversely, when Ford lined up alongside Donald in Week 2, he was the one doing the smothering. While his 5-foot-11 frame may look like a liability, it affords him tremendous power and an unnaturally strong center of gravity. Even though Puka didn’t play last night, but Davante Adams did and played stellar. And Williams and Corum know how to do what the hell they do. title: Rams snap count review: Terrance Ferguson stakes a claim for TE#1
summary: Using a balanced offense and stifling defense, the Los Angeles Rams used the Monday Night Football platform to gain entry to the winning side of the ledger. L.A. knocked off the New York Giants by a 28-6 margin at SoFi Stadium. The Rams not only welcomed back Aaron Donald after a  two-year hiatus, but appear […]
full_text: Terrance Ferguson is ready for a breakout in his second season as a pro.(Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Using a balanced offense and stifling defense, the Los Angeles Rams used the Monday Night Football platform to gain entry to the winning side of the ledger. L.A. knocked off the New York Giants by a 28-6 margin at SoFi Stadium. The Rams not only welcomed back Aaron Donald after a two-year hiatus, but appear to have ushered in a new TE#1, Terrance Ferguson. The Rams opened the game in a two-tight end set and it was Ferguson and Davis Allen on the field. Ferguson went on to accumulate 36 snaps (58%) and six catches on nine targets. It wasn’t the sheer numbers that hint that he will be main tight end going forward, it was his role in the offense. L.A. deployed him inline, out of the slot, and in motion. He ran routes on over 70 percent of snaps and had a target share of 31 percent. After two weeks, Ferguson heads up the on it in routes run, target catches, yards, and touchdowns. While he did have a pair of dropped passes that must be cleaned up, Ferguson showed why the Rams drafted him in the top half of Round 2. He flashed his all-around skills, able to find the soft areas in the zone, catch the ball away from his body, and run after the catch. He’s definitely been working on blocking and it manifested with a solid effort. Fans have witnessed his abilities in the medium/deep areas of the field, Monday was time for work in the underneath/medium zones. Quarterback Matthew Stafford (62, 100%) I’ll be honest, those first few drives had me worried that “Bad Stafford” was going to show up and the Rams offense was going to be— force it in to Davante Adams and hope he makes the catch. But, Staff quickly righted the ship and ended up having a solid game, He jumped up the all-time charts for touchdown thrown (6th), most games with 4 TD’s thrown (6th), and most games with 300+ yards thrown (7th). Running back Kyren Williams (34, 55%) Blake Corum (28, 45%) If you set the fumbles aside, both had strong efforts. Williams consistently makes the first tackler miss in tight spaces. He did a good job of breaking plays outside for healthy gains. Corum’s burst really stands out and he runs with stellar vision. A solid one-two punch, but dammit, you gotta hold on to the football. Is there a RB controversy? Kyren Williams vs. Blake Corum through the 1st 2 weeks of the season, per @FantasyPtsData : Kyren + 51.1% RB rush share (excluding Ronnie Rivers garbage time) + 5 goal line touches (100% of snaps) + 54.8% route share (5 targets) + 11.4 XFP/G Corum + 48.9% RB rush share + 0 goal… — Dataroma (@ffdataroma) September 22, 2026 Wide receiver Davante Adams (40, 65%) Found the Fountain of MNF Youth. L.A. needed him to step up and he looked as if in his prime, just amazing route running and ability to high point the ball. Wish McVay would have fed him the ball a couple more times so that his personal best yards per game would be as a Ram. Konata Mumpfield (43, 69%) Very quiet, lot of reps with only two targets. Really made a run after catch effort on his single completion. Xavier Smith (26, 42%) One flat route target that should have been caught and a rough day getting any traction on returns. TuTu Atwell (11, 18%) Vintage TuTu, he runs a picture-perfect out route and gets his feet down for a catch on the sideline, then runs a fly where the pass is mis-fired, and completely disappears after that. Welcome back. Tight end Colby Parkinson (44, 71%) Kind of a quiet evening considering he was on the field almost 3/4 of the offensive snaps. Targeted twice on short passes and made both catches. Davis Allen (32, 52%) The dirty work guy, in the game on multiple tight end sets. He he’s really improved his blocking and was rewarded with a late game target, which he converted. Tyler Higbee (16, 28%) Simply not much for left him anymore. Insurance, I guess. Offensive line Alaric Jackson, Steve Avila, Coleman Shelton, Kevin Dotson, Warren McClendon (62, 100%) Strong effort by the big guys up front. They dominated the line of scrimmage, consistently opening run lanes to the tune of 165 total yards at 5.8 per tote. They allowed one sack where the defender split a double team, but overall, only allowed a pass rush pressure rate of 15 percent, one of the lowest Stafford has faced since joining the Rams in 2021. Rams OL PFF Grades in Week 2: Alaric Jackson – 81.2 PBLK | 77.4 RBLK Steve Avila – 74.8 | 77.4 Kevin Dotson – 64.4 | 68.3 Warren McClendon – 63.6 | 66.3 Coleman Shelton – 33.0 | 74.0 — Blaine Grisak (@BGMediaOnSI) September 22, 2026 Special teams Ethan Evans, Joe Cardona, Harrison Meevis New season, same old special teams output. Harrumph!! Hopefully, Meevis got that miss out of his system. He’s been solid over a short sample, not time to worry, yet. Defensive line Aaron Donald (33, 57%) The crowd went wild upon his entry, and so did opposing offensive blocking plans. To no one’s surprise, the “AD effect” was in full force on Day 1. Donald drew the attention of double-team blocking at a rate of 39% on 19 pass plays. Although he only accrued one pressure, he had a 28 percent pass rush win rate and a get-off rate 0.75 seconds, third best across the NFL for the season. Against 14 run plays, he booked three tackles with one for loss. That tackle for loss tied him for 4th place on the all-time list at 177. Kobie Turner (34, 59%) Tyler Davis (23, 40%) B raden Fiske (30, 52%) Poona Ford (18, 31%) Ty Hamilton (8, 14%) Stellar performance by the defensive interior. No single effort really stood out, mostly because all played so well. Maybe not enough reps to go around magnifies the hustle and effort. Edge Byron Young (41, 71%) Strong effort for Young, Pro Football Network gave him an 80.7 impact score. He not only pressured from outside, but was employed in numerous loops, which fit his athleticism and burst . He logged a sack and three quarterback hits. Josaiah Stewart (46, 79%) I was hoping Stewart would step up and stand out. A quiet outing. Wesley Bailey (19, 33%) Good to see the undrafted rookie competitive in his first pro action and he got a hustle sack to boot. I thought he clearly outplayed Johnson in the preseason and now doubling his snap count, makes a case for E#4. Desjuan Johnson (10, 17%) As of now there are snaps to go around, but when Myles Garrett returns, a decision will have to be made. Will Johnson be able to hold onto his place in the rotation, or be limited to mop up duty? Off-ball linebacker Nate Landman (49, 84%) Omar Speights (25, 43%) Both played as well as can be expected. Speights reps were down just a little from Week 1. Interestingly, Shaun Dolac did not get a single defensive snap. Safety Kamren Curl (58, 100%) On the Giants first possession of the game, they were in Rams territory and completed a short flat pass, Curl triggered downhill and made a stellar open-field tackle. If he misses, it’s a big play and the GMen are in the red zone. Instead it’s third and eight, Dart is injured dropping back to pass on the very next play. The game would have been very different had Curl missed that tackle. Quentin Lake (58, 100%) Played more of a true safety role and was solid. I think he’s at his best in this role, making tackles and coming downhill in coverage rather trying to stay attached to more athletic receivers Jaylen McCollough (30, 52%) Recipient of the reps that would have went to Kamren Kinchens, although the Rams defensive braintrust most often uses McCollough as a pseudo-linebacker, subbing in on the second line of defense on passing downs (Speights, usually). Didn’t stand out on my radar. Cornerback Trent McDuffie (58, 100%) L.A. is certainly getting their money’s worth from this big bucks capital outlay. Love his willingness in run fits. The Rams are primarily using him where he’s at his best, in man-to-man from both the slot and outside and he’s showing very sticky coverage from both. The Rams game plan had McDuffie shadowing the Giants…

title: Should Blake Corum be Rams RB1?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have a legitimate decision to make in their backfield. Kyren Williams remains the starter and has continued to produce, but Blake Corum is making a strong case for a larger role after two games. In Monday night’s 28-6 win over the New York Giants, both backs received exactly 12 carries. Williams […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - September 21:Rams Blake Corum (24) runs for yards as Giants Jevon Holland (8) and Tyler Nubin (27) defend on the play during first quarter action at SoFi Stadium on Monday, September 21, 2026. (Photo by David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams have a legitimate decision to make in their backfield. Kyren Williams remains the starter and has continued to produce, but Blake Corum is making a strong case for a larger role after two games. In Monday night’s 28-6 win over the New York Giants, both backs received exactly 12 carries. Williams finished with 85 yards, while Corum recorded 79 yards and added 13 receiving yards. The production is similar. The skill sets are not. Discussion #1: Running Ability – Speed/Agility Williams has proven that he can be an effective NFL running back. He consistently finds production and has been an important part of Sean McVay’s offense. However, there are times when Williams appears to lack an extra gear. He can be hesitant to hit a running lane, giving defenders time to close the gap. When the Rams create an opening, Corum appears more willing to attack it quickly. That’s where Corum’s explosiveness becomes intriguing. Corum averaged 6.6 yards per carry against New York and had a long run of 18 yards. Williams averaged 7.1 yards per carry with a 20-yard long, so the numbers don’t tell the entire story. Corum’s combination of acceleration, agility and elusiveness gives the Rams another dimension. He has the ability to make the first defender miss and turn a relatively small crease into a chunk play. Blake Corum was top 5 in the NFL in yards/carry last season for running backs with 100+ carries Picking up where he left off averaging 6.0 yards/carry the first to weeks of this season pic.twitter.com/GNbRwDixNo — Jake B 〽️ (@MichFootballBEL) September 22, 2026 The Rams don’t necessarily need to move away from Williams entirely. But Corum has shown enough to warrant consideration for a larger share of early-down carries. Advantage: Corum Discussion #2: Passing Game This is another area where Corum could provide something unique. Corum only caught one pass against the Giants, but he turned it into 13 yards. McVay could potentially expand Corum’s role through the screen game. Getting Corum into space with blockers in front of him could maximize his agility and acceleration. Rather than asking him to consistently create yards against a loaded box, the Rams could manufacture opportunities where his elusiveness becomes the primary advantage. A more prominent screen-game role could also force defenses to account for Corum differently when he enters the game. Blake Corum with the 13-yard catch and run to put the Rams in scoring position! @NYGvsLAR on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/me17vK64uc — NFL (@NFL) September 22, 2026 In fairness to Williams, the value he brings to the table in the passing game is as a blocker for Matthew Stafford in the pocket. Williams is not afraid to stick his nose in against a linebacker in order to protect his quarterback. To me, the scenario that makes sense here is to let Corum be used in first and second downs; providing a run:pass balance (again – using the screen game potentially on 2nd down), while Kyren works in a third down role. Advantage: Split Discussion #3” Ball Security This is where the argument for giving Corum more opportunities becomes even more interesting. Williams lost a fumble against the Giants, giving New York a short field that resulted in a field goal. One fumble doesn’t erase Williams’ production, but ball security has been a recurring concern. Williams is the NFL RB leader in fumbles lost since 2023, and Monday night’s turnover added another entry to that total. Rams RB career fumbles: Kyren Williams: 10 Blake Corum: 0 pic.twitter.com/dovxuRRFTH — Yahoo Fantasy Sports (@YahooFantasy) September 22, 2026 For a Rams offense that expects to compete in close games, possessions matter. Giving the ball away can completely change the complexion of a game. We have seen firsthand how Kyren’s ball security has hurt Los Angeles. 2024 vs. PHI. 2024 @ PHI (divisional). 2025 vs. SF. Corum also fumbled against New York, but he was able to recover his blunder. That means ball security isn’t necessarily a completely one-sided argument. But Williams’ history makes the issue particularly noteworthy. Advantage: Corum Conclusion Perhaps the answer isn’t simply Kyren Williams or Blake Corum. The Rams could potentially maximize both players by giving them different responsibilities. Blake Corum could be the RB1 on first and second down. His speed, agility, decisiveness and explosive potential could give the Rams a different element early in the series. He could attack running lanes, create yards after contact and be utilized in the screen game. Kyren Williams could then become the primary third-down back while also spelling Corum at various times on first and second down if he is the hot hand. This change means that Williams is not removed from the offense but simply reconfiguring their approach for using the tandem. It would mean the Rams are using both backs according to their strengths. After two weeks, Corum has already demonstrated that he can produce when given opportunities. The next step may be finding out what happens when the Rams give him more of them.

title: Rams Power Rankings roundup: L.A. drops despite dominant performance
summary: After a dominant performance over the New York Giants, the results are surprisingly mixed in terms of the Los Angeles Rams’ movement in this sample of NFL power rankings. In three instances, the Rams rose in the rankings; in three others, they dropped, while two remained unchanged. This sample of eight sites seems to represent […]
full_text: After a dominant performance over the New York Giants, the results are surprisingly mixed in terms of the Los Angeles Rams’ movement in this sample of NFL power rankings. In three instances, the Rams rose in the rankings; in three others, they dropped, while two remained unchanged. This sample of eight sites seems to represent the consensus and the average ranking of these eight prognosticators is 5.75, which is a slight increase over last week. Pete Prisco : Dropped from 5 to 8 “They bounce back in a big way against the Giants. The offense came alive, which it had to do.” Fox Sports Ralph Vacchiano : Held at 5 “OK, so maybe it was the jet lag in Week 1. The Giants were no match after Jaxson Dart’s injury, but the Rams have at least started to flex their superteam muscles with an impressive performance on Monday night.” NFL.com Nick Shook : Dropped from 7 to 8 “Without Myles Garrett and Puka Nacua, the Rams entered Week 2 with less fanfare and a lingering, bitter taste in their mouths from the season-opening loss in Australia. Both absences didn’t end up mattering much. Matthew Stafford and Davante Adams rekindled their productive connection, lighting up New York’s defense and running away with a win over a Giants team that lost Jaxson Dart on Drive No. 1.“ Mike Florio PFT : Up from 11 to 9 “Fortunately, they didn’t fly back from Australia the day before the Week 2 game.” USA Today Nate Davis : Up from 5 to 4 “Throwback uniforms, throwback DPOY. Forthcoming coach . All seems well after their Week 1 mulligan .“ SI Conor Orr : Up from 7 to 5 “There is nothing like not playing in Australia, is what I always say. In all seriousness, I think that everyone posting “Aaron Donald looks gassed” online are going to be among the silliest looking internet humans in our universe four weeks from now. He got so much better even over the course of this game. Myles Garrett can’t return soon enough.“ NFL Trade Rumors Ethan Woodie : held at 2 “LA’s defense was absolutely dominant, with CB Trent McDuffie making multiple huge plays, and DT Aaron Donald returning to the field for the first time after two years of retirement.” ESPN : Dropped from 4 to 5 “One thing we know about the QB1: Matthew Stafford is still capable of playing at an MVP level. Stafford and the Rams’ offense struggled in the season opener, but wide receiver Davante Adams said the team’s Week 2 offensive performance was closer to what the group expects to look like this season. On Monday night against the Giants, Stafford, the reigning MVP, completed 22 of 31 passes for 327 yards with four touchdown passes and an interception. He had that success without wide receiver Puka Nacua, who is dealing with soreness in his groin. — Sarah Barshop” Another strong showing against Denver in week three should have them trending in the right direction.
