full_text: Old friends will cross paths when the New England Patriots and Jacksonville Jaguars do so at EverBank Stadium. And not just offensive line coach Doug Marrone. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold for Sunday have been members of both locker rooms during their NFL careers. Here’s a glance through the list of former Patriots and former Jaguars leading up to the 1 p.m. ET kickoff. JACKSONVILLE Jakobi Meyers, wide receiver — Entering the NFL as an undrafted rookie out of North Carolina State in 2019, Meyers tallied 235 receptions for 2,758 yards and eight touchdowns across 60 games and 39 starts with the Patriots. The ex-quarterback threw a pair of touchdowns, received the club’s Ed Block Courage Award, and led the offense in receiving yards in back-to-back-to-back seasons. He departed for the Las Vegas Raiders as an unrestricted free agent 2023 and was sent to the AFC South at the trade deadline last November in exchange for the No. 117 and No. 182 overall picks in the 2026 draft class. A three-year, $60 million extension followed for the eventual Jaguars team captain. Since leaving Foxborough, Meyers has caught 236 passes for 2,737 yards and 16 touchdowns across 49 games and 46 starts. The 29-year-old wideout has had a hand in additional three scores as a rusher and passer. Jahlani Tavai, linebacker — After five seasons, the Patriots released Tavai ahead of the new league year. The 29-year-old linebacker had been under contract through 2027 after signing an extension that carried a $16 million base value. First landing in Foxborough as a member of the practice squad in 2021 after being waived by the Detroit Lions, Tavai went on to appear in 76 games, starting 51. The University of Hawaii product logged 350 tackles and 3.5 sacks while intercepting three passes and forcing three fumbles. He saw 2,606 snaps on defense and 1,293 snaps on special teams and was named New England’s recipient Ed Block Courage Award on the way to Super Bowl LX. The No. 43 overall pick in the 2019 NFL draft agreed to terms with the Jaguars amid training camp in August and stands four tackles into his stay on the active roster. NEW ENGLAND Chandler Brayboy, wide receiver — The Patriots added Brayboy to the practice squad following a workout midway through September. The 25-year-old wide receiver made his first NFL stop in Jacksonville. Signed by the Jaguars as an undrafted free agent in 2025, Brayboy spent the duration of his rookie year on the practice squad. After being retained on a futures contract in January, he was waived at the cutdown deadline in August. A former FCS All-American, CAA Special Teams Player of the Year and Elon team captain, Brayboy’s collegiate career spanned 2,660 receiving yards, 245 rushing yards, 1,568 kickoff return yards and 22 all-purpose touchdowns over the course of 55 games dating back to 2019. Greg Van Roten, guard — The Patriots hosted Van Roten on a visit during the first week of August. And after attrition hit New England’s offensive line in the preseason opener, the 36-year-old free agent circled back on a one-year deal to shore up the interior depth. He took over at right guard last week after tenured starter Mike Onwenu was carted off due to a broken ankle. A veteran of 146 games, including 105 starts, Van Roten began his career as an undrafted rookie in 2012. The former All-Ivy League offensive tackle out of Penn has since made stops with nine different NFL clubs. Count the Jaguars among the previous. Van Roten joined Jacksonville during the 2017 offseason on the heels of a CFL run with the Toronto Argonauts, yet was cut amid organized team activities that spring before playing a down. His career now stretches 6,938 offensive downs. Ironman campaigns arrived in 2024 and 2025.

title: Patriots host 2 safeties on tryouts after Craig Woodson, Dell Pettus injuries
summary: After losing both Craig Woodson and Dell Pettus to injuries during their Week 2 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers, the New England Patriots have brought in a pair of safeties on a tryout basis. Free agents Darren Hall and Malik Spencer both were in town on Tuesday, per the NFL transactions wire. Hall, 26, entered […]
full_text: After losing both Craig Woodson and Dell Pettus to injuries during their Week 2 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers, the New England Patriots have brought in a pair of safeties on a tryout basis. Free agents Darren Hall and Malik Spencer both were in town on Tuesday, per the NFL transactions wire. Hall, 26, entered the NFL as a fourth-round draft pick out of San Diego State in 2021. A career journeyman, the 6-foot-0, 195-pounder started out in Atlanta before stints in Indianapolis and Arizona. He later re-joined all three of those teams, including a return to the Falcons earlier this year. However, he was later placed on injured reserve and eventually released with a settlement. In total, Hall has appeared in 48 games with 12 starts. Spencer, 23, was an undrafted free agent earlier this year. The Michigan State product, who played in 38 games with 29 starts as a Spartan, spent his summer with the Commanders. He played in two preseason games before a hamstring injury landed him on injured reserve. The 6-foot-1, 191-pound defender was let go with a settlement earlier this month. The tryouts come in the aftermath of an injury-filled victory over the Steelers on Sunday. Woodson and Pettus were among a group of players unable to finish , with the former suffering a shoulder injury and the latter hurting his ankle. With them out, the team used a safety pairing of regular starter Kevin Byard and late-summer trade acquisition Jaylen Reed to close out the 20-3 win. In addition to those two, the Patriots also have Mike Brown and Elliott Davison as depth safeties on their practice squad. Head coach Mike Vrabel anticipated earlier this week that both might see increased opportunities leading up to the game against the Jaguars on Sunday. The Patriots’ Week 3 game in Jacksonville is schedule to kick off 1 p.m. ET on Sunday, Sept. 27.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: What placing Mike Onwenu on injured reserve means for the Patriots
summary: Two days after he left the New England Patriots’ win over the Pittsburgh Steelers on a cart, Mike Onwenu has officially been placed on injured reserve. As a consequence, he will miss at least the next four games. The nature of his ailment — reported as a fractured right ankle — is likely to keep […]
full_text: Two days after he left the New England Patriots’ win over the Pittsburgh Steelers on a cart, Mike Onwenu has officially been placed on injured reserve . As a consequence, he will miss at least the next four games. The nature of his ailment — reported as a fractured right ankle — is likely to keep him out longer than that and possibly end his season. In a follow-up move, the Patriots promoted punter Mitch Wishnowsky from the practice squad to the 53-man roster. Here is what Tuesday’s transactions mean for the team from a big-picture perspective. No surprises Coming out of Sunday’s game, Onwenu finding his way to injured reserve was the expected outcome. The injury itself and subsequently-reported diagnosis made this clear pretty quickly, and head coach Mike Vrabel also suggested as much when speaking to the media on Monday. “I don’t think he’ll be available here in the short term,” Vrabel said at the time. “I wouldn’t anticipate him being out there here in the next few weeks.” From that perspective, New England pulled no surprises out of its transactional bag on Tuesday because the follow-up was also bound to happen. Wishnowsky spent the first two weeks of the season on the practice squad, only to be standard-elevated for both games. With only one such elevation remaining for the 34-year-old, however, the Patriots had to make a move at some point. Regular punter Bryce Baringer, after all, will be out for two more games at least while himself on IR. Replacement wanted When Onwenu left the Steelers game in the late first quarter, the Patriots inserted veteran Greg Van Roten as their new right guard. His debut had its ups and downs, but the 36-year-old seems poised to remain in the lineup between center Jared Wilson and right tackle Morgan Moses for the time being. “I think he had a few plays that he’d like to have back, so would everybody,” said Vrabel about Van Roten on Monday. “But I thought he had some positive plays. To go through an entire game, there are going to be some good ones, some bad ones and some that we have to eliminate. I think that he stepped in there, was ready to go. Then we’ll have to figure out who’s the next guy, and if it is Greg, make sure that he’s as ready to go to work with Morgan and Jared as possible.” The trickle-down effect of Onwenu moving to IR will not be felt only at the starter level, though. Promoting Van Roten in his place means that the team is now down to Ben Brown as its lone interior offensive backup. And while first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu showed some inside/out versatility in training camp, he has been “trying to predominantly practice, be there, be ready to go playing tackle,” according to Vrabel. Other depth options available include tackle/guard hybrid Walter Rouse, who joined the team via trade ahead of roster cutdowns, as well as practice squadders Jake Kubas and Xavier Newman-Johnson. Uncertain future Mike Vrabel refrained from ruling Onwenu out for the remainder of the season on Monday, but the ankle injury that has now landed him on injured reserve is a serious matter. The 28-year-old staying sidelined for the rest of 2026 would not necessarily be a shocking development; on the contrary, a return at some point this season should be seen as a surprise. This does not just mean his short-term future is uncertain, however, but his long-term outlook as well. Onwenu is in the final year of his contract, a deal he renegotiated over the offseason to sacrifice total compensation for a more favorable package of guarantees. Still, he is on track to enter the open market in six months. IR keeps growing With Onwenu now on injured reserve, the list continues to grow . Eight players are currently on it, and that is not including players such as running backs Jam Miller and Terrell Jennings, who were sent to IR at one point but have since been let go with a settlement . Injured reserve (8): RB Myles Montgomery (39 | season-ending), WR A.J. Brown (1), WR Jeremiah Webb (29 | season-ending), TE Julian Hill (80 | season-ending), OT Marcus Bryant (52), RG Mike Onwenu (71), LB Khalil Jacobs (59), P Bryce Baringer (17) Out of the eight on IR, three — Myles Montgomery, Jeremiah Webb, Julian Hill — are done for the season unless also getting released with settlements at some point. The other five are all theoretically in a position to return later in the year. For some such as A.J. Brown, however, the outlook is much more positive than for Onwenu. Cap space decrease As with most NFL transactions, Tuesday’s also have an impact on New England’s salary cap space. According to Miguel Benzan (@patscap), the Patriots lost $955,555 by moving Onwenu to injured reserve, promoting Wishnowsky, and signing tight end Tanner Conner to the practice squad. This leaves the team with just under $6.5 million in available cap space, and a combined $51.1 million in cap commitments currently on IR.

full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; A New England Patriots fan cheers during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Bob DeChiara-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The good news is that the Patriots won on Sunday! It’s a game Aaron Rodgers is still Pondering as he took quite a few Spillanes. After taking seven hits, including four sacks, he probably felt like a Jacas and headed over to the nearest Barmore afterwards. He certainly didn’t Ellissit any sympathy, even if a Farmer was needed to plow him off the turf. I’ll stop now. Guess who didn’t think the Week 2 win was worth celebrating? Local sports talk radio (as usual) and a good number of the experts below. In fact the Pats should be thanking Old Man Rodgers for the win. All are very concerned about Drake Maye’s “slump”, loss of “accuracy”, and the “disjointed” offense that still needs to be “figured out”. All valid criticisms, but it’s always a good thing to get the W while cleaning up the early-season kinks. In Week 3 the Patriots head to Jacksonville as 2.5 point underdogs to the 1-1 Jaguars. The Jags opened with a 34-10 home win over the Browns in Week 1, then lost 20-13 at Denver in Week 2 after blowing a 13-3 third-quarter lead. This won’t be an easy ride, as QB Trevor Lawrence is a lot quicker than Aaron Rodgers, but I believe the Patriots catch a win Sunday to return home 2-1. GO PATS!! Around the AFC East: Buffalo Bills (2-0) vs. Los Angeles Chargers (0-2) New England Patriots (1-1) at Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1) New York Jets (1-1) at Detroit Lions (1-1) Miami Dolphins (0-2) vs. Kansas City Chiefs (2-0) AFC Matchups: Cincinnati Bengals (2-0) at Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1) Las Vegas Raiders (2-0) at New Orleans Saints (1-1) Baltimore Ravens (1-1) at Dallas Cowboys (1-1) Denver Broncos (1-1) vs. Los Angeles Rams (1-1) Tennessee Titans (0-2) at New York Giants (1-1) Houston Texans (0-2) at Indianapolis Colts (0-2) Cleveland Browns (1-1) vs. Carolina Panthers (1-1) 7th – Vinnie Iyer (Sporting News): The Patriots were bound to lean more on the running game and defense early with A.J. Brown’s injury limiting the passing potential of the Drake Maye offense. Mike Vrabel turned well to that game plan with big results against another one of his former teams, the Steelers . [+2] 7th – Nate Davis (USA Today): If you hadn’t heard, lifelong Seahawks fan Macklemore will not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium this week. The Pats have now won seven in a row … against teams not based in the Pacific Northwest . [+3] 7th – Ian Glendon (Full Press Coverage): The defense should collect the offense’s paycheck. Holding Pittsburgh to three points restored order. New England slips because unbeaten teams climbed past it; the offense still has to contribute more consistently . [-1] 10th – NFL Nation (ESPN): One thing we know about the QB1: Drake Maye’s accuracy isn’t what he’s accustomed to. After leading the NFL with a 72% completion percentage in 2025, Maye has completed 67.3% of his throws through two games — with one touchdown pass and four interceptions. Those performances came against two of the league’s top defenses (Seahawks and Steelers), but Maye isn’t satisfied with his performance. “It starts with me making good decisions, being in good plays,” he said . — Mike Reiss [nc] 11th – Frank Schwab (Yahoo! Sports): The Patriots won and they got some downfield passing going, but Drake Maye is still in a slump. He didn’t throw a touchdown Sunday and had only 208 yards. His Week 1 struggles can be excused because the Seahawks’ defense is incredible. The Steelers’ defense isn’t on that level and the Patriots were still underwhelming on offense. The Patriots are still figuring out their receiver rotation without A.J. Brown, but the passing offense needs to do more. Maye is 19th in adjusted EPA per play and 10th in success rate, which isn’t that bad considering half of his season so far was against Seattle, but it’s nowhere near his MVP form of last season . [nc] 11th – Ralph Vacchiano (FOX Sports): Take the win and thank old man Aaron Rodgers for that. For the second straight week, quarterback Drake Maye did not look good . [-1] 14th – Pete Prisco (CBS Sports): The defense came up big in the victory over the Steelers to get them to 1-1. The offense still looks disjointed at times . [+5] 14th – Mike Florio (ProFootballTalk): At this rate, they won’t have to worry about a difficult negotiation with Drake Maye in 2027 . [-1] 15th – Conor Orr (SI): We can wait until the Drake Maye and Patriots offensive line drama plays itself out. Spoiler, I don’t think there’s going to be much drama. The Patriots’ offensive line is okay, but much worse in the interim now that Mike Onwenu has broken his ankle. Maye is going to stop pressing and do his best Joe Burrow impression from the pocket. But the story of this team at the moment is just how dominant Christian Gonzalez has been . [-4] 18th – Nick Shook (NFL.com): It’s strange to have the Patriots stuck in the bottom half of the rankings after a win, but it’s also jarring to see New England’s offense struggle to find a consistent pulse. Drake Maye isn’t playing as poorly as his stat line suggests and still dropped a few dimes against the Steelers, but he’s also not operating comfortably in the offense, which lost right guard Mike Onwenu to an ankle injury on Sunday. If Maye’s not right, Sundays are going to be a chore for this group until he improves. The defense deserves a hat tip, though; it reduced Pittsburgh’s offense to rubble in Week 2 . title: Patriots place Mike Onwenu on injured reserve amid series of moves entering Week 3
summary: After being carted off in the first quarter of the home opener at Gillette Stadium, Mike Onwenu’s move has now become official. Onwenu, 28, sustained a broken right ankle 15 offensive snaps into Sunday’s 20-3 […]
full_text: After being carted off in the first quarter of the home opener at Gillette Stadium, Mike Onwenu’s move has now become official. The New England Patriots placed the starting right guard on injured reserve amid a series of transactions announced Tuesday afternoon. Onwenu, 28, sustained a broken right ankle 15 offensive snaps into Sunday’s 20-3 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. The injury arrived at the 1:08 mark in the opening quarter on a sack split between outside linebacker T.J. Watt and defensive tackle Derrick Harmon. Quickly ruled out after being taken to the locker room, he was replaced on the interior line by veteran August signing Greg Van Roten. Selected in the sixth round of the 2020 NFL draft at No. 182 overall, Onwenu’s tenure in Foxborough has spanned 100 games in the regular season. A former PFWA All-Rookie honoree, the 6-foot-3, 350-pound Michigan Wolverines product stands with 92 starts and 5,660 offensive snaps in his versatile Patriots career. “Again, I don’t think he’ll be available here in the short term,” head coach Mike Vrabel said during his Monday press conference when asked whether Onwenu’s injury would be season-ending. “So, I wouldn’t anticipate him being out there here in the next few weeks. If that changes and it ends up being longer than that, then we will let you guys know.” The organization promoted punter Mitch Wishnowsky to the 53-man roster and signed tight end Tanner Conner to the practice squad in corresponding moves. Wishnowsky, 34, reverted to the practice squad on Monday after serving as a standard elevation for the second time in as many weeks. The veteran right-footed specialist has averaged 45.3 yards per punt and 41.5 net yards per punt with no touchbacks through eight opportunities. He has doubled as New England’s holder in the absence of incumbent punter Bryce Baringer, who was placed on injured reserve following the league’s 53-man roster deadline in August and will miss at least two more games. Signed to the practice squad at its formation, the 6-foot-2, 220-pound Wishnowsky stands 107 games into his NFL career with 352 punts for 16,182 yards and a long of 74. The former Ray Guy Award winner out of Australia, Santa Barbara City College and the University of Utah entered the league in the fourth round of the 2019 draft at No. 110 overall. He spent six campaigns with the San Francisco 49ers before making stops with the Washington Commanders and Buffalo Bills. Conner, 28, takes the open spot on New England’s 17-man practice squad after being among a group of tight ends in for workouts to begin the week. The 6-foot-3, 240-pound Idaho State alum headed into the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2022. He made the Miami Dolphins’ initial active roster as rookie and went on to appear in 33 games during his first stint in the AFC East. Finishing 2025 on the practice squad of the New York Giants before being released in August, Conner has caught 12 passes for 107 yards across 251 snaps on offense and 413 snaps on special teams in his career. The Jacksonville Jaguars host next Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET kickoff at EverBank Stadium.

full_text: The New England Patriots entered their Week 2 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers with the task of replacing A.J. Brown, who had suffered a high-ankle sprain in the season opener. Among the candidates to fill Brown’s spot as a starting outside receiver was second-year man Kyle Williams, the speedster who looked good in preseason and entered the year poised for a bigger role. He keeps waiting for it, however. Versus Pittsburgh, after all, Williams’ role remained unchanged: he served as a rotational package player on offense, taking the. field for just 11 of 55 offensive snaps — a similar share than last week versus the Seahawks. Williams did manage to reel in a 10-yard pass on a 3rd-and-6 in the third quarter for his first catch of the season, but other than that and an incomplete target in the fourth period was quiet. To replace Brown, the Patriots instead relied on a three-receiver package of Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Mack Hollins. It was the same grouping they used down the stretch in Week 1. Even though the season is still long and Brown reportedly expected to miss five more games after this one, it seems Williams’ position on the depth chart is set in stone for now. Here is our full snap count report from the Patriots’ 20-3 win at Gillette Stadium . The most significant was starting right guard Mike Onwenu, who exited the game in the late first quarter due to what was later reported as a broken ankle. With him out, veteran Greg Van Roten — who arrived in training camp — was moved into the top lineup between center Jared Wilson and right tackle Morgan Moses. The other injury was suffered by rookie tight end Eli Raridon, who suffered a tight injury in the first half and was later ruled out for the remainder of the game. This means increased opportunities for Cameron Latu, another late addition to the roster. Latu played his first 14 snaps on offense against the Steelers, primarily serving as an in-line run blocker. Speaking of firsts, Caleb Lomu also played his first offensive snaps. The first-round draft pick replaced the aforementioned Morgan Moses for the final four snaps of the game. As opposed to Onwenu and Raridon, Moses was not removed from the game due to injury. Elsewhere on offense, TreVeyon Henderson out-snapped Rhamondre Stevenson following the latter’s first-quarter fumble. Under normal circumstances, Craig Woodson would have played more than his 46 snaps, but the shoulder injury he suffered in the third quarter forced him to exit the contest. The nominal next man up, Dell Pettus, had already exited the game at that point: Pettus suffered an ankle ailment in the second period. This meant that Jaylen Reed saw his first defensive snaps since arriving in Foxborough via trade in late August. The team also had to rely on its youth on the edge. With Dre’Mont Jones being lost for the game in the second quarter, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas ended up playing 54 and 49 snaps, respectively. In the meantime, Qunitayvious Hutchins also saw his first career reps on defense. The same was true for Channing Canada, who briefly replaced fellow cornerback Marcus Jones in the late second quarter. Outside of his brief injury scare, however, Jones was on the field for every snap; with Carlton Davis inactive due to injury, the Patriots made the veteran slot their No. 2 cornerback opposite Christian Gonzalez. In base sets, he lined up outside while kicking in in nickel and dime looks while Charles Woods was brought onto the field. Latu, Obiazor, Muasau and Jacas all registered tackles among them, with the latter adding his special teams performance to an already strong defensive showing. New England’s injuries also impacted the kicking game personnel. One position stands out in that regard: Dell Pettus (1), Craig Woodson (2) and Jaylen Reed (1) all saw snaps as the personal punt protector. full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Mark Andrews #89 of the Baltimore Ravens is tackled by Pete Werner #20 of the New Orleans Saints during the first quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images New Orleans Saints linebacker Pete Werner entered the 2026 season with a bigger role potentially waiting for him. For the first time in his career, Werner is playing without Demario Davis beside him. After spending years alongside one of the most important leaders on the Saints’ defense, Werner now has an opportunity to establish himself as one of the veteran leaders of the unit alongside Kaden Elliss. Through two games, he is making the most of that opportunity. Werner delivered an impressive performance in Sunday’s 24-17 win over the Baltimore Ravens, finishing with team-high 11 total tackles, including eight solo tackles. He also recorded a sack, three total pressures, a tackle for loss and a defensive stop. His impact as a pass rusher was particularly encouraging, as he earned a 79.6 pass-rush grade from Pro Football Focus. Werner’s performance came at an important time for New Orleans. The Saints trailed 14-3 at one point during the game, but the defense settled down and played a major role in helping complete the comeback. Baltimore managed just three points after halftime as New Orleans flipped the game. Werner was consistently around the football throughout the afternoon. Much like he was in the season opener agains the Detroit Lions. So far, he has shown that he is capable of taking on the increased responsibility. His ability to contribute against the run while also making an impact as a pass rusher gives New Orleans another versatile piece to build around. It is still early, but Werner is off to a strong start in his sixth season and looks to be drifting away from the inconsistency that plagued the early years of his career. The Saints may no longer have his mentor beside him, but Werner is showing that he is ready for breakout season.

title: Saints vs. Ravens: Game MVP
summary: The Saints pulled off the biggest upset of the football weekend, proving the old saying, “On any given Sunday, any team can beat any other team.” The Saints went into Baltimore as 8.5-point underdogs and won by 7 points. A game like that requires several players to play above expectations, and several of them did […]
full_text: The Saints pulled off the biggest upset of the football weekend, proving the old saying, “On any given Sunday, any team can beat any other team.” The Saints went into Baltimore as 8.5-point underdogs and won by 7 points. A game like that requires several players to play above expectations, and several of them did exactly that. Here are a few worth mentioning. Chase Young is a DMV native, so this was a homecoming of sorts for him, and he showed up big in his hometown, but for the away team. Young finished with 4 tackles, 2 sacks, 2 TFLs, and 3 QB hits. His impact on the defense is what helped keep Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry in check for the Ravens’ offense. This defense is flying under the radar, and they are dangerous. That’s largely in part due to Young and his play so far in the early part of this season. Devaughn Vele seems to be the player Tyler Shough looks for whenever it’s third-and-impossible. When those two can link up, it usually works out. Vele finished with 5 receptions for 64 yards and averaged 12.8 yards per reception. Him being able to serve as another vertical-stretch receiver to complement Chris Olave, especially while Jordyn Tyson has been sidelined, is great to see. Vele has a vital role in this emerging offense, and that should expand as this team continues to play throughout the season. Juwan Johnson is becoming the pass-catching tight end that every fan has been waiting to see. His play has elevated ever since Tyler Shough became the starting QB. Johnson finished the game with 4 receptions for 66 yards, including a major reception that converted a crucial third down. That reception went for a long of 25 yards. Johnson is a valuable safety blanket for Shough when everything breaks down, and it’s good to see him coming into his potential. Chris Olave is the primary target for Tyler Shough and is playing like the best player on this team. Olave finished the game with 8 receptions for 86 yards and 1 touchdown. Olave is finding himself playing like one of the best wide receivers in the game right now. His route running is elite, and now he’s been able to come down with contested catches, adding another element to his game. But the overall game MVP for this week is the QB himself, Tyler Shough. Shough finished this game 27 of 34—that’s a 79% completion percentage—for 252 yards and 1 TD. He added 9 carries for 23 yards and another TD on the ground. The Saints got down early in this game on the road, but Shough never allowed that to faze him or affect his play. When it seemed that the game might start slipping away, Tyler Shough kept elevating his play. The special thing about Shough, though, is that as he elevates his play, he’s also elevating the play of others around him. Even after losing starting LT Kelvin Banks Jr., Shough was still able to play extremely well. Games like this showcase to the rest of the league that the Saints not only have a starting QB, but they may indeed have their next franchise QB. The Saints will be set to face off against the Raiders on Sunday at 3:25 p.m. in the first home game of the season, and it’s a safe bet that the Dome will be rocking when the Black and Gold take the field. Who was your game MVP from Sunday, and will you be in that number when the Saints open up the Dome this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Week 2 Film Review: Highlights from the All 22
summary: If you read last week’s film preview for the Ravens you would’ve known that the Ravens offense runs through Zay Flowers. Although most think of Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry as the most dangerous players on the offensive side of the ball for Baltimore, Flowers is the real difference maker in Declan Doyle’s offense. The […]
full_text: If you read last week’s film preview for the Ravens you would’ve known that the Ravens offense runs through Zay Flowers. Although most think of Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry as the most dangerous players on the offensive side of the ball for Baltimore, Flowers is the real difference maker in Declan Doyle’s offense. The loss of Flowers this week undoubtably helped the Saints who were able to accomplish all three of my “Keys to Victory” from last week on their way to what many around the football world saw as a huge upset by the now Coach of the Year Favorite (+600 on FanDuel) Kellen Moore’s squad. Takeaways from the Film Containing the Boot #Saints defensive coordinator Brandon Staley did a great job coming up with answers for the boot plays the #Ravens used to gash the #Colts in week 1. pic.twitter.com/FRDCbaEXw1 — Andrew Lotz (@andrewlot3) September 22, 2026 Brandon Staley devised a great scheme and gameplan this week that proved to stifle one of the most dangerous quarterbacks in the league and an offense that seemed unstoppable after their first half showing in week 1 vs the Colts. Below we see the Saints responding to the boot action from Lamar with what looked like a Cover 4 scheme that allowed Carl Granderson to eliminate the run threat while waiting for the flat route. Most boot concepts will try to flood one side of the field and gash you in the middle while the defense worries about trying to limit passes to the sideline which absolutely killed the Colts last week. Staley seemed to take the approach of making Lamar make the more difficult pass in the concept, the deep out. While the Cover 4 defense above worked perfectly to blanket every receiver on the field (great communication by the Saints defense) below is a Cover 1 hole defense they also deployed to make Lamar take the hard throw (Deep comeback to #10). Each defense has it’s own weakness as the boot is hard to stop and a fundamentally great concept in football, however the Staley expertly mixed the two defenses in this week to limit the ability for Jackson to find his most dangerous receiver (#7 Bateman on the crossing route). Key to Victory Number 1 (Limit explosive plays off of play action and boot passes ) : Check. New Orleans: We Have a Quarterback I had all the confidence in the World in Tyler Shough after watching his first handful of games last year, but let’s be honest, the first half against Detroit was rough. Kelvin Sheppard (Lions Defensive Coordinator) clearly confused Shough in his first live action since last season and was able to affect his play by having his defense hit him early and often. Shough’s confidence from the second half last week carried over into the Ravens game as he noticeably more poised as the Ravens were doing a good job of pressuring him from multiple looks. Shough improved tremendously in the turnover department and had a much better feel for where rushers would be coming from; Key to Victory Number 2: (Take care of the football and correct pass protection issues): Check. The increased comfortability allowed Shough to show off his elite level of anticipation and timing that he has developed with his receiving core. The game tying touchdown pass to Chris Olave is shown below to illustrate just how dangerous Shough can be and why there are whispers about him being a dark horse in the MVP race (+3000 on FanDuel). This play (pictured below) is a perfect example of what makes Shough special as he is able to diagnose the miscommunication in the Ravens defense as they tried to defend this Bronco concept (Post + Corner) the instant Vele breaks to the corner route. This is the definition of a perfect play by a quarterback, and with the game on the line, Shough made these plays repetitively to lead the Saints to victory. Kaden Ellis Impact Kaden Ellis was all over the field on Sunday and, so far, had proven he was well worth the money it took to get him back from the NFL team that plays in Atlanta (their name doesn’t need to be mentioned). Elliss was able to effect the Ravens entire offense as he proved to be a mismatch when blitzing versus interior pass protectors (pictured below) and forced the Ravens to play Justice Hill more than they probably wanted to. This led to the Saints accomplishing Key to Victory Number 3: (Don’t let Henry get rolling) as Doyle’s hand was forced and the Ravens couldn’t justify keeping Henry on the field. This is a perfect example of what people refer to as the chess match inside of the chess match when it comes to football. The Saints knew they have to stop Derrick Henry and they chose to attack his running ability by exploiting his worst trait, pass protection (below is an example of Pete Werner getting a sack because of Henry’s confusion on his blocking assignment). This was a beautifully designed and executed gameplan by Staley’s defense that held the Ravens to just 3 points in the second half of Sunday’s matchup. Pete Werner lights up Lamar Jackson with the blitz! #Saints pic.twitter.com/Z2UFy6JFb1 — SleeperSaints (@SleeperSaints) September 20, 2026 End of the Day If you aren’t believing in this team now, can you even call yourself a Saints fan? Kellen Moore deserves more credit than he is getting for finding Tyler Shough, building an offense around him that has dynamic weapons, employing Brandon Staley, and inspiring this team to believe they are never out of a contest. Chris Olave noted after the win that, “I feel like since I’ve been here, we haven’t really beaten a good team” when asked if this was one of the best wins in his career, and I couldn’t agree more. This was the most impressive win the Saints have had since Sean Payton left New Orleans.

title: State of the NFC South: Week 2 recap
summary: The division had a better week overall: two teams won, while the other two struggled. Tampa Bay Buccaneers If you remember last week’s edition, I said that the Bucs should win their Week 2 game against the Cleveland Browns. Well, funny thing. After a long weather delay on what should have been the game’s final […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints and Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens hug after New Orleans' 24-17 win at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The division had a better week overall: two teams won, while the other two struggled. Tampa Bay Buccaneers If you remember last week’s edition, I said that the Bucs should win their Week 2 game against the Cleveland Browns. Well, funny thing. After a long weather delay on what should have been the game’s final drive, the Bucs couldn’t score, resulting in a 4-point loss to the Browns. This was an embarrassing loss; Deshaun Watson outplayed Baker Mayfield, and the defense really struggled. Tampa Bay’s season is far from over, but Todd Bowles’ seat is on fire. Carolina Panthers Now, to our first win from the division, my goodness, the Panthers destroyed the Falcons. We will get to Atlanta after this, but the Panthers won this game 34-3, and it was never really in doubt. Carolina’s defense played really well, and Bryce Young continues to have a really great start to the season. At the top of the division, Carolina plays the Browns next week, and just like last week with the Bucs, I’m guessing the Panthers will win. Atlanta Falcons Yeesh. Losing a game by 31 points is never great, but it was worse than the score says. The one bright spot was the Falcons’ rushing attack, but they had to abandon it because of the score. The QB play, with Penix and Tua out, was downright horrible. In Week 3, the Falcons will be getting Penix back against the Green Bay Packers, who are also struggling to start the season. New Orleans Saints Back to winning, the Saints had the shock of the week. In a game nobody expected New Orleans to win, they beat the Baltimore Ravens, a Super Bowl contender. It wasn’t a perfect game, far from it, but with Tyler Shough being confident all game, the defense holding Derrick Henry to under 100 rushing yards (insane), and Chase Young being a monster off the edge, the Saints stayed in the game all day. In the second half, they really controlled the momentum, and after some interesting decisions by the Ravens, it was over in Baltimore. Their next game is against the 2-0 Raiders, who have had a strong start to the season under former Saints OC Klint Kubiak. This will be a very fun game. NFC South standings: Carolina Panthers (1-1) New Orleans Saints (1-1) Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-2) Atlanta Falcons (0-2)

title: Are the Saints contenders after beating the Ravens?
summary: It’s time to start taking the New Orleans Saints a little more seriously. That might sound like an overreaction after just two games, but beating the Baltimore Ravens on the road is the kind of win that gets a team’s attention. The Saints entered Baltimore as underdogs and found themselves trailing 14-3 in the second […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints looks to pass while pressure by Trenton Simpson #32 of the Baltimore Ravens in the fourth quarter of a game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time to start taking the New Orleans Saints a little more seriously. That might sound like an overreaction after just two games, but beating the Baltimore Ravens on the road is the kind of win that gets a team’s attention. The Saints entered Baltimore as underdogs and found themselves trailing 14-3 in the second quarter. Instead of folding, New Orleans completely flipped the game after halftime, scoring the final 15 points to secure a 24-17 victory. Tyler Shough continues to show why there is growing excitement surrounding him as one of the NFL’s next star quarterbacks. He completed 27 of 34 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 23 yards on nine carries and the game-winning score with under two minutes remaining. Chris Olave added eight catches for 86 yards and a touchdown, while the defense held Lamar Jackson and the Ravens to only three points after halftime. Those are the types of complementary performances that can make a team dangerous. But this is where the overreaction comes in. The Saints are just two games in, and one road victory doesn’t suddenly erase every question surrounding a team that is still figuring itself out. New Orleans also trailed by double digits for the second consecutive week, meaning the team has plenty to clean up despite its ability to respond. Still, there is something different about beating a team like Baltimore in its own building. The Saints now return home for their first game at Caesars Superdome against the 2-0 Las Vegas Raiders. If they can carry the momentum from Baltimore into that matchup, the conversation around this team could change quickly. Are the Saints contenders? It is probably too early to say. But after Sunday, it is no longer unreasonable to ask the question.

title: Rookie Report: A shaky second game for the NY Giants’ 2026 draft class
summary: The New York Giants had a nightmare of an evening against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 2 on Monday Night Football. Just about everything that could go wrong for the Giants, did go wrong. The headline is obviously the knee injury suffered by quarterback Jaxson Dart, but that wasn’t the only storyline from the […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Malachi Fields on the field against the Los Angeles Rams. | Getty Images The New York Giants had a nightmare of an evening against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 2 on Monday Night Football. Just about everything that could go wrong for the Giants, did go wrong. The headline is obviously the knee injury suffered by quarterback Jaxson Dart, but that wasn’t the only storyline from the night. The Giants’ had six rookies playing major roles for them against the Rams, and how the Giants’ 2026 class develops will be one of the most important things to watch as the rest of the season unfolds. The Giants are relying heavily on their young players, and their rookies, this year. In fact, the Giants had the third-most snaps played by rookies of any team in the NFL in Week 2, and perhaps it also isn’t a coincidence that the Los Angeles Rams had the fewest snaps played by rookies. Rookie Snap Count % through Week 2 1. MIA 27.6% 2. CLE 16.4% 3. NYG 15.1% … 30. ARI 2.3% 31. DEN 1.1% 32. LAR 0.7% pic.twitter.com/dA2rPZ8FZV — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) September 22, 2026 That the Giants are asking so much of their rookies makes the team more prone to mistakes while the players develop. However, it does give them valuable experience to aid in their development. Let’s take a closer look and see how they did in their second game of NFL action. Arvell Reese (LB) ( 59 snaps, 95% ) The Giants’ first pick played almost every snap against the Rams, as well as contributing on special teams. We saw every facet of Reese’s skill set employed by Dennard Wilson against the Rams. Reese played the run, played in coverage as a linebacker, was walked up to the line of scrimmage to show pressure on simulated blitzes, and was asked to rush off the edge. Of those, Reese looked most comfortable playing downhill. He appeared largely disciplined in his run fits and is remarkably strong for a 241-pound linebacker. He is able to take on and stalemate offensive linemen when he engages with good leverage. He also showed off his power with an impressive bull rush off the edge to drive left tackle Alaric Jackson back into the pocket, and he might have been able to disrupt had Blake Corum not delivered a timely chip block. Reese looks less comfortable dropping into space and playing coverage. He typically processes quickly, but doesn’t quite play with a natural feel for coverage. Reese can be a step late to pick up players as they enter his zones, and shows some indecision as well. That said, his speed is absolutely an asset and he simply flies to the ball once he commits. Sisi Mauigoa (RG) ( 58 snaps, 100% ) We saw both the highs and lows of Mauigoa’s game in his play against the Rams. On the plus side, Mauigoa’s power and agility were on full display. At his best, he showed some of what he did against the Cowboys’ interior defensive linemen. Mauigoa was able to displace the Rams’ linemen laterally on zone blocks, vertically when blocking downhill, and move laterally to mirror pass rushers. He has great range as a pulling guard, and was a load for any defender not prepared to block him. On other plays, however, Mauigoa struggled mightily. In particular, he had a tough time with Aaron Donald in his first game back. Sisi struggled to deal with Donald’s technique, leverage, and explosive first step — Donald’s 0.75-second get-off was the third-fastest by a defensive tackle so far this season. There were times when Mauigoa was pushed backward despite the considerable size disparity, as well as times when he struggled to deal with Donald’s speed rushes. The arrow is still pointing up for Mauigoa and his good plays were impressive, but this game definitely made him look like a rookie. Colton Hood (CB) ( 62 snaps, 100% ) Hood got the start in place of the injured Deonte Banks, and it was a long night for the rookie. He played every one of the defensive snaps and was a factor in both run defense and pass coverage. Hood wasn’t always a positive factor, but he did flash the traits that made many consider him a fringe first-round talent. Hood is a tough, physical corner who started the game with a great tackle to limit Kyren Lacy to a 2-yard gain on the Rams’ second play. He doesn’t hesitate to take on bigger blockers or to get his hands dirty. He also has quick feet and fluid hips as a cover corner and flashes the ability to stick in receivers’ hip pockets as a man cover corner. Hood is still a work in progress in off coverages. He has a tendency to overreact to savvy route runners, biting on double-moves or stumbling after a fake. At best that can make him a bit slow to react and at worst he can give up separation that can lead to big plays. Hood flashes the ability to be a good cover cornerback, but isn’t there yet. The upside to playing so many snaps is that he got valuable experience against a great offense. Malachi Fields (WR) ( 47 snaps, 81% ) Fields had an inconsistent day against the Rams, which is to be expected from a rookie. He flashed the upside of what the Giants hope he can be with the diving 14-yard catch from Dart on 1st and 10 early in the first quarter. That play showed off the body control, concentration, and ball skills that the Giants hope will make Fields a weapon on third downs and in the red zone. He generally seemed to run his routes well enough, and did a good job of using his frame to try to create traffic on clear-outs or create natural rubs. The Giants continued to use Fields in condensed formations, frequently starting with him as a slot before motioning a player around him, condensing the offensive formation and leaving Fields him as an outside receiver. That said, Fields also struggled with the Rams’ physical coverage. His size and strength are assets in that regard, however his technique isn’t there yet. Considering he doesn’t have the quick-twitch athleticism to cut with exceptional suddenness, it can be difficult for Fields to generate separation against tight coverage. The Giants can work around that going forward while Fields works on improving his technique to get off physical coverage. The Giants also frequently made use of Fields as a blocker in the run game. He became their primary receiver in 22 or 13-personnel sets after Malik Nabers suffered his shoulder injury, and comported himself well enough. Those were primarily running plays, and Fields is a problem for perimeter defenders as a blocker. There were times where the Giants also used Fields as a pulling tight end or asked him to insert in the box as an extra blocker. He was, predictably, less of an impact player in those situations. However, he was able to lose slowly enough to do his job. Dominic Zvada (PK) and Ben Mann (LS) ( 13 snaps combined ) No slight to specialists, but I think it’s appropriate to lump these two together, as much of the time they’re working as a unit. Fittingly, we’ll start with the long snapper, and Mann was largely solid. His snaps appeared crisp and accurate, arriving on time and well placed for Jordan Stout as a punter and holder for Zvada. Mann did give a fair amount of ground when blocking for Stout on punts, but held up well on both of Zvada’s field goals despite facing the Rams’ starting defensive linemen. For his part, Zvada largely remains a weapon on kickoffs. He had one touchback, but otherwise did a good job of dropping his kicks around the 5-yard line to force a return. Unfortunately, Zvada was the Giants’ lone source of points against the Rams, but we did get to see his strong leg in action. His 52-yard field goal was not only accurate, but appeared as though it would have been good from 62 yards.
author: Chris Pflum

title: Jaxson Dart injury is ‘not an ACL’, but the timeline still isn’t good: Report
summary: There hasn’t been much in the way of good regarding the injury to New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart. At first it was believed that Dart only suffered an MCL strain when he was sandwiched between a pair of Los Angeles Rams defenders and could return inside of a month. It was then revealed Tuesday […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart | Getty Images There hasn’t been much in the way of good regarding the injury to New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart. At first it was believed that Dart only suffered an MCL strain when he was sandwiched between a pair of Los Angeles Rams defenders and could return inside of a month. It was then revealed Tuesday morning that an MRI revealed that his injury is worse than initially believed. The reporting hasn’t revealed the exact nature of the injury, but that Dart would be out indefinitely and season-ending surgery is on the table. That catches us up to Wednesday morning, when Mike Garafolo reported that Dart’s injury doesn’t involve his ACL. Garafolo said: “Ian Rapoport and I were both told yesterday, this is not an ACL. But, the MRI did tell a different story from what the Giants were initially expecting. There is more damage than what the evaluations on site showed.“ The Giants’ hesitancy to confirm the nature of the injury makes sense in the light of Garafolo and Rapoport’s reporting. ACL injuries are usually quickly confirmed and the recovery timelines are well understood. A different or complicated injury could be good news, worse news, or just bad news depending on what the continuing tests and opinions show. Garafolo added that Dart’s recovery could follow several different timelines depending on the exact nature of the injury. None of the potential timelines are “very good”, according to Garafolo, and Dart’s season being over remains on the table. “There are a lot of people involved. That means inside doctors [inside the Giants organization], outside doctors, that means Dart, the Giants. Everybody is going to come together and make a collective decision.” Dart, obviously, will lobby to take the quickest route back to the field. Dart is an incredibly competitive young man and even played through a high ankle sprain his final season at Ole Miss. However, that might not be best for his long term health. Garafolo says, “A lot of times when you have a young player, particularly at the quarterback position, these decisions are made with the long term interest of the player in mind.” The Giants had to take Dart’s uniform away from him after he tried to talk his way back onto the field Monday night. With that in mind, the Giants may need to protect Dart from himself as much as deal with his injury. Garafolo ends by saying that we should expect clarity on Dart’s status and timeline in the coming days. We’ll update with more as we get it.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants-Tennessee Titans storylines: Moving on without Jaxson Dart
summary: Jaxson Dart is likely not going to be under center for any of them, but the New York Giants still have 15 games to play in the 2026 NFL season. How will they do without their young quarterback, who played like a star in an impressive Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys? We begin […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart throwing the ball Monday right before being injured. | Getty Images Jaxson Dart is likely not going to be under center for any of them, but the New York Giants still have 15 games to play in the 2026 NFL season. How will they do without their young quarterback, who played like a star in an impressive Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys? We begin to find out Sunday at MetLife Stadium when the Tennessee Dabolls — er, Titans — come to East Rutherford, N.J. for a 1 p.m. matchup. Below are some of the storylines for the week. Winning without Dart The latest reporting from NFL Network insider Mike Garafolo is that “ there are a few timelines on the table , none of them very good, one of them season-ending” for the Giants quarterback. While we await word on that, it is obvious Dart will not play Sunday against Tennessee. And the Giants will be without him for the foreseeable future. How will the Giants fare without Dart, especially if he is out all season? It is possible that John Harbaugh and his veteran coaching staff squeeze every ounce of juice from this imperfect Giants’ roster and they finish in the neighborhood of .500. It is also possible that a four- or five-win season, the kind of disastrous year the Giants figured was off the table due to Harbaugh’s presence, is back on the table. Beginning with the 0-2 Titans, the Giants have a three-game stretch of games that should be winnable. Tennessee is a young, winless team coming to MetLife Stadium. They did, though, put a Week 2 scare into the Philadelphia Eagles. The 1-1 Arizona Cardinals come to MetLife in Week 4. They are expected to be one of the league’s weaker teams. The Giants visit the 0-2 Washington Commanders in Week 5. The Commanders could be without star quarterback Jayden Daniels, who suffered his second dislocated left elbow in as many seasons on Sunday against the Dallas Cowboys. If the Giants cannot win at least two of those three games, another long, miserable, losing season could follow. Harbaugh, one of the winningest head coaches of all time, is going to be challenged over the next 15 games. The veteran head coach promised on Tuesday that the Giants will “be fighting every step of the way.” “We haven’t even come close – not even close — to playing as well as we’re capable of playing as a football team,” Harbaugh said. “So, that’s really going to be the focus. I mean, it’s going to be something we’re going to have to, you deal with all the different challenges that you face and all the different adversity that you face, for sure. And even the prosperity, you learned that last week, you faced some of the prosperity, and prosperity sometimes can be more dangerous than adversity. “All these challenges to put your best effort out there, play your best football, so you can win a football game. And we’re going to do that. These guys are going to do that. That’s what you get excited about. The prospect of our team playing the best football that they can play. And that’s what we’re working on, working as hard as we can, working like crazy as a football team to do that all together.” The Giants referred to Dart’s injury as an in-game “gut punch.” Harbaugh does not expect that to cause a long-term letdown. “The guys want to go win. They want to go play,” Harbaugh said. “Guys play. They’ll play. They play for each other. They play for themselves. They play for their families. They play because they believe they can win the game. And it’s never one person, never one person that wins or loses a football game. It’s everybody. And the more good players you can have out there, the better chance you’re going to have. There’s no doubt about it. But you still have to be a complete team to win games. “If you get punched in the gut, are you going down? Are you going down? Are you going to crumple to the ground, as Jack Harbaugh would say, like a sack of sour apples and just fall to the ground and just rot away and wither away into the dust. Is that what you’re going to do?” To win games, the Giants are going to have to accomplish several things: They will have to get better play from quarterback Jameis Winston than the miserable 11 of 27 for 11 yards and an interception performance he gave them Monday night. They will have to find some way to get explosive plays from their offense. The longest non-Dart run they have in two games is a 13-yard carry by Cam Skattebo. They have one pass completion of more than 20 yards, a 33-yard grab by Darnell Mooney. The pass rush will have to remember that the regular season has started. They will need to find a way to cover some of the league’s best receivers. They need to hope that injuries to stars Brian Burns, Andrew Thomas, and Malik Nabers aren’t severe. Oh, and that other injuries don’t continue to pile up. We begin to find out how life after Dart will go Sunday against Tennessee. More injuries to worry about Dart suffered the worst and most significant injury on Monday night. Still, the game against the Rams saw several other significant injuries to Giants stars. Edge defender Brian Burns, who had a career-high 16.5 sacks last season, suffered a sprained left ankle. Left tackle Andrew Thomas apparently suffered a groin injury on the Giants’ final offensive possession. Wide receiver Malik Nabers left the game briefly with a shoulder injury. He had just one catch for 1 yard in the game. Cornerback Deonte Banks missed Monday’s game with a calf injury. His status for Week 3 is unclear. The initial injury report of the week comes out Wednesday afternoon. We find out more about the severity of these injuries then. With a short week before playing the Titans, it is fair to wonder just how short-handed the Giants are going to be in a game that not long ago looked like one the Giants should win. Remember the Titans This game has been circled on the calendar for a while simply because of the volume of former Giants — especially key Giants — who are now part of the Titans’ organization. Daboll, fired last season as Giants head coach, is now running the Tennessee offense. Daboll, of course, was instrumental in the Giants’ decision to trade up last season to draft Dart. Robinson is second on the Titans with six receptions for 47 yards, just 7.8 yards per catch. He had the only 1,000-yard season of his career with the Giants last season. Bellinger has just one catch in two games, one of which he started. Schlottmann has started both Tennessee games at center. Through two games, Schlottmann’s Pro Football and Sports Network ‘Impact Score’ is 72.6. For the Giants, starting center John Michael Schmitz is at 73.6. Both scores are slightly below what PFSN considers league average, a score of 75.0. Where’s the pass rush? The Giants’ defense was supposed to be built around what they hoped would be a dominant pass rush. Burns is coming off a career-best season. Abdul Carter was drafted No. 3 overall in hopes he would be a game-wrecking pass rusher. He looked in the summer like he was about to fulfill that promise. Kayvon Thibodeaux has at times been a good, but not great, pass rusher. No. 5 overall pick Arvell Reese is an inside linebacker with pass rush potential. Interior defensive linemen Chauncey Golston and Darius Alexander have pass rush ability. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s defense used creative schemes to pressure Giants’ quarterbacks throughout training camp. Through two weeks of the regular season, none of that talent, potential, and summer promise has mattered. The pass rush has been non-existent. The Giants have one quarterback sack. Per NextGenStats, their 1.4% sack rate is 31st in the league. Only the woeful Miami Dolphins, who do not have a sack yet, are worse. The Giants’ pressure rate of 26.1, again per NGS, is the worst in the league. The ball is coming out quickly against New York, with the 2.69-second time to throw against the Giants 26th overall. That is .41 seconds faster than league average. Still, the pressure rate isn’t good enough.…

title: Advanced stats for the Giants’ 28-6 loss to the Rams
summary: In John Harbaugh’s first season as head coach of the Baltimore Ravens, he lost a road game to Tony Dungy’s Indianapolis Colts 31-3 in Week 6 to drop the Ravens to 2-3 on the season. A few weeks later his team was manhandled by the Giants 30-10, dropping them to 6-4. That team wound up […]
full_text: Jevon Holland intercepts a pass against the Rams. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In John Harbaugh’s first season as head coach of the Baltimore Ravens, he lost a road game to Tony Dungy’s Indianapolis Colts 31-3 in Week 6 to drop the Ravens to 2-3 on the season. A few weeks later his team was manhandled by the Giants 30-10, dropping them to 6-4. That team wound up making it to the AFC Championship Game before being eliminated by eventual Super Bowl champion Pittsburgh. Stinkers happen, and Sunday night was certainly one of them for the Giants. The issue is how you react to them. Harbaugh’s 2008 team reeled off four wins in a row in between those losses to the Colts and the Giants. His Giants team now has the chance to do something similar, with the most navigable part of their schedule coming up. For the moment, though, they have to own this stinker of a loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Jaxson Dart’s injury makes it all the more difficult, but that’s why they’re paying Harbaugh the big bucks. As Ed mentioned in The Feed on Tuesday, we’re going to start trying something new after games. We’ll continue to show you Pro Football Focus grades, but say less about them than in the past. In their place, we’ll try to show a number of other advanced stats from various sources to give you a better feel for the team as a whole, and specifically how the quarterback is doing. PFF grades You might guess that few Giants scored well in PFF’s eyes in Monday night’s game. You would be correct. Here are the grades for the offense: Andrew Thomas was the only Giants offensive player to play well, grading 74.5 overall. Thomas gave up a hit and a hurry, but from an “Other than that Mrs. Lincoln, how did you like the play?” perspective, that one QB hit was the one that injured Jaxson Dart’s knee. Similarly, Jermaine Eluemunor was charged with one sack (on the same play) and a hit, the only sack of the night on a Giants QB among 11 total pressures, which is not terrible. Still, we can see the entire Giants interior OL with grades in the 40s and Sisi Mauigoa in particular with an awful 23.3 pass block grade. John Michael Schmitz is down there too, in part because sometimes he decides to block air rather than a pass rusher: As @nickfalato mentioned last night's show — second straight week JMS didn't get a hand on a pass rusher on a screen and killed a big play. So much space ahead. Great play call. One of many bad JMS plays in pass protection from last night. Clock is ticking for him as starter. pic.twitter.com/a9pFtKRhIq — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) September 22, 2026 Other than that, there isn’t much positive to say about anyone on the offense. A couple of the receivers (Isaiah Likely, Darnell Mooney) played fairly well, while Theo Johnson (38.0) continues to be a liability. Here are the defensive grades: It’s a very similar story, with one player performing well, a few more in the average category, and a bunch being well below par, even terrible. The most notable was Jevon Holland, who had a spectacular game – an interception (for the second game in a row), 2 forced fumbles, 7 tackles and an assist, no missed tackles, and only one completion for 9 yards. This is reminiscent of his rookie and Year 3 play, which is what got him his big contract. Among starting safeties, Holland is ranked No. 1 after two games, just ahead of the Rams’ Quentin Lake (who also had a great game last night), Julian Love, and Kyle Hamilton. Let’s hope that continues, because his backfield mate Tyler Nubin (29.3 last night) is ranked 64th of 69 safeties. A few other Giants played at least fairly well on defense last night: Dru Phillips (69.5), who only played 30 snaps and wasn’t targeted at all; Brian Burns (67.2), who had a QB hit, a hurry, and a run stop before leaving with an ankle injury; Abdul Carter (67.0), who had the Giants’ only sack of Matthew Stafford; and D.J. Reader (63.8), though both Carter and Reader had two missed tackles. On the other hand, Tremaine Edmunds had an awful game (28.5), with a missed tackle and 3 receptions in 3 targets including a TD. Shelby Harris (40.7) and Josh Tupou (40.2) played poorly as well, and Arvell Reese (50.5) did not distinguish himself either. Advanced metrics Jameis Winston did not have an auspicious season debut, to say the least: Winston was dead last among starting quarterbacks in both expected points added/play and completion % over expected…and it wasn’t particularly close except for the aged Aaron Rodgers being almost as bad in EPA/play. Matthew Stafford was in the upper right quadrant and second overall in EPA/play, which tells you about how effective the Giants’ pass defense was. Not to be outdone, the Giants’ defense said, hold my beer: The Giants were on par overall with the wretched Atlanta Falcons for worst performance of the week, but somewhat surprisingly, six teams were as bad or even worse on defense, including two who actually won their games (Kansas City and Buffalo). Here’s a different perspective on team offense and defense in Week 2, using defense-adjusted value over average ( DVOA ) as the metric: DVOA through Week 2 1. SF (OFF #2, DEF #5, ST #12) 2. BUF (OFF #1, DEF #19, ST #9) 3. BAL (OFF #3, DEF #11, ST #22) 4. KC (OFF #6, DEF #10, ST #20) 5. SEA (OFF #15, DEF #2, ST #15) 6. CIN (OFF #12, DEF #7, ST #10) 7. DAL (OFF #4, DEF #20, ST #4) 8. NYJ (OFF #14, DEF #3, ST #26)… pic.twitter.com/tOtaGWZCij — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) September 22, 2026 The results are not identical but fairly similar for most teams. The Giants are still in the lower left (bad on both offense and defense) quadrant, but if you’re looking for solace, they have more company than EPA/play gives them, including next week’s opponent Tennessee, which almost beat the Eagles but apparently played poorly while doing so. EPA/play says otherwise. However you slice it, the Giants were bad. In Winston’s defense, his teammates didn’t give him much help. Here is how he ranks in a few Next Gen Stats that are not about him but about the guys he was throwing to and the guys blocking for him: Winston’s receivers had the lowest average separation of any other quarterbacks (2.3 yards). His tight window percentage (TW%) of 33.3% was thus the largest of any QB (the next three – Jared Goff, Daniel Jones, Jordan Love – all lost their games). Winston’s pressure rate of 58.6% (QBP%) also led the NFL, and four of the top five in that category lost their game: If you’re looking for a silver lining, the Giants’ special teams are performing well (the plot below is for two games, not just Week 2): Special Teams EPA through Week 2 1. LV +10.7 2. CIN +10.3 3. NYG +9.9 … 30. HOU -10.1 31. MIA -12.1 32. TEN -13.5 pic.twitter.com/b0tDZbaX3x — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) September 22, 2026 Fortunately for the Giants, their next three games are against Tennessee, Arizona, and Washington, collectively with one win among them. Last year, when Dart went down with a concussion, Winston kept the Giants competitive against both Detroit and Green Bay. Despite his poor outing Monday night, he’s one of the best backups in the NFL. All three opponents have their own questions at QB, the Commanders being in the same boat as the Giants with their star starting quarterback out due to injury. If John Harbaugh and his staff are as good as the buzz around them was when they were hired, the Giants should still be able to win some games. Let’s see whether the juice was worth the squeeze.
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: NY Giants news: Jaxson Dart’s season in doubt, Jevon Holland, Jordan Stout, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants look to rebound against the Tennessee Titans. The Giants’ major questions run deeper than injuries after blowout loss to Rams | The Athletic The Giants are supposed to be better equipped to weather that type of adversity because […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants look to rebound against the Tennessee Titans. The Giants’ major questions run deeper than injuries after blowout loss to Rams | The Athletic The Giants are supposed to be better equipped to weather that type of adversity because they have veteran backup Jameis Winston, who recently signed a two-year, $13 million extension. But the Giants got the version of Winston that showed why he went from No. 1 pick to backup. With Winston spraying the ball all over the field Monday night, the offense never found any rhythm. The search for schematic answers likely began as Harbaugh watched the game tape on the flight home. He didn’t wait that long to take the pulse of his players, as he made his way around the postgame locker room and huddled with small groups. As discouraging as Monday’s result was, players vowed not to let it carry over. “For us to come in here and lose this game, obviously it sucks,” right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “But you get punched in the face, you’ve got to get back up and keep going because we’ve still got 15 more rounds.” Chris Simms on the play that Dart got hurt The play where Dart got hurt was in disarray before the snap. pic.twitter.com/b4WKB6p0wS — Chris Simms (@CSimmsQB) September 22, 2026 Jaxson Dart’’s injury a gut punch to Giants and John Harbaugh’s potential storybook season | SNY.tv That uncertainty could follow the Giants into the 2027 draft. If they struggle without Dart and land a high first-round pick, Harbaugh and Schoen could face a decision they had hoped was behind them: Stick with a quarterback whose promise they have seen but whose development remains incomplete, or consider starting over. The question would not simply be whether Dart is talented enough. It would be whether they have seen enough to commit to him — and whether they can trust him to remain on the field. Six things we learned from Giants’ Week 2 loss: The scary Jameis Winston Experience will now make or break season | New York Post It’s time for Jameis Winston to show if he’s worth that new extension. If Jaxson Dart is going to be sidelined for two to four weeks – the typical recovery timeline experts associate with what the Giants fear is a sprained MCL – then there are worse times for it to happen than against the softest part of the schedule. Jameis Winston pins Giants’ passing woes on early-down failures | USAToday.com Winston said Los Angeles got ahead and then knew a pass was coming, making the passing game difficult. “They knew a pass was coming. When you know a pass is coming — it’s very challenging to throw the ball when (they) know that a pass is coming,” Winston said. “We have just got to execute better. We are focusing on being in better down the distance. We went in third-and-long a lot, so I have to execute better on first and second down… Pressure is for the unprepared. You keep preparing. You be ready. So, whatever happens, happens.” Malik Nabers’ shoulder injury explained: Why Giants should be concerned about WR | NJ.com “Which means he’s done this before, allowing it to be much easier to pop out (as you can see by the benign play it happened on),” Dr. Jesse Morse wrote on X. “The question becomes: How much new damage did this cause?” This could lead to him playing next week with a brace, him missing a couple weeks — or possibly worse (if fracture. The adrenaline was pumping, so that allowed him to get through the game. But now that the pain and swelling has started, getting the range of motion back might be challenging.” Odell Beckham Jr. was on the field for three plays on Monday night | Pro Football Weekly Beckham was on the field for only three snaps. Out of 58 total offensive plays. By way of comparison, Malachi Fields had 47 snaps. Malik Nabers played 43. Darnell Mooney was on the field for 42. Even Braxton Berrios — primarily a special-teamer — had five offensive snaps. In Week 1, Beckham was on the field for 11 of 69 snaps. He has been targeted zero times, through two games. NFL Week 2 grades for all 32 teams | CBSSports.com New York Giants: D. This was a nightmare loss for the Giants, who had to play nearly the entire game without Jaxon Dart, who suffered a knee injury in the first quarter. It one thing became clear from this game, it’s that the offense will be in some serious trouble if Dart is out for an extended period of time. Once Jamies Winston came in, the Giants’ couldn’t run the ball and he couldn’t complete a pass, which is how this game turned into a blowout. The bigger issue for the Giants might be their defense. After an impressive Week 1 performance, things got ugly in L.A. They couldn’t cover Davante Adams and they got steamrolled by a Rams offense that rushed for 165 yards. The Giants also struggled to put pressure on Matthew Stafford, who took advantage of that by picking them apart. The loss of Dart hurts much more than losing the game and the Giants will now cross their fingers and hope their QB won’t have to miss very much time. title: Survey: How many games will the injured Giants win?
summary: The New York Giants trip to take on the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football was a perfect storm of bad outcomes. The Giants were out-schemed and out-executed by arguably the most talented team in the NFL. And to add injury to insult, the Giants also lost QB Jaxson Dart to a knee injury […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart leaves the field after an injury. | Getty Images The New York Giants trip to take on the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football was a perfect storm of bad outcomes. The Giants were out-schemed and out-executed by arguably the most talented team in the NFL. And to add injury to insult, the Giants also lost QB Jaxson Dart to a knee injury on their 11th play of the game, and edge defender Brian Burns to a sprained ankle late in the game. The Giants don’t have time to lick their wounds from their loss to the Rams. They have a quick turnaround as they fly back from California and immediately need to begin preparing for the Tennessee Titans. As of this writing, we don’t know the status of Dart, Burns, left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), wide receiver Malik Nabers (shoulder), and cornerback Deonte Banks (calf). While none of the players’ injuries appear to be long-term, it’s possible that the team could be without many of their best and most important players for the coming weeks. And it’s possible that those who are able to play this week could be limited in what they’re able to do or how well they’re able to play. If there’s a silver lining to the rash of injuries that struck the Giants in LA, it’s that they happen to coincide with the softest part of the Giants’ schedule. The Giants will face the Tennessee Titans (0-2), Arizona Cardinals (1-1), Washington Commanders (0-2), and New Orleans Saints (1-1) over the next four weeks, who have a combined record of 2-6 after two weeks. The Titans and Cardinals are struggling to get their respective rebuilds on track, while the Cardinals, Commanders, and Saints have significant injury concerns of their own. The Commanders lost QB Jayden Daniels to a dislocated elbow, while the Saints lost left tackle Kelvin Banks to a fractured ankle. The Cardinals could also be without starting corner Will Johnson , who could miss the remainder of the season with a neck injury. So with all that in mind, we want to know what you think the Giants’ record will be after these next four games. full_text: Ryan Schernecke | Kutztown Athletic Department Jaxson Dart injury and the sadness surrounding it aside, the business of the NFL continues for the New York Giants. The team continued with that business on Tuesday, bringing a pair of names that should be familiar to the team’s practice squad. Schernecke is a rookie right tackle out of Division II Kutztown University. He was initially signed by the Giants as a priority free agent after the 2026 NFL Draft. He was waived at the end of the preseason and signed to the practice squad. Schernecke was dropped from the practice squad last week to make room for cornerback Jaden Robinson. Ravenell is a 6-foot-5, 300-pound defensive tackle who played in 14 games for the Tennessee Titans last season. Dennard Wilson, now Giants defensive coordinator, was in that role with the Titans in 2025. The Giants initially claimed Ravenell off waivers from the Titans on July 7, then waived him with a non-football injury on July 25. Veteran defensive tackle visits Veteran defensive tackle Dean Lowry, who some thought was going to sign with the team before Week 1, visited with the Giants on Tuesday. Lowry, 32, is a 6-foot-6, 296-pound defensive end who was a fourth-round pick by the Green Bay Packers in 2016. Lowry spent seven years with the Packers, one with the Minnesota Vikings, and the last two with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Lowry has played in 132 regular-season games with 85 starts. Statistically, he has 16.5 career sacks and 271 tackles. Lowry spent last season on injured reserve due to a torn ACL. He was released by the Steelers in the cutdown from 90 to 53 players.
