 1. Buffalo Bills (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Lions 41-31 
 Week 2 ranking: 1 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Josh Allen is going to make defenses pay either way.

 Allen has kept his eyes downfield through two games, averaging a career-best 9.7 yards per attempt on his deepest average depth of target (10.5) since 2018, his rookie season. That has led to three touchdowns on throws of 20-plus air yards. But Allen is just as dangerous when defenses bail out to protect against the deep ball. Of his 92 rushing yards on 20 carries this season, 70 have come on six scramble plays. -- Nick Suss 

 

 
 

 

 2. Seattle Seahawks (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Cardinals 31-7 
 Week 2 ranking: 2 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Drew Lock is one of the NFL's best backup QBs.

 He's not the same player who turned the ball over 25 times in 24 games over his first three seasons in Denver. Or the one who couldn't beat out Geno Smith after a  trade to Seattle in 2022. Lock has gotten plenty of help from receiver  Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Seattle's defense, but he has also played like a starter. Since stepping in  for an injured Sam Darnold one series into the season opener, Lock has completed almost 73% of his passes, with four touchdowns, zero turnovers and only two sacks. His Total QBR of 86.4 ranks fourth. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 3. San Francisco 49ers (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Dolphins 35-13 
 Week 2 ranking: 5 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Brock Purdy looks poised for his best season.

 Purdy has been one of the league's most productive quarterbacks since taking over the starting job in 2022. Now in his fifth season, he's completely comfortable in coach Kyle Shanahan's offense and is coming off his best training camp. That hot start has teammates such as linebacker  Fred Warner openly wondering whether Purdy can compete for league MVP honors. Through two weeks, Purdy is atop the league in QBR (94.9) despite a supporting cast that has already been thinned by injury. If he stays healthy, there's reason to believe Purdy will post his best year yet. -- Nick Wagoner 

 

 
 

 4. Kansas City Chiefs (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Colts 33-30 (OT) 
 Week 2 ranking: 8 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Patrick Mahomes can deal from under center.

 With  the addition of running back Kenneth Walker III , Mahomes has shown that he can be surgical when passing from under center, especially on play-action passes. On under-center plays, Mahomes threw a touchdown against the Colts and has already recorded 107 passing yards. It's one of the biggest changes from last season, when the clear majority of the Chiefs' snaps with Mahomes were in the shotgun -- 80.6% of their formations (excluding quarterback kneel-downs), third most in the league. -- Nate Taylor 

 

 
 

 5. Los Angeles Rams (1-1) 
 Week 2 result:  Beat the Giants 28-6 
 Week 2 ranking: 4 

 One thing we know about the QB1:   Matthew Stafford is still capable of playing at an MVP level.

 Stafford and the Rams' offense struggled in the season opener , but wide receiver Davante Adams said the team's Week 2 offensive performance was closer to what the group expects to look like this season. On Monday night against the Giants, Stafford, the reigning MVP, completed 22 of 31 passes for 327 yards with four touchdown passes and an interception. He had that success without wide receiver Puka Nacua , who is dealing with soreness in his groin .  -- Sarah Barshop 

 

 
 

 6. Philadelphia Eagles (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Titans 24-20 
 Week 2 ranking: 6 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Jalen Hurts is carrying this team.

 The thought heading into the season was Hurts and the passing offense would need time to acclimate to coordinator Sean Mannion's system , meaning the Eagles would have to rely on their defense and ground game early. The defense did not dominate as expected  against Washington and Tennessee, while the running game has been spotty behind an offensive line still trying to find its footing. Meanwhile, Hurts led the team to a Week 1 win with three touchdowns and another victory Sunday via a go-ahead touchdown drive in the closing seconds. He is tied for second in touchdown passes (five) and ahead of schedule in this new scheme. -- Tim McManus 

 

 
 

 7. Baltimore Ravens (1-1) 
 Week 2 result: Lost to the Saints 24-17 
 Week 2 ranking: 3 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Lamar Jackson is facing a lot of pressure.

 Baltimore's revamped offensive line has struggled in protection. The Ravens' two lowest pass block win rates with Jackson as the starting QB have come in the first two weeks this season. Baltimore had a 38% pass block win rate at the Colts in Week 1 and a 33% win rate in Week 2. Jackson and the Ravens should have a more favorable matchup this week against the Cowboys, who have two sacks this season. -- Jamison Hensley

 One thing we know about the QB1: Bo Nix might not be all that fond of September.

 Whether it's an issue with his mechanics or rushing into plays, Nix is caught up in the Broncos' propensity for slow starts under coach Sean Payton. In his first two seasons, Nix has thrown eight of his 23 interceptions in September -- including three games with at least two picks. And in the season-opening loss to the Chiefs, Nix had his first career three-fumble game and was sacked four times, tying a career high. The Broncos escaped with a win in Week 2 after Nix and the offense got things cranked up in the second half. But he did throw his second interception of the season. -- Jeff Legwold

title: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 3
summary: Can Baker Mayfield rebound? Are the Chargers doomed? Is the Eagles' new offense actually encouraging for Jalen Hurts? Get ready for Week 3 with seven takes.
full_text:
Week 2 is in the books! It came with big upsets ( Raiders over Chargers ! Browns over Bucs !) and devastating injuries (such as Commanders QB Jayden Daniels and Giants QB Jaxson Dart ). Week 3 feels like as murky a future week as ever.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions; those come later. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 This week, I'm starting with my concern for a big-ticket quarterback contract signed not even a month ago, my concern for one key AFC contender and my lack of concern for two others. Here are seven things I think ahead of Week 3.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Bucs regret the Mayfield deal 
 Chargers to pick top-10 in 2027 
 Patriots offense is fine, everyone 
 Hurts is settling into Eagles' offense 
 Jaguars trenches will be postseason downfall 
 Henry won't solve Ravens' late-game issues 
 Donald's workout regimen paid off 
 Five extra inklings 

 

 
 

 I think ... the Buccaneers are already regretting that Baker Mayfield deal 
 Mayfield has not played well through the first two games of the season.

 This does not mean he is a bad quarterback who is undeserving of a nice contract. Two game samples are, in a vacuum, barely above meaningless. (They're just meaningful enough that you should keep reading this column.) But it would have been nice to see how this season played out, to see if this two-game trend continued, before signing an extension.

 Mayfield and the Buccaneers looked destined for a prove-it season before the Buccaneers "surprised" Mayfield with an eleventh-hour offer that clearly met his expectations. It is a three-year deal , as Mayfield wanted, though it's really a two-year deal with a $55 million team option in 2029. Still, at $55 million per year, Mayfield is making Matthew Stafford and Trevor Lawrence sort of money ... Joe Burrow and Josh Allen sort of money.

 Mayfield's play has been decidedly below that level to start the season. Through two weeks, Mayfield is 29th among 32 quarterbacks in EPA per dropback and 27th in success rate. Of course, two-game samples are useless, so let's add last season. Since the start of 2025, Mayfield is 24th among 32 quarterbacks in EPA per dropback and 25th in success rate.

 

 But last season was a down year. Mayfield played through a strained knee that he suffered in Week 2 and endured shoulder pain (non-throwing side) after a big hit in Week 12. His 2025 offensive coordinator, Josh Grizzard, was fired at the end of the season. So, let's throw in 2024 as well. Since the start of that season, Mayfield's career year with offensive coordinator Liam Coen, Mayfield is 13th in EPA per dropback and 13th in success rate. There he is,  the guy the Bucs paid. We just had to go back a couple of seasons to find him.

 But even including the 2024 season, we find some problems. A big part of Mayfield's success in that season, and in the seasons to follow, is how well he played when pressured. His dropback success rate (34.9%) is eighth; his first-down/touchdown rate (29.7%) is third behind Burrow and Brock Purdy .

 But play under pressure tends not to be sticky. Pressured plays are either big wins (the passer beats the blitz with a deep throw) or disasters (the passer gets sacked), and that creates large swings in the outcome. Good play against pressure also relies heavily on athleticism. Mayfield has scrambled on 17.9% of his pressured dropbacks since the start of the 2024 season, second to Jayden Daniels . Mayfield's numerous 2025 injuries reflect his toughness, but they also reflect his playstyle. He gets sacked a lot (22.8% pressure to sack ratio, eighth highest) and takes more hits on scrambles down the field. It is reasonable to expect Mayfield's effectiveness against pressure to decline with age and accumulated hits; he's 31 years old! I'd argue it already has.

 This season, Mayfield's scramble rate has almost halved (9.2%) as the Buccaneers have prioritized throws behind the line of scrimmage, but his ability to escape is also underwhelming, leading to a 9.2% sack rate.

 Here's one of three sacks he took against the Browns. Cool concept here on third-and-7 from new offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, who motions receiver Emeka Egbuka into the bunch to create a natural pick for Chris Godwin Jr . to get into the slant. The Buccaneers get the hoped-for man coverage. This ball should be out to Godwin immediately.

 

 Mayfield is aggressively climbing the pocket despite the fact that there's plenty of room to stand and throw, and accordingly, he's too late to get the ball to Godwin by the time he reaches a throwing platform. Watch safety Ronnie Hickman , meant to rob the middle of the field, burn right by Godwin and give Mayfield hot pursuit; Hickman knows the scouting report on the quarterback. As Mayfield tries to escape, Hickman hawks him down.

 Here's another simple one from Week 1 against the Bengals. Rookie wideout  Ted Hurst III has a vertical route to the bottom of the screen, and the single-high safety is on the opposite hash when Mayfield drops back. A veteran quarterback needs to land on his back foot and send this throw, beating the deep safety to the spot by pulling that vertical route outside the numbers. Not an easy throw, but one a $55 million quarterback should be expected to attempt. Instead, he hitches, double-clutches and gets sacked.

 

 Mayfield's attempts breakdown has become worryingly polarized through two games of the Robinson offense. A harrowing 37.1% of Mayfield's pass attempts are behind the line of scrimmage, more than all quarterbacks save for Aaron Rodgers and Patrick Mahomes . But 16.1% of his throws go more than 20 yards downfield, as well; that's fifth-highest in the league. Such a spray chart is unhealthy. It indicates a quarterback is uncomfortable testing coverage and either checks it down in front of all defenders or sails it deep beyond all defenders.

 Again, this is a small sample. Seven of these eight deep throws came in Week 2 against the Browns, and the lack of success had more to do with miscommunications than anything else. If you're looking for a sunny side in the Buccaneers' offense through two games it's that clearing up those little mistakes should lead to big downfield connections.

 This is why the Buccaneers might regret that Mayfield deal. Not because his bad play through two games is written in stone, but because they could have collected a season's worth of additional data to inform their contract decision, and at little cost. What was Mayfield going to demand if he had a good year? Maybe $60 million instead of $55 million? Actual guarantees in 2029?

 

 These are peanut problems compared with the larger issue: Mayfield is a late-career breakout who relies heavily on his athleticism and accordingly is on a shorter time horizon than most quarterbacks over 30. He also plays an inherently erratic style, and Robinson has had little success tamping that down through two weeks. I enjoy when Mayfield is at his best and look forward to seeing it again, but paying for peaks makes the valleys difficult to endure. The Buccaneers likely never had a better alternative than paying Mayfield a sizable veteran contract, but I sure would have liked to turn every stone before I consigned myself to that path.

 

 

 I think ... the Chargers will pick in the top 10 of next year's draft 
 I can't name 10 teams worse than the Chargers (0-2) through two weeks. I'm not even sure if I can name five.

 There is nothing about the Chargers that works right now. They remind me of the Nathaniel Hackett-led Broncos in…

title: Cowboys' CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens playing with 'no egos'
summary: Lamb and Pickens believe their off-field connection is helping their on-field production.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- One day recently, CeeDee Lamb walked out of the locker room and into the Dallas Cowboys ' weight room with George Pickens a stride behind as they laughed about something.

 During training camp, most days the Cowboys' star receivers walked onto the field in Oxnard, California, together. On off days, they were often together.

 About the only time, it seems, they are apart is when one lines up to Dak Prescott 's right and the other is to the quarterback's left.

 "I don't think you can get any much closer than we've been," Lamb said. "I feel like at the end of the day, we want what's best for each other and that's to be with one another and to grind.

 "I feel like we both have that alpha mentality, that alpha dog component to us so just rubbing off on one another and just keeping this thing going. We gotta keep being who we are and at the end of the day prove it to each other every day."

 

 Lamb and Pickens believe their off-field connection helps their on-field production. Last year, they both had more than 1,000 yards receiving, even with Lamb missing three full games and three quarters of a fourth because of injury.

 Pickens set career highs in catches (93), yards (1,429) and touchdowns (nine) while Lamb joined Michael Irvin as the only receivers in Cowboys' history to post five straight 1,000-yard seasons.

 The start to 2026 has been different, however, as the Cowboys (1-1) head toward Sunday's game against the Baltimore Ravens  (1-1) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 Lamb has caught 13 passes for 197 yards and three touchdowns. With 153 yards and two touchdowns last week against the Washington Commanders , Lamb has six career games with at least 100 yards and multiple scores, tying him with Tony Hill and Irvin for the second most in team history (Bob Hayes, 13).

 Pickens has nine catches for 68 yards. He had two drops in Week 1 against the Giants, including one that could have been a 76-yard touchdown.

 "I, of course, want to get him and CeeDee the ball," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I think CeeDee's playing great. I think George is playing really well. I mean, some of the catches he made [against Washington] were really big-time plays in big-time situations for us. ... He just didn't have the highlight-type catches and the explosive catches and things like that. But he draws a lot of attention out there.

 "Believe me, we're looking for ways to continue to get those guys the ball. And if you look at George last year, he didn't really take off until a couple games in, and the rest is history."

 

 Wide receiver is a position in the NFL known for its individuality. Some have had their own touchdown celebrations, such as  Dez Bryant throwing up the X or Terrell Owens  extending his arms for a "TO."

 They can be moody, especially if they don't get the ball enough. Every move can be -- and has been -- scrutinized by camera angles catching poor body language, a comment or a shake of the head.

 

 "We go through the same stuff just being at the same position," Pickens said. "So I feel like that makes us super close."

 Schottenheimer has said numerous times he wants to "build the best culture in professional sports." He said he has been around teams where the jealousy among receivers was a detriment.

 "I think it can affect a game. I mean, it can affect a playcaller. It can affect the quarterback, but there's not really a great way to handle it," Schottenheimer said. "And so that's why we're so fortunate, because our guys, they both want the ball. They both want to score touchdowns. They both want to celebrate, but I love how excited they get when the other guy gets it -- or even Ryan Flournoy , [ Jake Ferguson ] -- their excitement because they love playing the game, and they love this locker room that we've built."

 

 Quarterbacks can get caught in the middle of wide receivers' desires to be the top option. Prescott said he doesn't care about that. He throws it to whoever is open based on his read of the playcalls.

 "They can get mad," Prescott said. "Only one of them can get the ball at one time, so they'll probably be getting it the next play. So don't get mad and miss your opportunity."

 With Lamb and Pickens -- or Pickens and Lamb, if you prefer -- Prescott said "there's no egos."

 "Both of those guys are selfless," he added. "They want to see each other succeed. They're probably each other's biggest cheerleaders to that extent."

 When Pickens came to the Cowboys last year in a trade from the Pittsburgh Steelers it was with a narrative that painted him as tempestuous and broody, but he was immediately accepted by the entire organization, starting mostly with Lamb.

 "I feel like for him, he wanted to do it for [himself] personally just [welcoming] a new guy in," Pickens said. "That's why I was saying last year, the guys on the team were more welcoming than I've ever experienced from any other team. When I came here, they were all open arms, trying to get me hooked up on the playbook fast. But definitely CeeDee, especially, I feel like he took pride in that."

 Said Lamb, "That's my boy. I don't think he questions anything about where my loyalty stands with him and vice versa."

 

 There might be an expiration date on the duo's time together with Pickens playing on the $27.3 million franchise tag. It will be difficult for the Cowboys to pay two top-of-the-market receivers, though not impossible, and there is always the chance the Cowboys could use the franchise tag again on Pickens in 2027.

 Lamb and Pickens are not letting contractual futures impact what they want to accomplish.

 Offensive coordinator Klayton Adams said Lamb and Pickens are "total opposites." Certainly in fashion with Lamb being more stylistically inclined than Pickens. Lamb wears diamonds and flashy bracelets, even on the field. Pickens is just as happy in a T-shirt and pair of shorts.

 "I think CeeDee, probably personality wise, is I guess a little bit more like what I would expect a receiver just in terms of the way that he operates day to day," Adams said. "George, you just don't always know exactly what you're going to get. A little bit more unpredictable, but both are awesome in their own ways."

 And together, they are one of the best receiver duos in the league. Well, maybe not just one of the best.

 "Yeah, we definitely think we're the best," Pickens said. "Now for everybody else's brains and mindsets, I don't know what they're going to say. But for us, yeah, we're the best."

title: Tyler Shough's late-game heroics have Saints' confidence soaring
summary: The second-year quarterback has been at his best this season when the game is on the line. Can he keep that up?
full_text:
BALTIMORE -- New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough wouldn't quit.

 Shough and the Saints lined up for a potentially game-sealing touchdown against the Ravens (1-1) on fourth-and-goal in Baltimore. As Shough dove for the plane of the goal line, a defensive player swiped at his face mask and yanked his head back.

 Shough gripped the football hard as he was swallowed up in a mass of bodies, but he didn't let go.

 The officials signaled touchdown, giving the Saints (1-1) the go-ahead score and eventually a 24-17 win , their first of the season.

 "Yeah, that one hurt a little bit," Shough said later with a smile. "Yeah, I got kind of folded a couple times, but I was able to get in there. So we'd like to not make it as close. ... I was going to reach for it, but getting your head pulled off, it's tough."

 

 For Saints coach Kellen Moore, it was a moment that showed Shough is "as tough as they come."

 "He's a really special player, but his willingness to hang in there and play the really hard downs, I think the rest of the team sees that, recognizes that. There's a lot of respect for what he's doing right now," Moore said.

 It took the Saints five tries to get into the end zone after backing up from the Baltimore 2-yard line due to a penalty. But pushing through and getting the job done was a reversal of last week.

 In Week 1, the Saints came up just short of beating the Detroit Lions in overtime, losing 31-30. That result might have been acceptable for last season's Saints, who were already in a 1-7 hole by the time Shough made his first start in Week 9. Getting any momentum from their rookie second-round pick felt like a win.

 But the Saints knew they had something special in Shough going into this season, and edge rusher Chase Young said the time for accepting moral victories was over.

 But after Sunday's win, the Saints blasted music in the locker room so loudly it could be heard in the adjoining conference room. Going toe-to-toe with the Ravens proved the Saints' confidence in Shough was deserved. So now New Orleans will aim to build on that momentum heading into its first home game of the season against the  Las Vegas Raiders  on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "We can hang with anybody. Sometimes you have to learn how to win, learn how to finish. And I think we right on time," Young said. "... No more moral victories, man. We want W's, and if it come down to the wire, then we just got to tough it out. We want to win."

 It was the Saints' biggest win since Shough was named the starter. He won five games leading the team in 2025, all against teams that finished the season with a losing record.

 Since 2022, the Saints have beaten only four teams that finished the season with a winning record (the 2022 Seattle Seahawks and Philadelphia Eagles and the 2023 Indianapolis Colts and Tampa Bay Buccaneers ).

 

 Beating a Ravens team that had just put up 41 points in Week 1 seemed different, even to veterans such as wide receiver Chris Olave , who is now in his fifth season.

 "I feel like since I've been here, we haven't really beat a good team. I feel like it's been tough for us to be able to battle against good teams or great teams that make the playoffs every year," Olave said. "Baltimore ... is a contender in the AFC. So just to be able to battle, be able to show our resilience, be able to come in here and get a W was huge for us, and we got to carry it over to next week."

 The Saints have found a quarterback who not only can close out games but appears to play his best in the fourth quarter and big moments. Shough's play hasn't been without flaws, and at times it has been perplexing.

 During the early and middle parts of the two games, he has played some of his worst football, only to turn up the dial when it counted the most. According to ESPN Research, Shough's Total QBR has been a dismal 14.3 rating through three quarters of the two games (ranked 29th of 30 qualified passers), but in the fourth quarter and overtime, his 97.7 rating is second in the league.

 

 He has only 56 passing yards in the first quarter compared with 350 and three touchdowns in fourth quarters and overtime.

 But when it has counted, Shough has stepped up.

 On key third downs, he has made big plays, such as a pass to Juwan Johnson on third-and-8 that gained 24 yards. With backup tackle Asim Richards handling two blockers on his left and rookie running back CJ Donaldson picking up a rusher on his right, Shough took a hit while getting the ball to Johnson, who ran to the Baltimore 2-yard line.

 "It was a special play. Got a lot of juice and energy," Moore said, "Obviously it very much changed the entire game management moving forward after that. ... That was a huge play. Just great effort by Juwan. Give us a chance to hopefully get that touchdown."

 Shough also has converted all four fourth-down attempts this season, via two runs and two passes.

 "I love those moments just because in my head it's just another down, it's just another play." Shough said. "We've prepared for a lot of those moments. So on the outside it feels like, man, this may be the game, but it generally feels like let's just go play."

 Now, with the Raiders up next, the Saints hope Shough and the team can keep that play going through all four quarters instead of just the final frame.

 "He's just going to keep going for it. And I think that's just the way he plays," Moore said. "There's highs and lows in games. There's things that go our way, the things that don't go our way. And he just keeps going. ... I was proud of him."

title: Why Aaron Glenn is encouraged by the Jets' progress
summary: New York is an overtime loss away from being undefeated after allowing the fewest yards through two weeks.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Perhaps the strongest endorsement for New York Jets coach Aaron Glenn came more than a year ago, delivered by his previous boss.

 "If he can't [turn them around]," Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said at the 2025 NFL spring meetings in Orlando, Florida, "nobody can."

 Despite a firestorm of criticism in the aftermath of their 20-17 overtime loss to the Green Bay Packers , Glenn has the Jets looking like a competitive team so far in his second season. It's overshadowed by a handful of questionable coaching decisions from the fourth-quarter collapse Sunday, but he is encouraged by the progress and insisted they won't allow the crushing loss to define their season.

 Glenn can prevent that from happening by beating the next opponent, which happens to be -- drum roll, please -- Campbell and the Lions. It's a delicious storyline, but Glenn, who served as Campbell's defensive coordinator from 2021 to 2024, can't let that distract him. His primary job is to refocus his team after blowing a 10-point lead.

 

 "It's my responsibility to get our guys to be able to close the door," Glenn said. "I take that, and it's something I will never run from."

 There are some positives to build on, which should make it easier to move past the Green Bay debacle. In two games, the Jets already have run more plays with a lead (68) than they did the entire 2025 season (66). They dominated the Tennessee Titans in the opener, never trailing, and they were only one timely play away from burying the Packers.

 The Jets have their best total yardage margin (plus-258) through two games since 1982, currently the third-best margin in the NFL. The defense, with Glenn calling the plays, is ranked No. 1 in yards allowed (197 per game). They have surrendered only 30 points, including 20 in the fourth quarter and overtime -- perhaps a troubling trend.

 Defensive tackle Harrison Phillips said they will make "a conscious effort this week to step up the intensity" in the latter portion of practice, hoping there's a carryover to the game.

 The Jets allowed the Packers to score on three of their last four possessions. Before that, they held Green Bay's vertical passing attack in check, though some of that could be attributed to  Jordan Love 's reliance on short passing because of a spate of offensive line injuries.

 The takeaway-starved defense, which has gone a record 19 consecutive games without an interception, recorded its first takeaway of the season -- a fumble recovery. There could've been more, but they recovered only one of five fumbles by the Packers.

 Glenn took that as a positive, saying, "We're attacking the football. We're punching the football out, and I do know this: Those things are going to come around for us."

 

 Offensively, the Jets haven't put up big numbers (40 points), but they're getting consistent quarterback play -- something that didn't happen last season. Geno Smith , who threw an NFL-high 17 interceptions last season for the Las Vegas Raiders , has yet to commit a turnover. Ditto, the entire offense -- the first time since 1971 they've had no giveaways through the first two games.

 "I still think we have a really good team, a team of high potential and we just went into a shootout with a [2025] playoff team," running back Breece Hall said after Sunday's game. "So I think we have everything we need."

 It wasn't exactly a shootout, but there's no doubt the Jets have been better than last season on offense. Smith already has more passing yards in his first two starts (462) than Justin Fields recorded in his last four (460) from last season. They're still lacking explosive plays, so it might behoove offensive coordinator Frank Reich to get wide receiver Garrett Wilson more involved. Wilson was targeted only seven times Sunday, just twice after his third-quarter touchdown.

 "Absolutely, that's a point of emphasis every time we go out: try to make sure we get him the ball, and we have to continue to do that," Glenn said. "There are guys on this team -- Breece, [ Mason Taylor ], [ Kenyon Sadiq ], especially Garrett -- that we have to make sure that we get those guys involved."

title: Why there's hope Pittsburgh Steelers' O-line can improve
summary: Pittsburgh's young group has struggled to find consistency, but with adjustments, there's still time to improve.
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- Moments before calling for the snap at Gillette Stadium on Sunday, Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers surveyed the defense, paused and walked a couple of yards toward his line, quickly adjusting his protections as the play clock wound down.

 Left guard Mason McCormick craned his neck back to Rodgers, engaging with the quarterback before gesturing at center Zach Frazier . McCormick then pointed to running back Rico Dowdle , directing his attention to inside linebacker Robert Spillane on the other side of the line. As he walked back to the shotgun, Rodgers crossed his arms and made a shivering motion, one of his many cues to adjust the play.

 Then, confusion led to a collision.

 Dowdle ran to his right, preparing to throw a block in the gap between right guard Spencer Anderson and right tackle Dylan Cook .

 But the pressure was coming from Rodgers' left. Completely unblocked, linebacker Christian Elliss came off the edge and smoked Rodgers, sandwiching him in the backfield with Spillane. The pair knocked the ball loose, and it bounced backward for 36 yards as both teams struggled to secure it. Finally, left tackle Troy Fautanu jumped on the ball at the Steelers' 42-yard line to bring up fourth-and-43.

 

 That was a microcosm of the Steelers' 20-3 loss to the New England Patriots .

 "It's frustrating, just all around as an offense," Fautanu said after the game. "We couldn't really get anything going, and when we did, we just couldn't convert, we just couldn't score."

 Rodgers, who took a total of four sacks Sunday, was also strip-sacked one more time in the loss. That time, defensive tackle Christian Barmore muscled through Anderson to knock the ball loose, and Elijah Ponder scooped it up for the defensive touchdown.

 "They were giving us different looks, different pressures, different stunts," Fautanu said. "Obviously, the coaches go over it during the week. We've got to be able to go out there and execute and block our men regardless of if we're one-on-one. We've just got to do a better job."

 Things won't get any easier on Sunday, when the team hosts the Cincinnati Bengals ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ), who are tied atop the league's leaderboard with eight sacks through two weeks.

 Steelers coach Mike McCarthy on Sunday shouldered the blame, pointing to a need to refine details, improve communication and reduce volume in the game plan until his young team can get the basics down.

 "Our protections weren't clean," McCarthy said. "We had opportunities, whether it was communication and breakdowns, clearly in the first half that took away some opportunities for big plays. ... The consistency of winning in the trenches, we need to be better there. But the reality of it is the detail is not there, and that's on coaching. It starts with me."

 Though every part of the offense has been flawed through two weeks of the McCarthy era, the problems on the offensive line run deeper than fine-tuning the little things. And with a 42-year-old quarterback, establishing a strong offensive line is the foundation for a successful offense. The unit is still salvageable, but McCarthy's preseason priority of creating an interchangeable line has created significant regular-season growing pains.

 

 "In hindsight you go back and you look how many days did we line up with the same offensive line? We worked a lot of different combinations," McCarthy said Monday. "No excuses, but they need continuity. They need reps, they need consistency. So the consistency will come through the common concepts. ... Our consistency starting up front, we need to give our guys more laps, more time on task and make sure we're asking them to do things that they got plenty of reps in."

 Through two weeks, the Steelers' offensive line has a pass block win rate of 52.5%, ranked 13th in the NFL, according to ESPN Analytics and NFL Next Gen Stats. Its run block win rate, however, is just 68.4%, the second lowest in the league. The Steelers are averaging 74.5 rushing yards per game (29th) and are averaging just 0.89 rushing yards before first contact (31st).

 "Something's got to change," Fautanu said. "I don't know if it's that we're not working hard enough as an offense or we're not working hard enough as an O-line. Just not connecting well with each other."

 Though McCarthy didn't overhaul the offensive line's personnel, he did significantly rearrange the group.

 During organized team activities, the Steelers coach elected to move Fautanu and McCormick from the right side of the line to the left. The pair already had chemistry from working together throughout the 2025 season, and the move solidified the left side of the line as 2023 first-round pick Broderick Jones worked back from injury.

 

 Anderson, the team's top in-house replacement option for Isaac Seumalo , moved to right guard, while Cook, who finished the 2025 season at left tackle after Jones' injury, moved to right tackle.

 Rather than emphasizing cohesion among the presumed starting five offensive linemen -- none of whom have more than four years of NFL experience -- McCarthy played a number of line combinations this preseason.

 Prior to being traded, Jones got reps at right and left tackle. Rookie first-round pick Max Iheanachor , who missed a chunk of the preseason with an injury, rotated in at right tackle when healthy. Veteran interior offensive linemen Brock Hoffman and Ryan McCollum also got a lot of reps at a number of positions throughout training camp.

 The starting O-line played 19 snaps together in each of the first two preseason games, and none of them were with the entire starting offense, as Rodgers didn't play in the preseason. Cook was the only starter to play in the third game, and even then, he started out of position at left tackle.

 Through two weeks of the regular season, Anderson and McCormick have each allowed nine pressures, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, tied for 20th most in the NFL. Fautanu has allowed eight pressures, while Dylan Cook five and center Zach Frazier four.

 Cook has also allowed two sacks, tied for third most in the NFL through two weeks, and Anderson and Fautanu have allowed one apiece.

 "We need more consistency," Steelers offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio said Monday. "I don't know if there's one particular thing to point to, just seems like it moved around a little bit, but I think communication's got to be better and just consistency of what we're trying to get done."

 

 There are, however, a couple of things that could improve the unit. Not only will more time together help the group work through some of the communication kinks, but intentionally changing how they practice -- with more reps together and a lower volume of plays -- should also help.

 "Certainly the reps, the looks, the guys starting to settle in," Angelichio said. "As we go into the third week of the season, I think that stuff should start to play itself out certainly in the next couple of weeks, and that's what we're hoping for."

 McCarthy could also opt to replace Cook with Iheanachor. The first-round pick missed two preseason games, but he showed promise once he returned and made his debut in the third game. And when Fautanu missed one snap with an ankle injury against the Atlanta Falcons , the Steelers slid Cook to left tackle, and Iheanachor made a brief appearance at right tackle.

 "Max has taken a step each and every week," McCarthy said. "I thought he had a really good day Thursday in the padded work, the individual work. He's definitely making big steps. So it's getting better."

 Though he's a more raw prospect with just five years of organized football under his belt, Iheanachor earned rave reviews from coaches and teammates throughout the preseason. McCarthy could also consider replacing Anderson with Hoffman. The Steelers drafted guard Gennings Dunker in the third round earlier this year, but he has been inactive each of the first two weeks.

title: Why 49ers' Brock Purdy looks poised for his best season yet
summary: Purdy is dominating through two weeks of the 2026 season despite many injuries at wide receiver. And it all started in training camp.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Sitting comfortably on a couch in the bowels of Levi's Stadium, a question after a late August practice leaves San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy carefully considering the lessons he has learned over the past four seasons and where it might take him in 2026.

 The query is simple: "Is this the best training camp you've ever had?" The response, much like his job, is more nuanced. Purdy takes a moment to ponder the offseason film sessions with quarterbacks coach Mick Lombardi and then compares where he is now to some of the highest points of his career, including the team's run to Super Bowl LVIII .

 Finally, Purdy concludes that yes, he is putting the finishing touches on his best training camp. But even more than that, he knows what it could mean for the 2026 season.

 "It's my fifth year and I feel confident with the plays and everything," Purdy told ESPN. "I go back and watch that Super Bowl year and it's like, 'Dude, honestly, I could have been better.' I made plays. But fundamentally as a quarterback and being consistent with my footwork, with my eyes, with throwing the ball aggressively, those were areas that I could have been better. I've honed into that."

 Two weeks into the season, Purdy's words seem prescient. He has been almost perfect in blowout wins over the Los Angeles Rams and the rebuilding  Miami Dolphins .

 

 Purdy leads the NFL in Total QBR (95.0), completion rate (80.4%) and completion percentage over expectation (11.1%). He has yet to throw a ball off-target or taken any sacks. And along the way, he has posted his 13th career game with a 130-plus passer rating and eighth contest with a 140-plus passer rating -- the most such games by a player in his first five seasons.

 Some of those stats are a bit deep in the weeds, but here's one that's not: Once Purdy hits 1,500 career regular-season pass attempts -- he's at 1,409 -- he will almost certainly hold the career mark for the highest passer rating by a qualified quarterback.

 "He's special," said running back Christian McCaffrey  on Sunday. "I think that'd be the word I'd use for it. ... I don't know what the stats are, but it's unbelievable to watch that. How decisive he is, how good he is at throwing on time and then also creating when he has to. When he's at the helm, we feel good."

 Despite that year-over-year consistency, the Niners believe there's still another level Purdy can reach this season. Linebacker  Fred Warner was already touting him as an MVP candidate after his Week 2 outing (DraftKings currently gives him the third-best odds at +800). And even with an already lengthy list of injuries at receiver ( Ricky Pearsall ,  De'Zhaun Stribling , Christian Kirk and Demarcus Robinson will miss all or parts of the season), Purdy proved in 2025 that he can elevate a deficient supporting cast with his own improvement.

 Purdy's pursuit of his best season began soon after the last campaign ended, when Shanahan and his staff gave their annual "get better" tape for each player to study over the offseason. Purdy's tape focused on a few foundational principles: not hanging on to big-play reads for too long so the ball can come out quicker and the offense can stay ahead of the chains; understanding when to better use his legs; and knowing when to take shots down the field without being reckless.

 All of those things showed up during training camp, whether it was on days when he consistently took checkdowns for easy completions or other days when he pushed the ball downfield for big plays.

 Warner, who had some serious battles against Purdy and the top offense in camp, said the game now seems to move slowly for Purdy. Warner noted Purdy has evolved in the ways he manipulates defenses with cadence and motion, knows every coverage defenses can throw at him and then has the athletic ability and creativity to make a play when things break down.

 "All those little things that kind of make a great quarterback in this league, he does all those things at a high level," Warner said.

 

 And while Purdy didn't mind the occasional training camp interception, so long as it came because of trying something new, even those were few and far between.

 "I thought he had his best training camp, just in terms of being aggressive with things, but not stupid," Shanahan said. "I think the more he plays, just with experience, the easier [it becomes to recognize defenses] and things like that. But he played so good right away that it's not like, 'Oh, he's so much better in this area.' I just think you gradually become a vet and get used to everything that you've seen."

 Indeed, if experience is part of the reason Purdy looks poised for his best season, the other half of the equation comes from time on task with Shanahan. Purdy is five starts away from passing Jimmy Garoppolo for the most starts by a QB under Shanahan (63), meaning he's already eclipsed signal-callers such as Matt Ryan, Robert Griffin III and Matt Schaub. Ryan's 2016 MVP season provides the benchmark for all Shanahan quarterbacks, as he posted a league-leading 79.6 QBR and finished second in passing yards (4,944) and touchdowns (38).

 The close relationship with Shanahan has allowed Purdy to see the game how his coach does, understand why Shanahan calls certain plays at certain times and learn how to adjust if the defense throws a curveball.

 Out of Purdy's 59 starts with Shanahan, that relationship was possibly never more evident than his 58th two weeks ago. As the Rams stayed in sub-packages with the idea of taking away the deep ball, Purdy complied for much of the game.

 One of the only times they deviated from that approach wasn't even supposed to happen. With second-and-6 at the Rams' 39-yard line late in the second quarter, Purdy stepped to the line of scrimmage with a playcall that had his progression focused to the left of the formation, where wide receiver  Mike Evans , tight end  Luke Farrell and running back  Kaelon Black were the primary options.

 Robinson ran a deep route from the right side of the formation, making him the sole option if the Rams provided a certain look. When Purdy dropped back, he saw the Rams defensive backs stick to their zone matching rules as safety Kamren Kinchens took a couple of steps toward the line of scrimmage.

 Purdy quickly worked off Evans, Farrell and Black before firing deep for Robinson. It worked, and the touchdown throw gave the Niners a lead they would not relinquish.

 "For Brock to be tapped into that and the 2% chance that actually is going to open up, and he has the confidence to step into it and rip it, I love to see him just continue to get more and more confident," fullback Kyle Juszczyk said.

 

 It was one of only six throws Purdy even attempted traveling 10-plus air yards in Melbourne, but he followed that by going 10-of-10 on such passes against Miami for 211 yards and a touchdown. And on Sunday, Purdy continued to use his legs -- another improvement mentioned on his "get better tape" -- with a rushing touchdown and 30 rushing yards. He became the first player in league history to complete at least 90% of his passes while throwing for 285-plus yards with two touchdowns and a rushing score in a single game.

 The disparity between the two games speaks not only to the level of the defense on the other side, but also to how Purdy is making the correct decisions over and over based on what defenses present him.

 Whether Purdy can continue his early-season trajectory will depend on plenty of factors outside of his control. The 49ers are slated to face the top-tier defenses of  Denver  and  Seattle  in Weeks 4 and 5, respectively. The Seahawks, in particular, should provide the stiffest test after they limited the Niners to nine points and 204.5 yards per game in the teams' final two meetings of last season.
